keyConcept: For equal-substance mixing, the equilibrium temperature is the mass-weighted average of the initial temperatures; the common specific heat cancels.
commonMistake: Including the specific heat among the relevant quantities, forgetting that it cancels when both masses are the same liquid.

optionExplanations.0: The specific heat appears on both sides of the energy balance and cancels, so T_eq does not depend on it.
optionExplanations.2: T_eq equals the plain average of the initial temperatures only in the special case m_A = m_B.
optionExplanations.4: The masses act as weights in the average, so they influence T_eq whenever they differ.

formulaNotes: m_A c (T_A - T_eq) = m_B c (T_eq - T_B) => T_eq = (m_A T_A + m_B T_B)/(m_A + m_B).

shortExplanation: Joule heating gives E = I^2 * R * t, so R = E/(I^2 t) = 20 J / (1 A^2 * 10 s) = 2 ohm.
solutionSteps: Known values: I = 1 A, t = 10 s, dissipated energy E = 20 J.
Dissipated energy in a resistor: E = P*t = I^2 * R * t.
Solve for R: R = E/(I^2 * t).
Check units: J/(A^2 * s) = W*s/(A^2 * s) = W/A^2 = ohm.
keyConcept: Joule's law: dissipated energy E = I^2 R t.
commonMistake: Dividing energy by time only (getting power, 2 W) and then misreading it as 20 or 0.2 ohm through a power-of-ten slip.

optionExplanations.1: 200 ohm multiplies instead of divides by the 10 s interval.
optionExplanations.3: 0.2 ohm results from dividing 2 by 10 a second time, applying the time twice.
optionExplanations.4: 20 ohm comes from equating R with the energy value 20 J without dividing by the time.

shortExplanation: For an ideal fluid in steady flow the volumetric flow rate S*v is conserved, so halving the cross-section doubles the speed.
solutionSteps: Continuity equation for an incompressible fluid in steady flow: S1*v1 = S2*v2.
The narrow section has S2 = S/2.
The flow rate itself stays constant along the duct; only the speed changes.
Hence the speed doubles in the narrow part.
keyConcept: Continuity equation: the product cross-section * speed is constant along a duct for an incompressible fluid.
commonMistake: Thinking the flow rate changes at the constriction; it is precisely the conserved quantity, and it is the speed that adjusts.

optionExplanations.1: The flow rate cannot change in stationary flow, otherwise fluid would accumulate somewhere in the duct.
optionExplanations.2: Same reasoning: the flow rate is constant, not doubled; it is the velocity that doubles.
optionExplanations.3: Halving the speed would violate conservation of the flow rate: with half the area the fluid must move faster, not slower.

shortExplanation: Uniform circular motion means the particle travels along a circle with constant angular velocity, which is equivalent to a constant magnitude of the tangential velocity.
solutionSteps: 'Circular' fixes the trajectory: an arc of a circumference.
'Uniform' fixes the rate: the angular velocity is constant in time.
Since v = omega * r with r fixed, constant angular velocity is equivalent to constant speed along the circle.
The velocity vector changes direction (there is a centripetal acceleration), but its magnitude does not.
Therefore the correct definition is: motion on a circumference with constant angular velocity and constant magnitude of the tangential velocity.
keyConcept: In uniform circular motion omega is constant and the speed v = omega*r is constant; only the direction of the velocity changes.
commonMistake: Saying the tangential velocity vector is constant: its magnitude is constant, but its direction rotates continuously.

optionExplanations.2: An increasing angular velocity contradicts constant speed, since v = omega*r would grow with omega.
optionExplanations.3: Constant nonzero angular acceleration describes uniformly accelerated circular motion, where the speed changes with time.
optionExplanations.4: A constant tangential velocity vector would mean straight-line motion; on a circle the direction changes at every instant, and uniform motion has zero angular acceleration.

formulaNotes: v = omega * r; in uniform circular motion omega = constant, angular acceleration = 0, centripetal acceleration = v^2/r.

shortExplanation: Frequency counts cycles per unit time, so its SI unit is the inverse second: 1 Hz = 1 s^-1.
solutionSteps: Frequency f = number of cycles / time, so its dimension is 1/time.
In SI units this gives 1 Hz = 1 s^-1.
The factor 2π appears only when converting to angular frequency: omega = 2π f, measured in rad/s, which is a different quantity.
keyConcept: Hertz is the inverse second: one cycle per second.
commonMistake: Confusing frequency f (Hz = s^-1) with angular frequency omega (rad/s), which differ by a factor 2π.

optionExplanations.0: The second measures time; frequency is the reciprocal of time, so Hz cannot equal s.
optionExplanations.1: The 1/(2π) factor belongs to the conversion between omega and f, not to the definition of the hertz.
optionExplanations.2: rad/s is the unit of angular frequency omega = 2π f, not of frequency itself.

formulaNotes: f = 1/T => [f] = s^-1; omega = 2π f with [omega] = rad/s.

shortExplanation: The friction gives a deceleration a = F/m = 5/7 m/s^2, so the stopping time is t = v/a = 30/(5/7) = 42 s.
solutionSteps: Known values: m = 7 kg, initial speed v = 30 m/s, friction force F = 5 N.
Newton's second law: deceleration a = F/m = 5/7 m/s^2 (about 0.714 m/s^2).
With constant deceleration, the speed decreases linearly: v(t) = v - a*t.
Stopping when v(t) = 0: t = v/a = 30/(5/7) = 30*7/5 = 42 s.
Units check: (m/s)/(m/s^2) = s.
keyConcept: Constant force means constant deceleration a = F/m, and stopping time t = v/a.
commonMistake: Dividing 30 by 5 (using force instead of acceleration) to get 6 s, or halving the correct result.

optionExplanations.1: 21 s is half the correct time, a slip such as using v/2 or doubling the acceleration.
optionExplanations.2: 6 s comes from t = v/F = 30/5, skipping the mass; force must first be converted into acceleration.
optionExplanations.3: The data are sufficient: mass, speed and force fully determine the constant deceleration and hence the time.

shortExplanation: Work is force times displacement for each stretch: 3 N * 100 m + 2 N * 100 m = 300 J + 200 J = 500 J.
solutionSteps: Both forces are parallel to the displacement, so W = F*d on each stretch with no angle factor.
First stretch: W1 = 3 N * 100 m = 300 J.
Second stretch: W2 = 2 N * 100 m = 200 J.
Total work: W = W1 + W2 = 300 + 200 = 500 J.
The work is positive because the forces point along the motion.
keyConcept: Work of a constant force parallel to the displacement is W = F*d, and works on successive stretches add up.
commonMistake: Multiplying an average force by the wrong distance or by using 200 m with a single force value, giving 1000 J or other spurious totals.

optionExplanations.0: 100 J underestimates the result; even the weaker 2 N force alone does 200 J over its stretch.
optionExplanations.2: A negative sign would mean the forces oppose the motion, but here they drag the crate forward.
optionExplanations.3: 1000 J would follow from applying a 5 N force (the sum of the two forces) over the full 200 m; each force acts only on its own 100 m stretch.

formulaNotes: W = F*d (force parallel to displacement); W_total = 3*100 + 2*100 = 500 J.

shortExplanation: Kinetic energy is (1/2)mv^2 and depends only on the speed squared, so moving in the negative x direction does not make it negative.
solutionSteps: Kinetic energy is defined as K = (1/2) m v^2, where v is the magnitude of the velocity (the speed).
The direction of motion enters through the velocity vector, but K uses v^2, which is the same for +v and -v.
Hence K = (1/2) m v^2, a positive scalar, regardless of the direction along the axis.
keyConcept: Kinetic energy is a scalar proportional to the square of the speed; it is never negative.
commonMistake: Attaching the minus sign of the velocity component to the energy, forgetting that squaring removes the sign.

optionExplanations.0: mv is the magnitude of the momentum, a different quantity with different units.
optionExplanations.3: -mv mixes up momentum with energy and wrongly imports the direction sign.
optionExplanations.4: A negative kinetic energy is impossible: v^2 is nonnegative and so is (1/2)mv^2.

formulaNotes: K = (1/2) m v^2 >= 0 for any direction of motion.

shortExplanation: The two stretches take 80/20 = 4 s and 20/10 = 2 s, so the average speed is total distance over total time: 100 m / 6 s = 16.7 m/s, about 17 m/s.
solutionSteps: Time for the first stretch: t1 = 80 m / 20 m/s = 4 s.
Time for the second stretch: t2 = 20 m / 10 m/s = 2 s.
Total distance: 80 + 20 = 100 m. Total time: 4 + 2 = 6 s.
Average speed: v_avg = 100/6 = 16.7 m/s, i.e. about 17 m/s.
Note this is not the arithmetic mean of 20 and 10, because the two speeds are held for different times.
keyConcept: Average speed = total distance / total time, not the plain average of the speeds.
commonMistake: Averaging 20 and 10 to get 15 m/s, which would be correct only if the two speeds lasted equal times.

optionExplanations.0: 13 m/s would be near the distance-weighted harmonic value for a 50/50 split, but here 80 of the 100 m are covered at the faster speed.
optionExplanations.1: 15 m/s is the arithmetic mean of the two speeds, valid only for equal time intervals, not equal distances split 80/20.
optionExplanations.3: 18 m/s overweights the faster stretch even more than the correct time-based computation.

shortExplanation: Resistance R = rho*L/S is inversely proportional to the cross-section, so the wire with area S2 = 4S1 has one quarter of the resistance: R1 = 4R2.
solutionSteps: Both wires are iron (same resistivity rho) and have the same length L.
Resistance of a wire: R = rho*L/S.
R1 = rho*L/S1 and R2 = rho*L/S2 = rho*L/(4S1).
Divide: R1/R2 = (rho*L/S1)/(rho*L/(4S1)) = 4.
Hence R1 = 4R2: the thinner wire has four times the resistance.
keyConcept: Resistance is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area: thicker wire, lower resistance.
commonMistake: Inverting the proportionality and giving the larger resistance to the thicker wire (writing 4R1 = R2).

optionExplanations.1: 4R1 = R2 reverses the relation: the wire with the larger cross-section conducts better and has the smaller resistance.
optionExplanations.2: A factor 2 would follow from doubling the area, or from wrongly taking the square root of the area ratio; the areas differ by a factor 4.
optionExplanations.4: Equal resistances would require equal cross-sections, but S2 is four times S1.

formulaNotes: R = rho*L/S; with S2 = 4S1: R2 = R1/4, i.e. R1 = 4R2.

shortExplanation: At constant pressure an ideal gas obeys V/T = constant, so the volume scales by the same factor as the absolute temperature: V2 = 10 l * 1.2 = 12 l, an increase of 2 l.
solutionSteps: For an isobaric transformation of an ideal gas, Gay-Lussac/Charles' law gives V1/T1 = V2/T2.
Solve for the final volume: V2 = V1 * (T2/T1) = 10 l * (1.2T/T) = 12 l.
Compute the change: 12 l - 10 l = +2 l, so the volume has increased by 2 l.
keyConcept: In an isobaric process V is directly proportional to the absolute temperature T (V/T = constant).
commonMistake: Adding 1.2 as if it were an absolute increment instead of multiplying the volume by the factor 1.2.

optionExplanations.0: An increase of only 1 l would correspond to a temperature factor of 1.1, not 1.2.
optionExplanations.1: The volume cannot stay fixed: at constant pressure a temperature rise forces the gas to expand.
optionExplanations.2: The temperature increases, so at constant pressure the volume must increase, not decrease.

formulaNotes: Isobaric process: V1/T1 = V2/T2, with T in kelvin (absolute temperature).

shortExplanation: Centripetal acceleration is a = v^2/R = (2 m/s)^2 / 4 m = 1 m/s^2.
solutionSteps: In uniform circular motion the centripetal acceleration has magnitude a = v^2 / R.
Substitute the values: a = (2 m/s)^2 / (4 m) = 4 / 4 = 1.
Check units: (m/s)^2 / m = m/s^2, so a = 1 m/s^2.
keyConcept: Uniform circular motion: centripetal acceleration a = v^2 / R, directed toward the center.
commonMistake: Reporting the numerical value with velocity units (m/s) instead of acceleration units (m/s^2).

optionExplanations.0: The number 1 is right but m/s is a unit of velocity, not of acceleration.
optionExplanations.2: Both v and R are given, so a = v^2/R is fully determined; no other data are needed.
optionExplanations.4: 0.5 m/s^2 would come from v/R = 2/4, but the correct formula squares the velocity.

formulaNotes: a_c = v^2 / R = omega^2 R.

shortExplanation: At the instant it slips from the boy's hands the bottle still shares the train's motion, so for a ground observer its speed equals the train's speed V.
solutionSteps: Before release, the bottle moves with the boy, i.e. with the train, at horizontal speed V relative to the ground.
Releasing it does not instantly change its velocity: at the exact moment of release no impulse has yet acted.
Therefore the ground observer sees the bottle moving with the same speed as the train at that instant.
Only afterwards does gravity add a growing vertical component while the horizontal component stays (neglecting air resistance) equal to V.
keyConcept: Velocity is continuous: an object released from a moving vehicle initially retains the vehicle's velocity (inertia).
commonMistake: Thinking the bottle starts from rest for the ground observer; zero initial speed holds only in the train's reference frame.

optionExplanations.0: The speed at the release instant is fixed by the train's motion; the later fall time affects the final speed, not the initial one.
optionExplanations.2: Mass is irrelevant to kinematics here; the initial velocity is determined purely by the shared motion with the train.
optionExplanations.3: Zero speed is what the observer on the train would measure, not the observer on the ground.

shortExplanation: The uniform field exerts a constant force on the charge perpendicular to its initial velocity, so the motion is like projectile motion: uniform along the initial direction and uniformly accelerated across it, giving a parabolic trajectory.
solutionSteps: The uniform electric field E exerts a constant force F = qE on the positive charge, directed along the field.
The initial velocity is perpendicular to the field, so the force has no component along the initial motion: that velocity component stays constant.
Along the field direction the charge undergoes constant acceleration a = qE/m, starting from zero velocity in that direction.
Uniform motion in one direction combined with uniformly accelerated motion in the perpendicular direction produces a parabolic trajectory, exactly as in projectile motion.
keyConcept: A constant force perpendicular to the initial velocity produces parabolic motion (the electrostatic analogue of projectile motion).
commonMistake: Confusing the electric case with a magnetic field, where the force stays perpendicular to the velocity and bends the path into a circle instead of a parabola.

optionExplanations.0: A charge in an electric field always feels the force F = qE, so it cannot continue unaffected.
optionExplanations.1: The field accelerates the charge along the field direction, so the motion cannot remain perpendicular to the field.
optionExplanations.4: The velocity component along the field grows but the perpendicular component never disappears, so the motion only asymptotically tilts toward the field without ever being parallel to it.

formulaNotes: F = qE, a = qE/m; trajectory y = (a/(2 v0^2)) x^2, a parabola.

shortExplanation: The equilibrium temperature is the mass-weighted average T_eq = (m1 T1 + m2 T2)/(m1 + m2); since m1 >> m2, the average is dominated by m1 and ends up close to T1.
solutionSteps: In an insulated container the heat lost by one body equals the heat gained by the other: m1 c (T1 - T_eq) = m2 c (T_eq - T2).
Since both bodies are the same material, the specific heat c cancels: T_eq = (m1 T1 + m2 T2)/(m1 + m2).
With m1 >> m2 the weight of T1 dominates: T_eq is approximately T1.
At equilibrium both bodies have the same temperature, and it lies much closer to T1 than to T2.
keyConcept: Thermal equilibrium temperature is a heat-capacity-weighted average; the body with the far larger heat capacity barely changes temperature.
commonMistake: Assuming the equilibrium temperature is simply the midpoint (T1 + T2)/2, which holds only for equal heat capacities.

optionExplanations.0: At equilibrium the two bodies must have equal temperatures; neither can remain hotter than the other.
optionExplanations.1: Closer to T2 would require m2 to dominate the average, but m2 is the much smaller mass.
optionExplanations.3: The walls are perfectly insulating, so the room plays no role; the final temperature is set only by the two bodies.

shortExplanation: Gravity follows an inverse-square law, so F/2 requires r^2 = 2 R_T^2, i.e. r = sqrt(2) R_T.
solutionSteps: Newton's law of gravitation: F = G M m / r^2, so the force scales as 1/r^2.
At the surface: F = G M m / R_T^2. We want the distance r where the force is F/2.
Set G M m / r^2 = (1/2) G M m / R_T^2.
Cancel G M m: 1/r^2 = 1/(2 R_T^2), so r^2 = 2 R_T^2.
Take the square root: r = sqrt(2) R_T, about 1.41 Earth radii from the center.
keyConcept: Inverse-square law: halving the force multiplies the distance by sqrt(2), not by 2.
commonMistake: Doubling the distance to halve the force, which actually reduces the force to F/4 because of the square in the denominator.

optionExplanations.0: At r = 4 R_T the force drops to F/16, far below F/2.
optionExplanations.3: At r = (1/2) R_T the inverse-square law would give a larger force (4F), not a smaller one.
optionExplanations.4: At r = 2 R_T the force is F/4, since (1/2)^2 = 1/4, not 1/2.

formulaNotes: F proportional to 1/r^2; F(r)/F(R_T) = (R_T/r)^2 = 1/2 gives r = sqrt(2) R_T.

shortExplanation: The container is rigid, so the gas volume never changes; since the work of a gas is W = integral of p dV and dV = 0 throughout, the work done is zero.
solutionSteps: Identify the transformation: heating a gas in a rigid, sealed container is an isochoric (constant-volume) process.
The work done by a gas is W = integral of p dV over the transformation.
Since the volume is fixed at 2 m^3, dV = 0 at every instant.
Therefore W = 0: all the heat supplied goes into internal energy (raising temperature and pressure), not into work.
keyConcept: In an isochoric process a gas does no work because work requires a volume change (W = p dV).
commonMistake: Multiplying the pressure change by the volume (50 kPa * 2 m^3 = 100 kJ) as if Delta(p)V were work; without expansion there is no work.

optionExplanations.0: 200 kJ would be 100 kPa * 2 m^3, a p*V product, not the work of a constant-volume process.
optionExplanations.2: 100 kJ comes from (150 - 100) kPa * 2 m^3, but pressure change times volume is not work; work needs a volume change.
optionExplanations.3: 300 kJ is 150 kPa * 2 m^3, again a p*V product with no physical role here since the gas never expands.

formulaNotes: W = integral p dV; isochoric process: dV = 0 so W = 0, and Q = Delta U.

shortExplanation: The current is proportional to the drift velocity (I = n q A v_d) and the power dissipated is P = I^2 R, so the energy dissipated per second is proportional to the square of the drift velocity.
solutionSteps: The current in a conductor is I = n q A v_d, where n is the charge-carrier density, q the carrier charge, A the cross-section and v_d the drift velocity; hence I is proportional to v_d.
The energy dissipated per unit time (power) by the Joule effect is P = I^2 R.
Substitute I proportional to v_d: P proportional to v_d^2.
So the energy dissipated in 1 s grows with the square of the drift velocity.
keyConcept: Joule heating P = I^2 R combined with I = n q A v_d gives P proportional to v_d^2.
commonMistake: Stopping at the linear relation I proportional to v_d and forgetting that the dissipated power depends on the square of the current.

optionExplanations.1: Linear proportionality would follow from P = I R (wrong formula); the correct P = I^2 R makes the dependence quadratic.
optionExplanations.2: Inverse proportionality would mean faster carriers dissipate less, contradicting P = I^2 R with I proportional to v_d.
optionExplanations.3: The dissipation cannot be independent of v_d: with zero drift velocity there is no current and no dissipation.

formulaNotes: I = n q A v_d; P = I^2 R = (n q A)^2 R v_d^2.

shortExplanation: For motion from rest, X = (1/2)(F/M)t^2, so t = sqrt(2MX/F). Quadrupling F divides the time by sqrt(4) = 2, giving t_2 = t/2.
solutionSteps: The body starts from rest with acceleration a = F/M, so the distance covered is X = (1/2)a t^2 = (1/2)(F/M)t^2.
Solve for the time: t = sqrt(2MX/F).
With the new force F' = 4F over the same distance X: t_2 = sqrt(2MX/(4F)) = sqrt(2MX/F)/2.
Therefore t_2 = t/2, independently of the actual value of F.
keyConcept: In uniformly accelerated motion from rest, the time to cover a fixed distance scales as 1/sqrt(a), so multiplying the force by 4 halves the time.
commonMistake: Assuming time is inversely proportional to force (t/4) instead of inversely proportional to the square root of force (t/2).

optionExplanations.0: Doubling the time would mean the stronger force makes the body slower, which contradicts a larger acceleration.
optionExplanations.2: t/4 would follow only if time were inversely proportional to force, but t depends on 1/sqrt(F), so quadrupling F only halves the time.
optionExplanations.4: The value of F cancels in the ratio t_2/t = sqrt(F/F') = 1/2, so the answer does not depend on F.

formulaNotes: X = (1/2)(F/M)t^2 for motion from rest; hence t proportional to 1/sqrt(F) at fixed X and M.

shortExplanation: Gravity is a conservative force, so its work depends only on mass and vertical drop: W = mgh. Both skiers descend the same height h, so the lighter skier (smaller m) receives less work from the weight force.
solutionSteps: The work done by the weight force is W = mgh, where h is the vertical drop, regardless of the path followed.
Both skiers start at the same mountain top and end in the same valley, so h is the same for both.
Since W is proportional to the mass m, the skier with smaller mass has smaller W.
Therefore the weight force does less work on the lighter skier.
keyConcept: The work of gravity is path-independent and equals mgh, so it depends on mass and height difference only.
commonMistake: Thinking the shape or length of the slope matters: gravity is conservative, so only the vertical drop counts.

optionExplanations.2: The work would be equal only if the skiers had equal masses; W = mgh is proportional to mass.
optionExplanations.3: The length of the slope is irrelevant because gravity's work depends only on the height difference, not on the distance travelled.
optionExplanations.4: The detailed shape of the slope is irrelevant for a conservative force: any path between the same two heights gives the same work mgh.

formulaNotes: W_gravity = mgh, with h the vertical height difference between start and end points.

shortExplanation: In free fall from height h, the final speed is v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2*10*20) = sqrt(400) = 20 m/s.
solutionSteps: Known values: h = 20 m, g = 10 m/s^2, initial speed 0.
Apply the free-fall relation v^2 = 2gh (from energy conservation or kinematics).
Take the square root: v = 20 m/s.
keyConcept: For a body falling from rest, v = sqrt(2gh) links final speed to the height of the fall.
commonMistake: Computing g*h = 200 or halving incorrectly instead of applying v = sqrt(2gh).

optionExplanations.1: 20 m/s is obtained correctly from sqrt(2*10*20); the other values do not satisfy v^2 = 2gh.
optionExplanations.2: 25 m/s would require a height of about 31 m, not 20 m.
optionExplanations.3: 5 m/s is roughly the speed after just half a second of fall, not after the full 20 m drop.

formulaNotes: v^2 = 2gh for free fall from rest; equivalently mgh = (1/2)mv^2.

shortExplanation: At constant volume the pressure is proportional to the absolute temperature (Gay-Lussac's law): a 10% rise from 300 K to 330 K raises the pressure from 20 bar to 20*1.1 = 22 bar.
solutionSteps: The tank is rigid, so the gas volume is constant: p/T = constant (Gay-Lussac's law).
Initial state: p1 = 20 bar, T1 = 300 K. A 10% increase gives T2 = 330 K.
p2 = 22 bar.
keyConcept: For a fixed amount of gas at constant volume, pressure scales linearly with absolute temperature.
commonMistake: Applying the 10% increase to a Celsius temperature instead of the absolute (Kelvin) temperature.

optionExplanations.1: The pressure cannot stay at 20 bar: heating a sealed rigid tank necessarily raises the pressure.
optionExplanations.2: 33 bar would correspond to a temperature increase of 65%, not 10%.
optionExplanations.4: 15 bar would mean the pressure dropped on heating, contradicting p proportional to T at constant volume.

formulaNotes: Gay-Lussac's law: p1/T1 = p2/T2 at constant volume, with T in kelvin.

shortExplanation: Taking right as positive with v0 = +1 m/s and a = -5 m/s^2, the displacement over 10 s is x = 1*10 + (1/2)*(-5)*10^2 = 10 - 250 = -240 m, i.e. 240 m to the left.
solutionSteps: Choose rightward as positive: v0 = +1 m/s, a = -5 m/s^2, t = 10 s.
Apply x = v0*t + (1/2)*a*t^2.
The negative sign means the net displacement is 240 m to the left: the object decelerates, stops after 0.2 s, then moves leftward for the rest of the interval.
keyConcept: Displacement in uniformly accelerated motion is x = v0*t + (1/2)*a*t^2, with signs fixed by the chosen positive direction.
commonMistake: Reporting only the magnitude and keeping the original rightward direction, instead of tracking the sign of the result.

optionExplanations.2: The data are sufficient: an initial velocity, a constant acceleration, and a time interval fully determine the displacement.
optionExplanations.3: 260 m to the right adds the magnitudes of the two terms (250 + 10) and keeps a rightward sign, instead of subtracting the leftward term from the rightward one.
optionExplanations.4: 490 m to the left drops the 1/2 factor on the acceleration term: (-5)*100 + 1*10 = -500 + 10 = -490 m instead of the correct -240 m.

shortExplanation: During a phase change (melting, boiling, etc.) the absorbed heat goes into breaking intermolecular bonds as latent heat, so the temperature stays constant even though the system absorbs heat Q.
solutionSteps: Recall that absorbed heat can either raise the temperature (Q = m*c*deltaT) or drive a phase change (Q = m*L) at constant temperature.
During melting or boiling, the energy absorbed is used to change the state of the substance, not to increase molecular kinetic energy.
Therefore a system undergoing a phase change can absorb heat Q while its temperature remains constant.
keyConcept: Latent heat: during a phase change, absorbed heat does not change the temperature.
commonMistake: Assuming that absorbing heat always means the temperature must rise.

optionExplanations.0: It is not impossible: any substance melting or boiling absorbs heat at constant temperature.
optionExplanations.1: A specific heat of zero would mean any heat causes an infinite temperature change, not zero change; no real system has c = 0.
optionExplanations.4: A system cannot be at absolute zero, and being cold does not prevent temperature from rising when heat is absorbed.

shortExplanation: Equal volumes in identical glasses give the same liquid height h, so the hydrostatic pressure rho*g*h at the bottom is larger for the denser fluid, which is water.
solutionSteps: Identical glasses with the same volume of liquid have the same liquid height h.
The pressure at the bottom due to the liquid is p = rho*g*h (plus atmospheric pressure, identical in both cases).
Since g and h are the same for both, the pressure depends only on the density rho.
Water is denser than olive oil, so the pressure at the bottom is larger in the glass of water.
keyConcept: Hydrostatic pressure p = rho*g*h grows with fluid density at equal depth.
commonMistake: Thinking equal volumes imply equal pressure, forgetting that pressure depends on density as well as height.

optionExplanations.1: Atmospheric pressure adds the same amount to both glasses, so it cancels out of the comparison.
optionExplanations.3: Pressure at the bottom is rho*g*h, which explicitly depends on the density.
optionExplanations.4: Olive oil is less dense than water, so with the same height it produces a smaller bottom pressure.

formulaNotes: p_bottom = p_atm + rho*g*h; same h and g, so larger rho gives larger p.

shortExplanation: Resistors in parallel share the same potential difference V, so each current is i = V/R; the smaller resistance R2 carries the larger current, hence i2 > i1.
solutionSteps: In a parallel connection both resistors have the same potential difference V across them (the battery voltage).
By Ohm's law, i1 = V/R1 and i2 = V/R2.
Since R1 > R2 and V is the same, dividing by the larger resistance gives the smaller current: i1 < i2.
Therefore i2 > i1.
keyConcept: In parallel, voltage is common and current is inversely proportional to resistance.
commonMistake: Assuming the larger resistance carries the larger current, or confusing parallel with series (where currents are equal).

optionExplanations.0: The potential difference is known to be the same for both branches: it is the battery voltage, so the comparison is possible.
optionExplanations.2: Equal currents would require equal resistances, but R1 > R2.
optionExplanations.3: i2 < i1 would hold only if R2 were the larger resistance, which is the opposite of what is given.

formulaNotes: i = V/R with common V: R1 > R2 implies V/R1 < V/R2.

shortExplanation: Weight is a force (W = m*g), so its SI unit is the newton, which in base units is kg*m/s^2.
solutionSteps: Weight is the gravitational force on a body: W = m*g.
Mass is measured in kg and acceleration g in m/s^2.
Multiplying the units: kg * m/s^2, which defines the newton (N).
keyConcept: The newton in SI base units: 1 N = 1 kg*m/s^2.
commonMistake: Confusing weight (a force, in newtons) with mass (in kilograms).

optionExplanations.0: kg/(m*s^2) corresponds to pressure (N/m^2 = Pa), not force.
optionExplanations.1: kg*m/s is the unit of momentum (mass times velocity), not force.
optionExplanations.3: kg is the unit of mass, not of weight; weight is a force.

shortExplanation: Power is work per unit time: 100 W means 100 joules of work every second.
solutionSteps: Power is defined as P = W/t, work done per unit time.
1 watt = 1 joule per second.
So 100 W means the engine does 100 J of work in 1 s.
commonMistake: Inverting the ratio and reading 100 W as 1 J in 100 seconds.

optionExplanations.2: 1 J in 100 s corresponds to a power of 0.01 W, not 100 W.
optionExplanations.3: 100 J in 1 minute is 100/60 ≈ 1.7 W, far less than 100 W.

formulaNotes: P = W/t, so W = P*t = 100 W * 1 s = 100 J.

shortExplanation: The mass is m = 3200 N / 10 m/s^2 = 320 kg. With an upward acceleration a = 1 m/s^2, Newton's second law gives T = m(g + a) = 320 * 11 = 3520 N.
solutionSteps: Find the mass from the weight: m = W/g = 3200/10 = 320 kg.
Take upward as positive. Newton's second law on the elevator: T - mg = ma.
Solve for the tension: T = m(g + a) = 320 * (10 + 1).
T = 320 * 11 = 3520 N, larger than the weight because the acceleration points upward.
keyConcept: For upward acceleration, rope tension exceeds the weight: T = m(g + a).
commonMistake: Subtracting instead of adding the acceleration (using g - a), or forgetting to convert the weight to a mass first.

optionExplanations.0: 35200 N results from multiplying the weight (not the mass) by (g + a).
optionExplanations.1: 2880 N comes from T = m(g - a), which would apply to a downward acceleration.
optionExplanations.4: 28800 N results from multiplying the weight by (g - a) instead of using the mass.

formulaNotes: T - mg = ma (upward positive) => T = m(g + a) = 320 kg * 11 m/s^2 = 3520 N.

shortExplanation: Capacitors in parallel share the same voltage V, so q = C*V for each. Since C3 = 4*C2 = 4*(2*C1) = 8*C1, it follows that q3 = 8*q1.
solutionSteps: In parallel, all capacitors have the same potential difference V.
The charge on each is proportional to its capacitance: q1 = C1*V, q2 = C2*V, q3 = C3*V.
Express C3 in terms of C1: C2 = 2*C1 and C3 = 4*C2, so C3 = 4*2*C1 = 8*C1.
Therefore q3 = 8*C1*V = 8*q1.
keyConcept: In parallel, charge is proportional to capacitance because the voltage is common.
commonMistake: Treating the connection as a series one (where charges would be equal) or inverting the proportionality.

optionExplanations.0: q3 = 0.125*q1 is the inverse of the correct ratio: it would require C3 = C1/8.
optionExplanations.3: q3 = 2*q1 corresponds to C3 = 2*C1, but C3 is 8 times C1.

formulaNotes: q = C*V with common V; C3 = 4*C2 = 8*C1 => q3 = 8*q1.

shortExplanation: The second vector makes 90° - 15° = 75° with the x axis, so the angle between the vectors is 75° - 30° = 45°; the dot product is 10*10*cos45° = 50*sqrt(2).
solutionSteps: Convert both directions to angles from the x axis: the first is at 30°; the second is 15° from the y axis, i.e. 90° - 15° = 75° from the x axis.
The angle between the two vectors is 75° - 30° = 45°.
Apply the dot product formula: a·b = |a||b|cos(theta) = 10*10*cos45°.
keyConcept: Dot product a·b = |a||b|cos(theta), with theta the angle between the vectors.
commonMistake: Using 15° directly as if it were measured from the x axis, which gives a wrong angle between the vectors.

optionExplanations.1: The data are sufficient: both magnitudes and both directions are fully specified.
optionExplanations.2: 5*sqrt(2) is a factor of 10 too small; the product of the magnitudes is 100, not 10.
optionExplanations.4: 50*sqrt(3) would follow from an angle of 30° between the vectors, but the actual angle is 45°.

shortExplanation: Air exerts a buoyant force proportional to the immersed volume; the larger body displaces more air, receives a larger upward buoyant force, and thus the dynamometer supporting it reads a smaller force.
solutionSteps: Each dynamometer reads the weight minus the buoyant force of the air: F = m*g - rho_air*g*V.
The two bodies have the same mass, so m*g is identical for both.
The buoyant force rho_air*g*V is larger for the body with the larger volume.
Therefore the dynamometer holding the larger body reads a smaller force.
keyConcept: Archimedes' principle applies in air too: buoyant force = rho_air*g*V(displaced).
commonMistake: Ignoring air buoyancy and concluding that equal masses must give equal readings.

optionExplanations.0: The buoyant force pushes upward, so a larger volume reduces, not increases, the reading.
optionExplanations.1: The reading has nothing to do with internal voids; only mass and displaced air volume matter.
optionExplanations.2: The shape is irrelevant for a fully immersed body: buoyancy depends only on the displaced volume.
optionExplanations.4: Equal readings would hold only in vacuum; in air the buoyant force differs because the volumes differ.

formulaNotes: Reading F = m*g - rho_air*g*V; same m*g, larger V => smaller F.

shortExplanation: At constant pressure the work done by the gas is W = p*deltaV = 100 kPa * 6 m^3 = 600 kJ; the first law gives Q = deltaU + W = 300 + 600 = 900 kJ absorbed.
solutionSteps: Compute the work done by the gas in the isobaric expansion: W = p*deltaV = 100*10^3 Pa * 6 m^3 = 6*10^5 J = 600 kJ.
Apply the first law of thermodynamics: Q = deltaU + W.
Insert the values: Q = 300 kJ + 600 kJ = 900 kJ.
Q is positive, so the gas absorbs 900 kJ of heat from the surroundings.
keyConcept: First law: Q = deltaU + W, with W = p*deltaV for a constant-pressure process.
commonMistake: Forgetting the work term and answering with deltaU alone, or getting the sign convention wrong and claiming heat is released.

optionExplanations.1: The gas both expands and gains internal energy, so it must absorb, not release, heat.
optionExplanations.2: 300 kJ ignores the 600 kJ of work the expanding gas does on the surroundings.
optionExplanations.3: No heat exchange (adiabatic) would force deltaU = -W, i.e. internal energy would drop during expansion, contrary to the given data.

shortExplanation: With the same weight, spring A stretches by 6 cm and spring B by 12 cm; since k = F/x, the spring that stretches half as much has twice the constant, so KA = 2 KB.
solutionSteps: Compute the elongations from the rest length of 12 cm: xA = 18 - 12 = 6 cm; xB = 24 - 12 = 12 cm.
Hooke's law for the same applied weight F: F = KA*xA = KB*xB.
So KA/KB = xB/xA = 12/6 = 2.
Therefore KA = 2 KB.
keyConcept: For equal force, spring constant is inversely proportional to elongation (k = F/x).
commonMistake: Using the final lengths 18 and 24 cm instead of the elongations 6 and 12 cm, which gives the wrong ratio 4/3.

optionExplanations.0: The ratio 3/2 comes from comparing the total lengths 18/12 or 24/18 rather than the elongations.
optionExplanations.1: Equal constants would produce equal elongations under the same weight, but the stretches differ.
optionExplanations.4: KA = (1/2) KB inverts the correct relationship; the stiffer spring is the one that stretches less.

formulaNotes: F = k*x => KA*6 = KB*12 => KA = 2 KB.

shortExplanation: The elastic energy is U = (1/2)k*x^2, a quadratic function of the deformation, so its graph is a parabola with vertex at the origin, symmetric for compression and stretching.
solutionSteps: Write the elastic potential energy of a spring: U(x) = (1/2)*k*x^2.
This is a quadratic function of x with no linear or constant term.
Its graph is an upward parabola with vertex at (0, 0).
The energy is the same for +x and -x, consistent with the symmetry of the parabola.
keyConcept: Elastic energy U = (1/2)k*x^2 is quadratic in the deformation.
commonMistake: Confusing the energy U = (1/2)k*x^2 (parabola) with the force F = -k*x (straight line through the origin).

optionExplanations.1: A straight line through the origin describes the elastic force versus x, not the energy.
optionExplanations.2: A line not through the origin would give nonzero energy at zero deformation, which is impossible.
optionExplanations.3: A hyperbola would imply the energy diverges at x = 0 or behaves as 1/x, neither of which holds.

shortExplanation: The temperature rise is deltaT = 37 - 27 = 10 °C, so c = Q/(m*deltaT) = 42/(10*10) = 0.42 J/(g°C).
solutionSteps: Compute the temperature change: deltaT = t_fin - t_in = 37 - 27 = 10 °C.
Use the calorimetry formula: Q = m*c*deltaT, so c = Q/(m*deltaT).
Insert the values: c = 42 J / (10 g * 10 °C).
keyConcept: Specific heat from calorimetry: c = Q/(m*deltaT).
commonMistake: Mixing up units and reporting the numerical value in cal/(g°C) instead of J/(g°C), or using a wrong deltaT.

optionExplanations.1: The number 0.42 is correct only in joules; expressed in calories the value would be about 0.1 cal/(g°C), so the calorie unit is wrong.
optionExplanations.2: 4.2 J/(g°C) is the specific heat of water, and would follow from a deltaT of 1 °C instead of 10 °C.
optionExplanations.4: 42 J/(g°C) forgets to divide by both the mass and the temperature change.

shortExplanation: The relative velocity of the first car with respect to the second is v1 - v2 = 10 - 20 = -10 m/s: the first car falls behind at 10 m/s.
solutionSteps: Take the common direction of travel as positive: v1 = 10 m/s, v2 = 20 m/s.
Relative velocity of car 1 with respect to car 2: v_rel = v1 - v2.
The negative sign means that, seen from the faster car, the first car moves backward at 10 m/s.
keyConcept: Relative velocity: v(1 rel 2) = v1 - v2, sign included.
commonMistake: Taking the difference in the wrong order (v2 - v1 = +10 m/s) or adding the speeds as if the cars moved in opposite directions.

optionExplanations.2: +10 m/s is the velocity of the second car relative to the first, not the reverse.
optionExplanations.3: 20 m/s is simply the speed of the second car, not a relative velocity.
optionExplanations.4: Zero relative velocity would require equal speeds.

shortExplanation: The closing speed is 9 - 7 = 2 m/s, so covering the 10 m gap takes t = 10/2 = 5 s.
solutionSteps: Compute the relative (closing) speed of the rear rider with respect to the front one: v_rel = 9 - 7 = 2 m/s.
The gap to close is d = 10 m.
Time to catch up: t = d/v_rel = 10/2.
t = 5 s.
keyConcept: Catch-up problems reduce to distance divided by relative speed.
commonMistake: Dividing the distance by one of the actual speeds (10/9 or 10/7) instead of the relative speed.

optionExplanations.0: 7 s matches no consistent combination; it mistakes the front rider's speed for a time.
optionExplanations.3: 3 s would require a closing speed of about 3.3 m/s, larger than the actual 2 m/s.
optionExplanations.4: 10 s would follow from a closing speed of 1 m/s, but the speed difference is 2 m/s.

shortExplanation: The horizontal launch does not affect the vertical fall, so t = sqrt(2h/g) = sqrt(2*4/9.8) ≈ 0.9 s.
solutionSteps: In projectile motion the horizontal and vertical motions are independent; the initial horizontal speed does not change the fall time.
Vertical motion is free fall from rest: h = (1/2)*g*t^2.
Solve for t: t = sqrt(2h/g) = sqrt(2*4/9.8).
keyConcept: Fall time depends only on the height: t = sqrt(2h/g), independent of horizontal speed.
commonMistake: Thinking the horizontal speed shortens or lengthens the fall, or using h = g*t^2 without the factor 1/2.

optionExplanations.0: 0.4 s would correspond to a height of about 0.8 m, not 4 m.
optionExplanations.1: 4.4 s is far too long; falling for 4.4 s would cover nearly 95 m.
optionExplanations.3: 1.7 s would follow from forgetting the factor 2 in a wrong rearrangement; it corresponds to a fall of about 14 m.

shortExplanation: R1 and R2 are both connected directly across the battery, so the full 30.0 V appears across R1 and I1 = V/R1 = 30.0/10.0 = 3.0 A.
solutionSteps: From the figure, R1 and R2 are in parallel across the source, so each resistor has the full battery voltage: V1 = V = 30.0 V.
Apply Ohm's law to R1 alone: I1 = V/R1 = 30.0 V / 10.0 Ohm.
I1 = 3.0 A. (R2 carries its own separate current of 30.0/5.0 = 6.0 A, which does not affect I1.)
keyConcept: In a parallel connection each branch sees the same voltage, and each branch current follows from Ohm's law applied to that branch alone.
commonMistake: Combining the resistors in series (15 Ohm) and computing 30/15 = 2 A, or dividing the total current equally between unequal resistors.

optionExplanations.1: 9.0 A is the total current delivered by the battery (3.0 + 6.0), not the R1 branch current.
optionExplanations.2: Current is not blocked by the smaller resistor in parallel; both branches conduct, each set by its own resistance.
optionExplanations.4: 6.0 A is the current through R2 (30 V across 5 Ohm), not through R1.

figureExplanation: The circuit drawing shows the battery on the left with R1 and R2 as two separate vertical branches joined to the same top and bottom wires, i.e. a pure parallel connection.
formulaNotes: Ohm's law: I = V/R. Parallel branches: same V across each branch.

shortExplanation: The components along x and y are equal when the force bisects the axes, i.e. when it makes 45° with each axis; forming 45° with the y axis gives Fx = F sin45° = F cos45° = Fy.
solutionSteps: Write the components for a force making angle theta with the y axis: Fy = F*cos(theta), Fx = F*sin(theta).
Equal components require sin(theta) = cos(theta).
This holds for theta = 45°.
So the components are equal when F1 forms an angle of 45° with the y axis (and hence also 45° with the x axis).
keyConcept: Equal Cartesian components occur when the vector makes 45° with both axes.
commonMistake: Thinking a force aligned with one axis has 'equal' components, when in fact one component is zero and the other equals the full magnitude.

optionExplanations.1: Perpendicular to the y axis means along x: then Fx = F and Fy = 0, which are unequal.
optionExplanations.2: Parallel to the y axis gives Fx = 0 and Fy = F, again unequal.
optionExplanations.4: The magnitude equals a component only when the force lies along an axis, which makes the other component zero, not equal.

shortExplanation: At constant temperature Boyle's law gives p*V = constant; doubling the volume halves the pressure.
solutionSteps: For an ideal gas at constant temperature, Boyle's law holds: p1*V1 = p2*V2.
The final volume is V2 = 2*V1.
The pressure has halved.
keyConcept: Isothermal process: pressure and volume are inversely proportional (p*V = const).
commonMistake: Assuming pressure grows with volume, or thinking the actual temperature value is needed when only its constancy matters.

optionExplanations.1: Doubling would occur if the volume were halved, not doubled.
optionExplanations.2: One quarter of the initial pressure would require the volume to quadruple.
optionExplanations.4: The temperature value is irrelevant: it cancels because it is the same before and after.

shortExplanation: The scalar (dot) product is a number, a·b = ab*cos(theta); for perpendicular vectors theta = 90° and cos90° = 0, so the result is the scalar zero.
solutionSteps: Recall the definition: a·b = |a|*|b|*cos(theta), where theta is the angle between the vectors.
The result of a scalar product is always a number (scalar), never a vector.
For perpendicular vectors theta = 90°, and cos(90°) = 0.
Therefore a·b = ab*0 = 0, a scalar equal to zero.
keyConcept: The dot product of perpendicular vectors is zero because cos90° = 0.
commonMistake: Confusing the scalar product with the vector (cross) product, whose result is a vector perpendicular to the plane of a and b.

optionExplanations.1: A 'vector of magnitude 0' misidentifies the nature of the result: the dot product is a scalar, not a vector.
optionExplanations.3: The value ab would require the vectors to be parallel (cos0° = 1), not perpendicular.
optionExplanations.4: A vector perpendicular to the plane describes the cross product a x b, not the scalar product.

formulaNotes: a·b = |a||b|cos(theta); theta = 90° => a·b = 0 (scalar).

shortExplanation: The same weight stretches A by 4 cm and B by 2 cm. Since F = k*x with the same F, the spring that stretches twice as much has half the constant, so k_A = (1/2) k_B.
solutionSteps: Extension of A: 10 cm - 6 cm = 4 cm; extension of B: 8 cm - 6 cm = 2 cm.
Hooke's law for the same hanging weight F: F = k_A * (4 cm) = k_B * (2 cm).
Divide: k_A / k_B = 2/4 = 1/2, so k_A = (1/2) k_B.
keyConcept: For the same force, spring extension is inversely proportional to the elastic constant (F = k*x).
commonMistake: Comparing the full lengths (10 cm and 8 cm) instead of the extensions from the 6 cm rest length.

optionExplanations.0: k_B = (1/2) k_A inverts the correct relation; the spring with the smaller extension (B) is the stiffer one, not the softer one.
optionExplanations.1: k_A = (4/5) k_B comes from taking the ratio of the total lengths 8/10 instead of the ratio of the extensions 2/4.
optionExplanations.4: Equal constants would require equal extensions under the same load, but A stretches 4 cm while B stretches only 2 cm.

formulaNotes: Hooke's law: F = k*x, where x is the extension from the natural length.

shortExplanation: The velocity of a point in uniform circular motion is tangent to the circle, with magnitude v = omega*r. Here omega = 33*2*pi/60 = 3.46 rad/s and r = 0.10 m, giving v = 0.35 m/s, about 0.33 m/s.
solutionSteps: Convert the rotation rate: omega = 33 rev/min * 2*pi rad/rev / 60 s/min = 3.46 rad/s.
Speed on a circle of radius r = 0.10 m: v = omega*r = 3.46 * 0.10 = 0.35 m/s.
The velocity vector in circular motion is always tangent to the circular path, so the answer is tangent with magnitude about 0.33 m/s.
keyConcept: In uniform circular motion v = omega*r and the velocity is tangent to the circle.
commonMistake: Forgetting to convert rounds per minute into radians per second before multiplying by the radius.

optionExplanations.0: 33 m/s wrongly treats the number of revolutions per minute as if it were already the speed in m/s.
optionExplanations.1: 3.3 m/s would follow from using r = 1 m or from a factor-of-10 slip in the unit conversion; with r = 10 cm the speed is ten times smaller.
optionExplanations.3: The radial direction is the direction of the centripetal acceleration, not of the velocity, which is tangent to the path.

formulaNotes: v = omega*r, with omega in rad/s: omega = 2*pi*f.

shortExplanation: The net force is the weight minus the upward push: mg - P = 20 - 5 = 15 N downward. Dividing by m = 2 kg gives a = 7.5 m/s^2 directed downward.
solutionSteps: Compute the weight: mg = 2 * 10 = 20 N, downward.
Find the net force: F_net = 20 N - 5 N = 15 N, downward (gravity exceeds the applied force).
Apply Newton's second law: a = F_net/m = 15/2 = 7.5 m/s^2, downward.
keyConcept: Newton's second law uses the vector sum of all forces: a = F_net/m.
commonMistake: Using gravity alone (giving 10 m/s^2) and ignoring the 5 N upward force.

optionExplanations.1: 10 m/s^2 downward ignores the 5 N upward force entirely, which would be free fall.
optionExplanations.3: 7.5 m/s^2 upward has the correct magnitude but the wrong direction: the 20 N weight exceeds the 5 N upward force, so the acceleration points down.
optionExplanations.4: 15 m/s^2 downward takes the 15 N net force as if it were the acceleration, skipping the division by the 2 kg mass.

formulaNotes: F_net = mg - P (down positive); a = F_net/m.

shortExplanation: Gravitational force follows an inverse-square law, F proportional to 1/d^2. To reduce the force by a factor of 16 the distance must increase by sqrt(16) = 4, so d' = 4d.
solutionSteps: Newton's law of gravitation: F = G*m1*m2/d^2.
So d'^2 = 16 d^2, hence d' = 4d.
keyConcept: Inverse-square law: multiplying the distance by n divides the force by n^2.
commonMistake: Treating the force as inversely proportional to d instead of d^2, which leads to d' = 16d.

optionExplanations.0: d' = 16d assumes F is proportional to 1/d; because of the square, a factor 16 in force needs only a factor 4 in distance.
optionExplanations.1: Bringing the masses closer (d/4) would make the force 16 times larger, not smaller.
optionExplanations.3: d' = 2d would reduce the force by 2^2 = 4, not 16.

formulaNotes: F = G*m1*m2/d^2; scaling d -> n*d gives F -> F/n^2.

shortExplanation: From F = m*a, one newton is the force giving a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s^2, so 1 N = 1 kg m/s^2.
solutionSteps: Newton's second law: F = m*a.
Units: [F] = [m]*[a] = kg * (m/s^2).
Therefore 1 N = 1 kg m/s^2.
keyConcept: The newton is a derived unit defined through F = m*a.
commonMistake: Confusing the units of force with those of energy (kg m^2/s^2, the joule) or of momentum (kg m/s).

optionExplanations.0: kg m^2/s^2 is the joule, the unit of energy and work, not of force.
optionExplanations.2: kg m/s is the unit of momentum (mass times velocity), not of force.
optionExplanations.4: 9.8 kg m/s^2 mixes up the definition of the newton with the weight of a 1 kg mass on Earth; the definition itself carries no factor 9.8.

formulaNotes: F = m*a implies N = kg * m/s^2.

shortExplanation: At the top of the toss the speed is zero, so energy conservation gives v = sqrt(2*g*h) = sqrt(2*10*1) = sqrt(20) = 4.5 m/s.
solutionSteps: At maximum height the vertical speed is zero.
Energy conservation (or kinematics): (1/2)*m*v^2 = m*g*h, so v = sqrt(2*g*h).
v = sqrt(2*10*1) = sqrt(20) = 4.47 m/s, about 4.5 m/s.
keyConcept: For a vertical launch, v0 = sqrt(2*g*h_max); the time of flight is not needed.
commonMistake: Thinking the flight time is required: the maximum height alone fixes the launch speed.

optionExplanations.0: 20 m/s confuses the value of v^2 (which equals 20 m^2/s^2) with the speed itself.
optionExplanations.1: The time of flight is unnecessary: v0 = sqrt(2*g*h) is fully determined by the 1 m height.
optionExplanations.2: 3.3 m/s roughly corresponds to sqrt(g*h) = sqrt(10), forgetting the factor 2 in v^2 = 2*g*h.

formulaNotes: v^2 = 2*g*h at the release point, so v = sqrt(2*g*h).

shortExplanation: Starting from rest with constant acceleration, x = (1/2)*a*t^2 = (1/2)*15*10^2 = 750 m.
solutionSteps: Uniformly accelerated motion from rest: x = (1/2)*a*t^2.
Substitute a = 15 m/s^2 and t = 10 s: x = 0.5 * 15 * 100.
keyConcept: Position under constant acceleration from rest: x = (1/2)*a*t^2.
commonMistake: Dropping the factor 1/2 (getting 1500 m) or forgetting to square the time (getting 75 m).

optionExplanations.0: 150 m equals a*t without squaring the time properly; that number is actually the final speed in m/s, not the position.
optionExplanations.1: 75 m comes from (1/2)*a*t with t not squared.
optionExplanations.3: The data are sufficient: initial position can be taken as the origin, initial velocity is zero, and a and t are given.

shortExplanation: The friction force must dissipate the whole kinetic energy of the bullet over 30 cm: F = (1/2)*m*v^2 / s = 90 J / 0.30 m = 300 N.
solutionSteps: Kinetic energy of the bullet: (1/2)*m*v^2 = 0.5 * 0.002 kg * (300 m/s)^2 = 90 J.
Work-energy theorem: the constant friction force removes all this energy over s = 0.30 m, so F*s = 90 J.
keyConcept: Work-energy theorem: F*s equals the kinetic energy lost when the body stops.
commonMistake: Forgetting to convert grams to kilograms or centimeters to meters before computing.

optionExplanations.0: 450 N comes from using s = 0.20 m or from dropping the 1/2 in the kinetic energy and then miscombining; the consistent calculation gives 300 N.
optionExplanations.1: 150 N would follow from using m*v^2 over 1.2 m or from a factor-of-2 slip; correctly, 90 J / 0.30 m = 300 N.
optionExplanations.3: 90 N is numerically the kinetic energy in joules (90 J), mistaken for the force without dividing by the 0.30 m penetration depth.

shortExplanation: Gravity is conservative, so its work depends only on the change in height: W = m*g*(hA - hB) = 10*10*(3-2) = +100 J. The work is positive because the body moves downward.
solutionSteps: Work of gravity along any path: W = -Delta(U) = m*g*(h_initial - h_final).
Substitute: W = 10 kg * 10 m/s^2 * (3 m - 2 m) = 100 J.
The body descends, gravity points downward along the net displacement, so W = +100 J.
keyConcept: The work of a conservative force depends only on the initial and final heights, not on the path.
commonMistake: Thinking 'conservative' means the work is zero on any path; it is zero only on closed paths.

optionExplanations.1: -100 J has the wrong sign: the body moves down, in the same direction as gravity, so gravity does positive work.
optionExplanations.3: A conservative force does zero work only over a closed loop; here the height changes by 1 m, so the work is nonzero.
optionExplanations.4: +10 J forgets to multiply by g (it is m*Delta(h) instead of m*g*Delta(h)).

formulaNotes: W_gravity = m*g*(hA - hB); sign is positive when the body descends.

shortExplanation: Both bodies drop the same height without friction, so energy conservation gives the same final speed v = sqrt(2*g*y0) = 4 m/s. B takes tB = v/g = 0.4 s, while A accelerates at g*sin(45 deg) over a path 1/sin(45 deg) times longer, giving tA = sqrt(2)*tB.
solutionSteps: Speeds: with no friction, (1/2)*m*v^2 = m*g*y0 for both, so vA = vB = sqrt(2*10*0.8) = 4 m/s (mass cancels).
Free fall time for B: y0 = (1/2)*g*tB^2, so tB = sqrt(2*0.8/10) = 0.4 s.
For A: acceleration along the incline a = g*sin(45 deg) = 10/sqrt(2) m/s^2; path length L = y0/sin(45 deg) = 0.8*sqrt(2) m.
Check: vA = a*tA = (10/sqrt(2))*(0.4*sqrt(2)) = 4 m/s, consistent.
keyConcept: Without friction the final speed depends only on the height dropped, while the incline lengthens the travel time.
commonMistake: Assuming equal times because the heights are equal: the incline reduces the acceleration and lengthens the path, so A arrives later.

optionExplanations.1: The speeds cannot differ: energy conservation with the same drop height gives the same speed regardless of mass or path, and the times cannot be equal.
optionExplanations.3: Mass does not affect either speed: both m*g*h = (1/2)*m*v^2 terms cancel the mass, so vA equals vB.
optionExplanations.4: tA = (1/sqrt(2))*tB would make A faster than free fall, which is impossible since the incline gives a smaller acceleration over a longer path.

formulaNotes: v = sqrt(2*g*h); on the incline a = g*sin(theta), L = h/sin(theta), so t_incline = t_freefall / sin(theta).

shortExplanation: The dynamometer reads less than the weight mg = 100 N, so the net force m*g - P = 10 N points downward, giving a = 1 m/s^2 directed downward.
solutionSteps: Forces on the mass: dynamometer tension P = 90 N upward, weight mg = 10*10 = 100 N downward.
Newton's second law (down positive): m*a = mg - P = 100 - 90 = 10 N.
a = 10/10 = 1 m/s^2, directed downward.
keyConcept: A reading below the true weight means the acceleration (not necessarily the velocity) points downward.
commonMistake: Concluding the elevator is 'moving downward': the reading fixes the direction of the acceleration, while the velocity could be downward and increasing or upward and decreasing.

optionExplanations.1: An upward acceleration would make the reading larger than 100 N, not smaller.
optionExplanations.2: The dynamometer tells us about acceleration, not velocity: the elevator could be moving upward while slowing down.
optionExplanations.3: 9 m/s^2 confuses the tension value per unit mass (90 N / 10 kg) with the net acceleration; the correct net force is only 10 N.

formulaNotes: P = m*(g - a) for downward acceleration a; here 90 = 10*(10 - a) gives a = 1 m/s^2.

shortExplanation: At constant volume, pressure is proportional to absolute temperature (P/T = constant). Doubling the pressure doubles the temperature: 2 * 400 K = 800 K.
solutionSteps: Isochoric transformation of an ideal gas: P1/T1 = P2/T2.
keyConcept: Gay-Lussac's law: at constant volume, P is directly proportional to the absolute temperature.
commonMistake: Halving instead of doubling the temperature, or working in Celsius instead of kelvin.

optionExplanations.1: 600 K corresponds to adding 200 K rather than multiplying by the pressure ratio 2.
optionExplanations.3: 200 K would follow if pressure were inversely proportional to temperature, but at constant volume they are directly proportional.
optionExplanations.4: The temperature must change: with V fixed, P can only double if T doubles (ideal-gas law P*V = n*R*T).

formulaNotes: P*V = n*R*T with V constant gives P1/T1 = P2/T2.

shortExplanation: The initial velocity is purely vertical (only a z-component), so the stone goes straight up and comes straight back down to its launch point on the floor, P(0,0,0).
solutionSteps: Initial velocity (0,0,3) m/s has zero horizontal components (vx = vy = 0).
Gravity acts only along z, so no horizontal motion ever develops: x(t) = 0 and y(t) = 0 for all t.
The stone rises, stops, and falls back along the z axis, landing at the starting point on the floor: P(0,0,0).
keyConcept: With zero horizontal velocity and only gravity acting, motion is purely vertical.
commonMistake: Mixing up the components: the '3' is the vertical speed in m/s, not a coordinate of the landing point.

optionExplanations.1: The trajectory is fully determined: vertical launch, only gravity, so it must land where it started.
optionExplanations.3: P(0,0,3) puts the landing point 3 m above the floor, but 'falling down' means reaching z = 0; the 3 was a speed, not a height.
optionExplanations.4: P(3,0,0) would require a horizontal velocity along x, but vx = 0 at all times.

shortExplanation: The elastic energy is U = (1/2)*k*x^2 = 0.5 * 100 * (0.02)^2 = 0.02 J. The compression must be expressed in meters.
solutionSteps: Convert the compression: x = 2 cm = 0.02 m.
Elastic potential energy: U = (1/2)*k*x^2 = 0.5 * 100 * (0.02)^2.
keyConcept: Elastic potential energy of a spring: U = (1/2)*k*x^2 with x in meters.
commonMistake: Leaving x in centimeters, which inflates the result by a factor of 10^4.

optionExplanations.0: 1 J would need a compression of about 14 cm; it typically results from mixing units (e.g. using x = 2 with k in N/m incorrectly scaled).
optionExplanations.1: 200 J comes from plugging x = 2 (centimeters treated as meters): 0.5*100*4 = 200; the unit conversion is missing.
optionExplanations.3: One of the listed values is indeed correct (0.02 J), so this catch-all option does not apply.

shortExplanation: Empty, the hemisphere floats because the trapped air lowers its average density. Filled with water, its average density is that of shell material plus water, which is greater than water's density, so it sinks to the bottom.
solutionSteps: Floating condition: a body floats if its average density is less than the density of water.
Empty hemisphere: shell (denser than water) + enclosed air gives an average density below that of water, so it floats.
Filled hemisphere: it is now shell material (denser than water) plus water (same density as water), so the average density exceeds that of water.
The buoyant force can never balance the weight, so the hemisphere sinks all the way down.
keyConcept: Archimedes' principle: sinking or floating is decided by the average density of the object compared with water.
commonMistake: Thinking a submerged object can hover partway down: in a uniform liquid, if average density exceeds the liquid's, it sinks to the bottom.

optionExplanations.1: Standing still just below the surface would require the average density to equal exactly that of water, but the shell is strictly denser, so the total is denser than water.
optionExplanations.2: It floated when empty only thanks to the enclosed air; replacing that air with water removes the low-density volume that provided the extra buoyancy.
optionExplanations.3: In water of uniform density the buoyant force on a fully submerged body does not grow with depth, so there is no level at which it would stop before the bottom.

shortExplanation: Kinetic energy is (1/2)*m*v^2; since velocity has dimensions [L][T]^-1, its square is [L]^2[T]^-2, giving [M][L]^2[T]^-2.
solutionSteps: Kinetic energy: E = (1/2)*m*v^2 (the 1/2 is dimensionless).
Dimensions of v: [L][T]^-1, so v^2 has dimensions [L]^2[T]^-2.
Multiply by mass: [E] = [M][L]^2[T]^-2.
keyConcept: Dimensional analysis: energy always has dimensions [M][L]^2[T]^-2 (the joule is kg m^2/s^2).
commonMistake: Writing positive time exponents: dividing by time squared means the exponent of [T] is -2, not +2.

optionExplanations.1: [M][L][T] does not correspond to any standard mechanical quantity and lacks the squared length over squared time structure of v^2.
optionExplanations.2: [M][L]^2[T]^2 has the sign of the time exponent wrong: v^2 = (L/T)^2 divides by T^2.
optionExplanations.4: [M][L][T]^-2 is the dimension of force (mass times acceleration), not of energy.

shortExplanation: In an isothermal transformation P*V is constant: 0.9 bar * V = P2 * 0.9V, so P2 = 1 bar.
solutionSteps: Isothermal ideal-gas transformation (Boyle's law): P1*V1 = P2*V2.
Substitute: 0.9 * V = P2 * 0.9 * V.
Solve: P2 = 0.9/0.9 = 1 bar.
keyConcept: Boyle's law: at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional.
commonMistake: Scaling the pressure down together with the volume; compression at constant T must raise the pressure.

optionExplanations.1: 0.8 bar would mean the pressure drops when the gas is compressed, the opposite of Boyle's law.
optionExplanations.3: 1.2 bar overshoots: the volume shrinks by the factor 0.9, so the pressure rises by exactly 1/0.9, from 0.9 to 1 bar.
optionExplanations.4: The pressure cannot stay 0.9 bar: with T fixed, shrinking V forces P to rise so that P*V stays constant.

formulaNotes: P1*V1 = P2*V2 at constant temperature.

shortExplanation: Without friction the only work to be done against gravity is W = m*g*h, which depends only on the height gained. The two ramps lead to the same floor, so the work is the same.
solutionSteps: Gravity is a conservative force: the work needed to raise a body equals m*g*h, independent of the path.
Both ramps connect the same two floors, so the height difference h is identical.
Ramp B needs a larger pushing force over a shorter distance; ramp A a smaller force over a longer distance; the product (work) is the same.
keyConcept: Against gravity alone, work depends only on the height difference, not on the path taken.
commonMistake: Confusing force with work: the steeper ramp requires a bigger force, but not more work.

optionExplanations.0: The shorter ramp needs a proportionally larger force, so the product force*displacement is unchanged; shortness alone does not reduce the work.
optionExplanations.1: Work is not inversely proportional to displacement; along the longer ramp the required force is smaller in exactly the ratio that keeps the work equal.
optionExplanations.2: The work is not zero: the box gains potential energy m*g*h, which must be supplied by the worker.

formulaNotes: W = m*g*h for any frictionless path between two heights.

shortExplanation: The cross product a x b is perpendicular to both a and b, and the scalar product of perpendicular vectors is zero, so (a x b) . a = 0 for any a and b.
solutionSteps: By definition, a x b is a vector perpendicular to the plane containing a and b.
In particular, (a x b) is perpendicular to a.
The dot product of two perpendicular vectors is zero: (a x b) . a = |a x b|*|a|*cos(90 deg) = 0.
keyConcept: The scalar triple product (a x b) . a vanishes identically because a x b is orthogonal to a.
commonMistake: Believing the components are needed: the result is zero by geometry, independent of the specific vectors.

optionExplanations.0: No components are needed: perpendicularity of a x b to a holds for every pair of vectors, forcing the dot product to zero.
optionExplanations.1: |a|^2 would be the value of a . a, not of (a x b) . a.
optionExplanations.3: |a||b| ignores that the cross product is orthogonal to a, making the cosine of the angle in the dot product zero.

shortExplanation: The horizontal motion does not affect the fall time; only the vertical initial velocity matters. Coin C has the largest upward component (v0y = +5 m/s), so it stays in the air longest.
solutionSteps: Vertical and horizontal motions are independent: the time to reach the floor depends only on v0y (and the common starting height).
Compare vertical components: A has +1 m/s, B has 0, C has +5 m/s, D has +2 m/s.
A larger upward v0y means the coin first rises longer before falling, so the flight time increases with v0y.
Coin C (v0y = +5 m/s) therefore reaches the floor last.
keyConcept: Independence of motions: fall time is governed solely by the vertical component of the initial velocity.
commonMistake: Thinking a larger total speed or horizontal speed prolongs the flight; horizontal velocity has no effect on the fall time.

optionExplanations.0: Coin D goes up with only +2 m/s, less than coin C's +5 m/s, so D lands before C.
optionExplanations.1: Coin B has zero vertical launch speed, so it starts falling immediately and is among the first to land, not the last.
optionExplanations.2: Equal times would hold only if all vertical components were equal; here they range from 0 to +5 m/s.

shortExplanation: Capacitors in parallel share the same voltage V, so each charge is q = C*V. Hence q3/q1 = C3/C1 = 4, that is q3 = 4 q1.
solutionSteps: In parallel, all capacitors have the same potential difference V across them.
Charges: q1 = C1*V, q2 = 2*C1*V, q3 = 4*C1*V.
Ratio: q3 = 4*q1 (and also q2 = 2*q1, q3 = 2*q2).
keyConcept: Parallel connection: equal voltage, so charge is proportional to capacitance.
commonMistake: Applying the series rule (equal charge on every capacitor) to a parallel connection.

optionExplanations.1: q3 = 0.125 q1 would require C3 to be one eighth of C1; in fact C3 is four times larger, so q3 is larger, not smaller.
optionExplanations.3: q2 = 0.5 q1 inverts the proportionality: with double the capacitance at the same voltage, q2 is double q1, not half.
optionExplanations.4: q3 = 2 q1 would be true for C3 = 2C1, but C3 = 4C1, so the charge is four times q1; q3 = 2 q2 instead.

formulaNotes: q = C*V with V common to all parallel branches.

shortExplanation: Losing 120 kJ cools 0.5 kg of water by Delta(T) = Q/(m*c) = 120000/(0.5*4000) = 60 K. Starting from boiling at sea level (100 °C), the final temperature is 100 - 60 = 40 °C.
solutionSteps: At sea level water boils at 100 °C, the initial temperature.
Calorimetry: Q = m*c*Delta(T), so Delta(T) = Q/(m*c).
Half a liter of water has mass m = 0.5 kg; Delta(T) = 120000 J / (0.5 kg * 4000 J/(kg K)) = 60 K.
Final temperature: t2 = 100 °C - 60 °C = 40 °C.
keyConcept: Q = m*c*Delta(T), with the boiling point at sea level (100 °C) as the starting temperature.
commonMistake: Reporting the temperature drop (60 K) or mixing kelvin and Celsius scales instead of subtracting the drop from 100 °C.

optionExplanations.0: About 300 K is roughly 27 °C, which would require a drop of about 73 °C, not the 60 °C computed from Q = m*c*Delta(T).
optionExplanations.3: 20 °C would need an 80 °C drop (160 kJ released); it may come from confusing the drop of 60 with the remaining temperature.
optionExplanations.4: 80 °C corresponds to a drop of only 20 °C, i.e. to a released heat of 40 kJ, not 120 kJ.

formulaNotes: Delta(T) = Q/(m*c); 0.5 L of water = 0.5 kg.

shortExplanation: For fixed distance X = (1/2)*(F/M)*t^2, the time scales as t proportional to 1/sqrt(F). Quadrupling F multiplies the time by 1/sqrt(4) = 1/2, so t2 = t/2.
solutionSteps: Constant force on a frictionless plane gives constant acceleration a = F/M.
Starting from rest: X = (1/2)*a*t^2 = (1/2)*(F/M)*t^2, so t = sqrt(2*X*M/F).
With F' = 4F: t2 = sqrt(2*X*M/(4F)) = t/sqrt(4) = t/2.
keyConcept: At fixed distance from rest, travel time is inversely proportional to the square root of the force.
commonMistake: Assuming time is inversely proportional to the force itself (t/4), forgetting that the distance depends on t^2.

optionExplanations.1: 2t goes the wrong way: a larger force means a larger acceleration and therefore a shorter, not longer, time.
optionExplanations.3: The actual value of F cancels out in the ratio t2/t = sqrt(F/F') = 1/2, so no numerical value of F is needed.
optionExplanations.4: t/4 would follow if X grew linearly with t, but X grows as t^2, so a factor 4 in force gives only a factor 2 in time.

formulaNotes: X = (1/2)*(F/M)*t^2 implies t = sqrt(2*X*M/F), so t scales as F^(-1/2).

shortExplanation: Recycling substitutes already-processed material for virgin raw material, which cuts the energy needed for extraction and primary processing and the associated pollution.
solutionSteps: Producing goods from virgin raw materials requires extraction, transport and energy-intensive primary processing.
Recycled materials skip most of these stages, so less energy is consumed.
Lower energy use and avoided extraction also mean less pollution and fewer emissions.
Hence the benefit of recycled over virgin materials is reduced energy consumption and pollution.
keyConcept: Recycling saves the energy and environmental cost of extracting and processing virgin raw materials.
commonMistake: Assuming recycled input automatically lowers product quality or is only about cost, whereas the primary documented benefit is energy and pollution savings.

optionExplanations.1: Recycling decreases, not increases, overall energy consumption compared with primary production.
optionExplanations.2: Properly recycled materials can meet the same standards; quality reduction is not the point of using them.
optionExplanations.4: Cost effects vary by material and market; the consistent, defining advantage is environmental (energy and pollution).

shortExplanation: The passage opens by stating that with population growth and drought, 'The choice is clear—rethink how we grow food, or starve', i.e. ways of growing food will have to change in the future.
solutionSteps: Locate the claim in the first paragraph: population will rise to 8 billion and drought is predicted.
The stated conclusion is that we must 'rethink how we grow food, or starve'.
Rethinking how food is grown means current farming methods must change in the future.
The rest of the passage (vertical farms as a proposed solution) confirms this reading.
keyConcept: Completing the sentence requires the inference explicitly supported by the passage's opening argument.
commonMistake: Reversing cause and effect: population growth pressures farming methods, not the other way round.

optionExplanations.0: The passage says population growth pressures food production; growing methods do not increase the population.
optionExplanations.2: The passage warns that failing to change methods could lead to starvation; it does not say current methods are sustaining starvation.
optionExplanations.3: Drought is attributed to climate, predicted by climate simulations, not caused by farming methods.

shortExplanation: The drawing uses three coordinate axes forming equal angles of 120 degrees with each other, with parallel edges kept parallel, which is the definition of isometric orthogonal axonometry.
solutionSteps: Look at the reference axes shown beside the roof structure: the three axes meet at one point forming equal angles (120 degrees each).
Note that in the drawing of the structure, parallel edges remain parallel and there is no vanishing point.
A parallel projection with the three axes equally inclined and equally foreshortened is isometric orthogonal axonometry.
Perspective types are excluded because lines do not converge; an elevation is excluded because all three dimensions are visible.
keyConcept: Isometric axonometry: parallel projection with the three axes at 120 degrees and equal scale on each axis.
commonMistake: Confusing axonometry with perspective; in axonometry parallel lines never converge to a vanishing point.

optionExplanations.0: A front elevation shows only one face in true shape with no depth axis, while here three dimensions are visible.
optionExplanations.1: In a central perspective, receding parallel lines converge to a vanishing point, which does not happen here.
optionExplanations.4: An accidental perspective uses two vanishing points, but this drawing keeps all parallel edges parallel.

figureExplanation: The small axis diagram shows three axes at equal 120-degree angles, and the roof structure is drawn with parallel edges staying parallel, identifying an isometric axonometric projection.

shortExplanation: The curve is decreasing with vertical asymptote x = -1, passes through (0, 1) and crosses the x-axis at x = 1, matching y = 1 - log2(x + 1).
solutionSteps: Read the vertical asymptote: the curve shoots up along the dashed line x = -1, so the function contains log2(x + 1).
The curve is decreasing, so the logarithm must appear with a negative sign.
Check the y-intercept for y = 1 - log2(x + 1): at x = 0, y = 1 - log2(1) = 1. The graph passes through (0, 1). Consistent.
Check the x-intercept: y = 0 gives log2(x + 1) = 1, so x + 1 = 2 and x = 1, matching the crossing at x = 1.
Eliminate: y = -log2(x + 1) passes through (0, 0), and the increasing versions rise instead of falling.
keyConcept: A logarithm's vertical asymptote locates the shift (x + 1), while the sign of the log coefficient sets increasing or decreasing behaviour.
commonMistake: Choosing y = -log2(x + 1), which is also decreasing with the same asymptote but passes through the origin instead of (0, 1).

optionExplanations.1: y = 1 + log2(x + 1) is increasing and tends to -infinity at x = -1 from above the axis in the wrong direction.
optionExplanations.2: y = -log2(x + 1) crosses at the origin, but the graph passes through (0, 1) and crosses the x-axis at x = 1.
optionExplanations.3: y = log2(x + 1) is increasing, while the curve shown is decreasing.

figureExplanation: The graph falls from +infinity along the vertical asymptote x = -1, passes through (0, 1), crosses the x-axis at x = 1 and keeps decreasing slowly for larger x.

shortExplanation: A 20 cm segment at 1:100 represents a real length of 20 m; at 1:500 that same length is drawn as 2000/500 = 4 cm.
solutionSteps: Find the real length: at scale 1:100, drawn 20 cm corresponds to 20 * 100 = 2000 cm = 20 m.
Convert to the new scale: at 1:500, drawn length = real length / 500 = 2000/500 cm.
Compute: 2000/500 = 4 cm.
keyConcept: Scale 1:n means drawn length = real length / n; the real object length stays fixed when changing scale.
commonMistake: Multiplying by the ratio of scales in the wrong direction, getting 100 cm (1 m) or dividing 20 cm by 5 incorrectly.

optionExplanations.0: 0.1 m (10 cm) would correspond to dividing by 2, i.e. a scale of 1:200, not 1:500.
optionExplanations.1: 2 cm would represent only 10 m of real length at 1:500, half the actual 20 m.
optionExplanations.3: 0.2 m (20 cm) keeps the drawing unchanged, ignoring that the scale factor changed from 100 to 500.

figureExplanation: The item is a pure scale-conversion question; the page shows only the question text and the answer options, with no diagram needed.
formulaNotes: Drawn length = real length / scale factor: 20 cm * 100 = 2000 cm real; 2000 cm / 500 = 4 cm.

shortExplanation: A 2:1 scale is an enlargement: every real length is drawn twice as large, so 20 cm is represented by 40 cm.
solutionSteps: In a scale written drawing:real, the first number is the drawn length and the second the real length.
Scale 2:1 therefore means 2 cm on the drawing for every 1 cm of the real object.
Drawn length = 20 cm * 2 = 40 cm.
keyConcept: In a scale a:b, drawn length = real length * a/b; when a > b the drawing is an enlargement.
commonMistake: Reading 2:1 backwards as a reduction and dividing by 2 to get 10 cm.

optionExplanations.1: 10 cm would be the result of a 1:2 reduction, the reverse of the given scale.
optionExplanations.2: 200 cm would correspond to a 10:1 enlargement, not 2:1.
optionExplanations.3: 100 cm would correspond to a 5:1 enlargement, not 2:1.

figureExplanation: The item is a plain text question about the 2:1 scale; no drawing features are needed beyond the stated scale.

shortExplanation: The negation of a universal statement is an existential one: if it is false that all flowers are beautiful, then at least one flower must not be beautiful.
solutionSteps: The original claim has the form 'All F are B'.
Its negation is 'Not all F are B', which is logically equivalent to 'There exists at least one F that is not B'.
So the only guaranteed conclusion is that at least one flower is not beautiful.
Nothing follows about all flowers being non-beautiful, nor about no flower being beautiful.
keyConcept: not(for all x, P(x)) is equivalent to (there exists x with not P(x)).
commonMistake: Treating the negation of 'all are' as 'none are' or 'all are not', which are far stronger claims than the falsity of the universal.

optionExplanations.0: Saying all flowers are not beautiful claims every flower fails, but the falsity of the universal only guarantees one counterexample.
optionExplanations.2: Saying no flowers are beautiful is the contrary, not the negation; some flowers could still be beautiful.
optionExplanations.3: A claim about plants in general is a change of subject and does not follow from anything stated about flowers.

shortExplanation: 'Every applying candidate must submit a letter' means there is no case of applying without submitting, so it is equivalent to 'No candidate applies without submitting a recommendation letter'.
solutionSteps: Rewrite the rule as a conditional: if a candidate applies, then that candidate submits a recommendation letter.
A conditional 'if P then Q' is equivalent to 'it is never the case that P and not Q'.
