optionExplanations.1: 150 Hz would correspond to a 2 m wavelength.
optionExplanations.4: 300 Hz ignores the division by the 1.5 m wavelength.

formulaNotes: f = v/lambda = 300/1.5 = 200 Hz.

shortExplanation: A real image twice the object size means the image distance is 60 cm; the lens equation then gives f = 20 cm.
solutionSteps: A real image with magnification magnitude 2 means di = 2 * do = 2 * 30 = 60 cm.
Lens equation: 1/f = 1/do + 1/di.
f = 20 cm.
keyConcept: For a thin lens, |m| = di/do; combine this with 1/f = 1/do + 1/di to find the focal length.
commonMistake: Forgetting to double the object distance to get di, then solving the lens equation with the wrong image distance.

optionExplanations.0: 10 cm would place the object at 3f, producing a smaller image, not one twice the size.
optionExplanations.1: 15 cm would result from using di = 30 cm equal to the object distance.
optionExplanations.4: 30 cm just repeats the object distance; an object at the focal point gives no real image at all.

shortExplanation: Energy (and work) is measured in joules; 1 J is the work done by a force of 1 N acting over 1 m.
solutionSteps: Work and energy share the same unit, defined from W = F*d.
One newton acting through one meter does one newton-meter of work, named the joule.
So the unit of energy is the joule.
keyConcept: 1 joule = 1 newton * 1 meter.
commonMistake: Confusing the joule (energy) with the watt, which measures power, i.e. energy per unit time.

optionExplanations.0: The watt is the unit of power (joules per second), not energy.
optionExplanations.1: The newton is the unit of force.
optionExplanations.3: The volt is the unit of electric potential difference.

shortExplanation: Photon energy grows with frequency (E = h*f), and gamma rays have the highest frequency in the electromagnetic spectrum.
solutionSteps: Photon energy is E = h*f: higher frequency means higher energy.
Order the EM spectrum by increasing frequency: radio < microwave < infrared < visible < ultraviolet < X-rays < gamma rays.
Gamma rays sit at the top, so they carry the highest photon energy.
keyConcept: E = h*f: gamma rays have the highest frequency, shortest wavelength, and highest energy.
commonMistake: Picking ultraviolet because it is famously harmful, though X-rays and gamma rays are far more energetic.

optionExplanations.0: Infrared has a lower frequency than visible light, hence low photon energy.
optionExplanations.1: Radio waves have the lowest frequency and lowest energy of the spectrum.
optionExplanations.2: Ultraviolet is energetic but lies below X-rays and gamma rays in the spectrum.

formulaNotes: E = h*f = h*c/lambda; shorter wavelength means higher energy.

shortExplanation: With the object at twice the focal length (50 cm for f = 25 cm), the image also forms at 50 cm, so the magnification magnitude is di/do = 1.0.
solutionSteps: Lens equation: 1/f = 1/do + 1/di.
Magnification magnitude: |m| = di/do = 50/50 = 1.0.
This is the classic 2f case: object at twice the focal length gives a real, inverted, same-size image.
keyConcept: An object placed at 2f of a convex lens produces an image at 2f with magnification of magnitude 1.
commonMistake: Computing m = f/do = 0.5 or mixing up which distance belongs in the numerator.

optionExplanations.0: 0.33 would describe a strongly reduced image, as for an object much farther than 2f.
optionExplanations.2: 1.5 does not match this geometry; here di and do are exactly equal.
optionExplanations.3: 2.0 would require the image distance to be twice the object distance, which does not happen with the object at 2f.

formulaNotes: 1/f = 1/do + 1/di; |m| = di/do; object at 2f gives di = 2f and |m| = 1.

shortExplanation: Equilibrium means all forces balance, so the net (resultant) force on the object is zero.
solutionSteps: By definition, an object in equilibrium has no acceleration.
Newton's second law, F_net = m*a, then requires F_net = 0.
Individual forces (like weight and the normal force) may be large, but their vector sum is zero.
keyConcept: Equilibrium condition: the vector sum of all forces is zero.
commonMistake: Thinking equilibrium means no forces act at all; forces act but cancel each other exactly.

optionExplanations.1: The net force is not the weight; in equilibrium the weight is cancelled by other forces, leaving zero net force.
optionExplanations.2: A maximum net force would produce maximum acceleration, the opposite of equilibrium.
optionExplanations.3: A changing net force would cause changing acceleration, not equilibrium.

shortExplanation: The newton is built from base units as kg*m/s^2, making it a derived unit; the second, kilogram and ampere are SI base units.
solutionSteps: The SI system has seven base units, including the second (time), kilogram (mass) and ampere (electric current).
A derived unit is any combination of base units.
Force = mass * acceleration, so 1 N = 1 kg*m/s^2, a combination of base units.
Therefore the newton is the derived unit.
keyConcept: Derived units, like the newton (kg*m/s^2), are products or ratios of the seven SI base units.
commonMistake: Assuming the ampere is derived because current relates to charge; in SI the ampere is a base unit and the coulomb is derived.

optionExplanations.0: The second is the SI base unit of time.
optionExplanations.1: The kilogram is the SI base unit of mass.
optionExplanations.3: The ampere is the SI base unit of electric current.

shortExplanation: Newton's second law gives F = m*a = 3 kg * 5 m/s^2 = 15 N.
solutionSteps: Newton's second law: F = m*a.
Substitute: F = 3 kg * 5 m/s^2.
keyConcept: Net force equals mass times acceleration.
commonMistake: Adding the numbers (3 + 5 = 8) instead of multiplying, or swapping in a wrong value for the mass.

optionExplanations.0: 10 N would correspond to a 2 kg mass at this acceleration.
optionExplanations.2: 20 N would need a 4 kg mass at 5 m/s^2 or a 5 kg mass at 4 m/s^2.
optionExplanations.4: 30 N doubles the correct product, as if the mass were 6 kg.

shortExplanation: Work is force times displacement along the force: W = F*d = 10 N * 5 m = 50 J.
solutionSteps: Work done by a constant force along the motion: W = F*d.
Substitute: W = 10 N * 5 m.
W = 50 J. The 2 kg mass is extra information; work depends only on the force and the displacement.
keyConcept: W = F*d for a force applied along the direction of motion.
commonMistake: Trying to involve the mass (e.g. multiplying by 2 kg); the mass is irrelevant when force and distance are given.

optionExplanations.0: 20 J would come from wrongly using mass times distance (2*10) instead of force times distance.
optionExplanations.2: 40 J does not match any correct combination of the given force and displacement.
optionExplanations.4: 60 J would require a 12 N force or a 6 m displacement.

formulaNotes: W = F*d*cos(theta); here theta = 0, so W = 10*5 = 50 J.

shortExplanation: With the full 12 V across the 3 Ohm resistor, the dissipated power is P = V^2/R = 144/3 = 48 W.
solutionSteps: The resistor is connected directly to the battery, so the voltage across it is V = 12 V.
Use the power formula P = V^2/R.
Compute V^2 = 12^2 = 144.
Divide by the resistance: P = 144/3 = 48 W, matching the 48 W option.
keyConcept: Power dissipated in a resistor: P = V^2/R (equivalently P = I^2*R = V*I).
commonMistake: Computing the current I = 12/3 = 4 A and then multiplying incorrectly, landing on 12 W or 36 W.

optionExplanations.0: 12 W would follow from treating V/R-type reasoning as power; the correct formula squares the voltage.
optionExplanations.1: 24 W would be V*I/2; there is no factor of one half in resistive power dissipation.
optionExplanations.2: 36 W comes from computing 12*3; P = I^2*R gives 4^2*3 = 48 W, not 36 W.

formulaNotes: P = V^2/R; also P = V*I with I = V/R = 12/3 = 4 A, so P = 12*4 = 48 W.

shortExplanation: Each parallel branch has 8 V across it, so the branch currents are 8/2 = 4 A and 8/4 = 2 A; the battery supplies their sum, 6 A.
solutionSteps: In a parallel circuit, every branch sees the same voltage, here 8 V.
Current through the 2 Ohm resistor: I1 = 8/2 = 4 A.
Current through the 4 Ohm resistor: I2 = 8/4 = 2 A.
The total current from the battery is the sum of branch currents: I = 4 + 2 = 6 A.
keyConcept: In parallel circuits, the voltage is the same across each branch and branch currents add up to the total.
commonMistake: Adding the resistances (2 + 4 = 6 Ohm) as if they were in series and computing 8/6 A.

optionExplanations.0: 2 A is only the current in the 4 Ohm branch, not the total supplied by the battery.
optionExplanations.1: 4 A is only the current in the 2 Ohm branch; the 4 Ohm branch's 2 A must be added.
optionExplanations.3: 8 A would require a combined resistance of 1 Ohm, but the parallel combination of 2 Ohm and 4 Ohm is 4/3 Ohm.

shortExplanation: Capacitance is measured in farads: one farad equals one coulomb of stored charge per volt.
solutionSteps: Capacitance is defined as C = Q/V, charge stored per unit potential difference.
The SI unit of charge is the coulomb and of potential the volt, so capacitance is measured in coulombs per volt.
One coulomb per volt is named the farad.
keyConcept: The farad (F) is the SI unit of capacitance: 1 F = 1 C/V.
commonMistake: Confusing the unit of charge (coulomb) with the unit of the quantity that stores charge (farad).

optionExplanations.0: The ampere is the unit of electric current, charge flow per second.
optionExplanations.1: The coulomb is the unit of electric charge, which a capacitor stores, not the unit of capacitance itself.
optionExplanations.3: The ohm is the unit of electrical resistance, not capacitance.

shortExplanation: Using v = f*lambda, the frequency is f = v/lambda = 340/0.85 = 400 Hz.
solutionSteps: Write the wave equation v = f*lambda.
Solve for frequency: f = v/lambda.
Substitute the values: f = 340/0.85.
Compute: 340/0.85 = 400, so f = 400 Hz, matching the 400 Hz option.
keyConcept: Wave equation: speed = frequency * wavelength (v = f*lambda).
commonMistake: Multiplying speed by wavelength or misplacing the decimal when dividing by 0.85.

optionExplanations.0: 200 Hz would give a wavelength of 1.7 m, twice the stated value.
optionExplanations.1: 300 Hz would require a wavelength of about 1.13 m at 340 m/s, not 0.85 m.
optionExplanations.3: 500 Hz would correspond to a wavelength of 0.68 m, shorter than the given 0.85 m.

formulaNotes: f = v/lambda = 340 m/s / 0.85 m = 400 Hz.

shortExplanation: Wave speed is frequency times wavelength: v = 4 Hz * 2 m = 8 m/s.
solutionSteps: Recall the wave equation v = f*lambda.
Substitute f = 4 Hz and lambda = 2 m.
Multiply: v = 4 * 2 = 8 m/s, matching the 8 m/s option.
keyConcept: Wave equation: v = f*lambda.
commonMistake: Dividing frequency by wavelength (4/2 = 2) or adding them (4 + 2 = 6) instead of multiplying.

optionExplanations.0: 4 m/s would only be correct if the wavelength were 1 m.
optionExplanations.1: 6 m/s is the result of adding 4 and 2; the wave equation multiplies frequency and wavelength.
optionExplanations.4: 12 m/s would require a wavelength of 3 m at 4 Hz.

formulaNotes: v = f*lambda = 4 * 2 = 8 m/s.

shortExplanation: Violet light has the shortest wavelength of the listed colors, so it has the highest refractive index in glass and is bent the most by a prism.
solutionSteps: In glass, the refractive index increases as the wavelength of light decreases.
Of the visible colors, violet has the shortest wavelength and red the longest.
A higher refractive index means a larger deviation at each prism surface.
Therefore violet is deviated the most and red the least.
keyConcept: Dispersion: shorter wavelength -> higher refractive index in glass -> greater bending.
commonMistake: Choosing blue because it is often drawn at the edge of the spectrum; violet has an even shorter wavelength and bends more.

optionExplanations.0: Red has the longest wavelength and the lowest refractive index, so it is bent the least.
optionExplanations.1: Green lies in the middle of the visible spectrum and is deviated by an intermediate amount.
optionExplanations.2: Blue bends strongly but has a slightly longer wavelength than violet, so it deviates a little less.

shortExplanation: Dispersion occurs because different colors travel at slightly different speeds inside the glass, so each color has a slightly different refractive index and is bent by a different angle.
solutionSteps: In vacuum all colors travel at the same speed, but inside glass the speed depends on wavelength.
The refractive index n = c/v is therefore different for each color.
By Snell's law, a different index means a different refraction angle at the prism surfaces.
The colors emerge at different angles, spreading white light into a spectrum.
keyConcept: Dispersion arises because the refractive index (and hence light's speed in the medium) depends on wavelength.
commonMistake: Attributing the spectrum to reflection or absorption inside the prism instead of wavelength-dependent refraction.

optionExplanations.0: Absorption removes light energy; it does not split white light into a spectrum.
optionExplanations.2: Reflection changes direction but does not separate colors; the separation comes from refraction, not reflection.
optionExplanations.3: Pressure plays no role in how a prism separates colors.

shortExplanation: Power is energy per unit time; energy has dimensions ML^2T^-2, so dividing by time gives ML^2T^-3.
solutionSteps: Power = Work / time.
Work = force * distance; force has dimensions MLT^-2, so work has dimensions MLT^-2 * L = ML^2T^-2.
Divide by time T: ML^2T^-2 / T = ML^2T^-3.
keyConcept: Build dimensions step by step: force MLT^-2, work ML^2T^-2, power ML^2T^-3.
commonMistake: Stopping at the dimensions of energy (ML^2T^-2) and forgetting to divide by time.

optionExplanations.0: MLT^-1 is the dimension of momentum.
optionExplanations.1: ML^2T^-2 is the dimension of energy or work, not power.
optionExplanations.3: MLT^-2 is the dimension of force.

shortExplanation: Since KE depends on m to the first power and v squared, the maximum percentage error is 2% + 2*3% = 8%.
solutionSteps: KE = (1/2) m v^2, so the fractional error is dKE/KE = dm/m + 2*(dv/v).
The constant 1/2 contributes no error.
Substitute the percentages: 2% + 2*3% = 2% + 6% = 8%.
keyConcept: In a product of powers, percentage errors add weighted by each exponent.
commonMistake: Adding the errors directly (2% + 3% = 5%) and forgetting to double the speed error because v is squared.

optionExplanations.0: 5% comes from adding 2% and 3% without accounting for the square on v.
optionExplanations.3: 6% counts only the doubled speed error and ignores the mass error.

formulaNotes: For KE = (1/2)mv^2: %error(KE) = %error(m) + 2*%error(v)

shortExplanation: Electric potential is energy per unit charge, a pure number with magnitude only, so it is a scalar; the other listed quantities all have direction.
solutionSteps: Electric field is force per unit charge and points in a definite direction, so it is a vector.
Impulse equals force times time, inheriting the direction of the force, so it is a vector.
Current density describes the direction and magnitude of charge flow per area, so it is a vector.
Electric potential is work per unit charge, defined by magnitude alone, so it is a scalar.
keyConcept: A scalar has only magnitude; potential (energy per charge) needs no direction to be specified.
commonMistake: Confusing electric potential (scalar) with the electric field (vector) because both describe the same region of space.

optionExplanations.0: The electric field has a direction at every point, making it a vector.
optionExplanations.1: Impulse is force times time and points along the applied force, so it is a vector.
optionExplanations.2: Current density has both magnitude and the direction of charge flow, so it is a vector.

shortExplanation: The particle is at rest when its velocity dx/dt = 6t − 12 equals zero, which happens at t = 2 s.
solutionSteps: Velocity is the time derivative of position: v(t) = dx/dt.
Differentiate x(t) = 3t^2 − 12t + 5 to get v(t) = 6t − 12.
Solve: t = 2 s.
keyConcept: Momentary rest means velocity (the derivative of position) is zero, not position.
commonMistake: Setting the position x(t) equal to zero instead of the velocity.

optionExplanations.0: At t = 1 s the velocity is 6*1 − 12 = −6 m/s, so the particle is still moving.
optionExplanations.2: At t = 3 s the velocity is 6*3 − 12 = +6 m/s, already moving in the positive direction again.

formulaNotes: v(t) = dx/dt = 6t − 12; v = 0 at t = 2 s

shortExplanation: The object takes v/g = 20/10 = 2 s to reach the top and the same time to fall back, for a total of 4 s.
solutionSteps: Time to reach the highest point: at the top v = 0, so t_up = v0/g = 20/10 = 2 s.
By symmetry the fall back to the launch height takes the same time: t_down = 2 s.
Total time in the air: 2 + 2 = 4 s.
Check with y(t) = 20t − 5t^2 = 0, giving t = 0 or t = 4 s.
keyConcept: For vertical launch and return to the same height, total flight time is 2*v0/g.
commonMistake: Computing only the time to the highest point (2 s) and forgetting the descent.

optionExplanations.0: 2 s is only the time to reach the peak, not the full flight.
optionExplanations.2: 6 s would require an initial speed of 30 m/s with g = 10 m/s^2.

shortExplanation: In a constant-volume process the gas does no work (W = p*dV = 0), so by the first law of thermodynamics all heat supplied goes into internal energy: Q = ΔU.
solutionSteps: An isochoric process means the volume stays constant, so dV = 0.
Work done by the gas is W = integral of p dV = 0 when the volume does not change.
Apply the first law: Q = ΔU + W.
With W = 0, this reduces to Q = ΔU: the heat supplied equals the change in internal energy.
keyConcept: First law of thermodynamics with W = 0 at constant volume: Q = ΔU.
commonMistake: Confusing isochoric (constant volume) with isothermal (constant temperature), which is the case where internal energy stays constant.

optionExplanations.0: With no volume change the gas cannot do work, so the work is zero, not positive.
optionExplanations.1: Internal energy is constant only in an isothermal process; here the temperature (and hence U) changes as heat is added.
optionExplanations.3: At constant volume, adding heat raises the temperature and therefore the pressure changes (p/T = constant).

formulaNotes: Q = ΔU + W; isochoric: W = 0, so Q = ΔU

shortExplanation: Carnot efficiency is 1 − T_cold/T_hot = 1 − 300/400 = 0.25 = 25%.
solutionSteps: Write the Carnot efficiency formula: eta = 1 − T_sink/T_source (temperatures in kelvin).
Substitute: eta = 1 − 300/400.
Convert to a percentage: 25%.
keyConcept: Carnot efficiency eta = 1 − T_c/T_h with absolute (kelvin) temperatures.
commonMistake: Computing T_c/T_h = 75% and forgetting to subtract it from 1.

optionExplanations.0: 75% is the ratio 300/400 itself, not 1 minus that ratio.
optionExplanations.1: 33% would come from the incorrect ratio (400−300)/300 instead of dividing the difference by the source temperature.
optionExplanations.3: 100% efficiency is impossible for any heat engine operating between two finite temperatures.

shortExplanation: Bernoulli's principle states that along a horizontal streamline, higher fluid speed corresponds to lower pressure, so the pressure decreases.
solutionSteps: Write Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal pipe (constant height): p + (1/2)*rho*v^2 = constant.
If the speed v increases, the term (1/2)*rho*v^2 increases.
Since the sum must stay constant, the pressure p must decrease.
keyConcept: Bernoulli: p + (1/2)*rho*v^2 = constant along a horizontal streamline; speed up means pressure down.
commonMistake: Intuitively assuming faster flow 'pushes harder' and therefore has higher pressure.

optionExplanations.0: Pressure increasing with speed contradicts energy conservation along the streamline.
optionExplanations.2: Pressure can stay constant only if the speed does not change.
optionExplanations.3: The diameter influences the speed via continuity, but the pressure change is governed by the speed change, not by diameter alone.

formulaNotes: p + (1/2)*rho*v^2 = constant (horizontal flow)

solutionSteps: Write Newton's law of gravitation: F = G*m1*m2/r^2.
Compute the mass product and distance squared: 25 / 4 = 6.25.
keyConcept: Newton's law of universal gravitation: F = G*m1*m2/r^2.
commonMistake: Forgetting to square the distance (dividing by 2 instead of 4), which doubles the result.

optionExplanations.1: 8.34*10^-10 N results from dividing by r = 2 instead of r^2 = 4.
optionExplanations.2: 1.67*10^-9 N results from omitting the division by r^2 entirely (6.67*10^-11 * 25).
optionExplanations.3: 3.34*10^-9 N results from both omitting r^2 and doubling, which has no physical basis here.

shortExplanation: The buoyant force equals the weight of displaced liquid, which depends only on the immersed volume. A and B have equal volumes, so they receive equal buoyant forces regardless of their masses.
solutionSteps: Archimedes' principle: F_b = rho_liquid * g * V_displaced.
Both bodies are completely immersed and have the same volume V, so V_displaced is the same for both.
The liquid density and g are the same in both cases.
Therefore F_b(A) = F_b(B): the masses (and hence weights) of the bodies are irrelevant to the buoyant force.
keyConcept: Buoyant force depends on displaced fluid volume and fluid density, never on the mass of the immersed body.
commonMistake: Assuming a heavier body feels a larger buoyant force; mass affects the net motion (sinking or floating), not the buoyant force itself.

optionExplanations.1: There is no squared dependence on anything here; buoyancy is linear in displaced volume only.
optionExplanations.2: Tripling the mass triples the weight, not the buoyant force, since displaced volume is unchanged.
optionExplanations.4: One third would wrongly scale buoyancy inversely with mass; buoyancy does not involve the body's mass at all.

formulaNotes: F_b = rho_liquid * g * V; equal V implies equal F_b.

shortExplanation: After t seconds the speed is v = gt, and with mass m = P/g the kinetic energy is (1/2)(P/g)(gt)^2 = (1/2)Pgt^2.
solutionSteps: The body starts from rest, so after t seconds its speed is v = g*t.
Its weight is P = m*g, hence its mass is m = P/g.
Kinetic energy: KE = (1/2) m v^2 = (1/2) * (P/g) * (g*t)^2.
Check units: P (newtons) * g (m/s^2) * t^2 (s^2) gives N*m = joules, as required for energy.
keyConcept: Express mass through weight (m = P/g), then substitute v = gt into KE = (1/2)mv^2.
commonMistake: Treating the weight P as if it were the mass, or forgetting to square either g or t when substituting v = gt.

optionExplanations.0: (1/2)Pgt has units of N*m/s * s = N*m only if t appears squared; with a single t it is not an energy over time consistent with v = gt.
optionExplanations.3: 2Pgt^2 has the wrong numeric factor; the 1/2 from the kinetic energy formula must survive.
optionExplanations.4: (1/2)Pg^2t^2 keeps an extra factor of g: one g cancels with the 1/g from the mass.

formulaNotes: KE = (1/2)mv^2, m = P/g, v = gt -> KE = (1/2)Pgt^2. Equivalently KE equals work done by gravity: P * h with h = (1/2)gt^2.

shortExplanation: Efficiency is work out over heat in, so Q = W/eta = 3.6 kJ / 0.75 = 4.8 kJ.
solutionSteps: Efficiency definition: eta = W / Q_absorbed.
Solve for the absorbed heat: Q_absorbed = W / eta.
Substitute: Q_absorbed = 3.6 kJ / 0.75 = 4.8 kJ.
Sanity check: the absorbed heat must exceed the work output, and 4.8 kJ > 3.6 kJ.
keyConcept: eta = W/Q means the heat absorbed is always larger than the work delivered for eta < 1.
commonMistake: Multiplying instead of dividing by the efficiency, which gives 2.7 kJ, an absorbed heat smaller than the work output, which is impossible.

optionExplanations.0: 2.7 kJ comes from computing W * eta; heat absorbed can never be less than the work produced.
optionExplanations.2: 14.4 kJ would correspond to an efficiency of 25%, not 75%.
optionExplanations.4: 3.6 kJ would require a 100% efficient engine, contradicting the stated 75%.

shortExplanation: Sound is a mechanical (elastic) wave: it needs a material medium to propagate, and its speed is a property of that medium (about 340 m/s in air, faster in water and solids).
solutionSteps: Sound consists of pressure oscillations transmitted by particles of a medium, so it is a mechanical/elastic wave.
Because it relies on particle interactions, sound cannot travel in vacuum.
Its speed depends on the medium's elastic properties and density: roughly 340 m/s in air, about 1500 m/s in water, and several km/s in solids.
The only description matching all of this is: a wave propagating in an elastic medium with a medium-dependent speed.
keyConcept: Mechanical waves require a medium and travel at a speed set by that medium; only electromagnetic waves travel in vacuum.
commonMistake: Attributing to sound either propagation in vacuum or the speed of light (300 000 km/s), which belong to electromagnetic waves.

optionExplanations.1: No elastic wave can propagate in vacuum; 340 m/s is only the speed of sound in air.
optionExplanations.2: 300 000 km/s is the speed of light, about a million times faster than sound in air.
optionExplanations.4: Sound cannot travel in vacuum, and even in material media its speed varies with the medium instead of being fixed at 340 m/s.

shortExplanation: The equilibrium temperature is the mass-weighted average: (60*20 + 20*60)/(60+20) = 2400/80 = 30 degrees C.
solutionSteps: Both liquids are water, so they have the same specific heat and it cancels out.
Heat lost by hot water equals heat gained by cold water: 60*(T - 20) = 20*(60 - T).
Collect terms: 80T = 2400, so T = 30 degrees C.
Check plausibility: with three times more cold water, the result must lie much closer to 20 than to 60, and 30 does.
keyConcept: For equal specific heats, the final temperature is the average of the initial temperatures weighted by the masses (volumes) of water.
commonMistake: Taking the plain average (40 degrees C) and ignoring that there is three times as much cold water as hot water.

optionExplanations.0: 25 degrees C would need a cold-to-hot ratio of 7:1, not the actual 3:1.
optionExplanations.2: 40 degrees C is the unweighted average of 20 and 60, valid only for equal amounts of water.
optionExplanations.4: 35 degrees C overweights the hot water; the correct weights are 60 parts cold to 20 parts hot.

shortExplanation: Only a body carrying the same sign of charge as the rod can be repelled, so B must be positively charged; A's attraction proves nothing definite, since both a negative and a neutral sphere are attracted by induction.
solutionSteps: The rod is positively charged and never touches the spheres.

Sphere A is attracted: this happens if A is negatively charged, but ALSO if A is neutral, because the rod induces charge separation in the metal and the nearer (negative) side is attracted more strongly.
So A's behavior is inconclusive: A is negative or neutral.
Sphere B is repelled: induction on a neutral conductor always produces net attraction, never repulsion, so B cannot be neutral.
Repulsion requires a net charge of the same sign as the rod: B must be positively charged.
keyConcept: Repulsion is the only conclusive test of charge: attraction can be caused by opposite charge or by induction on a neutral conductor.
commonMistake: Concluding that A must be negatively charged; a neutral metallic sphere is also attracted to a charged rod through induced polarization.

optionExplanations.0: B cannot be neutral, because a neutral conductor is attracted (by induction), never repelled.
optionExplanations.3: It reverses the certainty: it is B, not A, whose charge is determined; B cannot be neutral.
optionExplanations.4: The claim about B is right, but A being negative is not certain: A could be neutral and still be attracted.

shortExplanation: The scalar projection of a on b is |a|cos(theta), and since a . b = |a||b|cos(theta), dividing the scalar product by |b| gives exactly that projection.
solutionSteps: The magnitude of the projection of a on b is |a| * cos(theta), where theta is the angle between the vectors.
The scalar product gives a . b = |a| * |b| * cos(theta).
Divide by |b|: (a . b)/|b| = |a| * cos(theta), which is the desired projection.
The vector product is unsuitable: |a x b| = |a||b|sin(theta) involves the sine, related to the perpendicular component and areas, not projections.
keyConcept: Scalar projection of a on b = (a . b)/|b| = |a| cos(theta).
commonMistake: Using the vector (cross) product, which measures the perpendicular component via sin(theta), or forgetting to divide the scalar product by |b|.

optionExplanations.0: The cross product divided by |b| gives |a|sin(theta) in magnitude (and is a vector), which is the perpendicular component, not the projection.
optionExplanations.2: The scalar product alone equals |a||b|cos(theta); it still contains the factor |b| and has the wrong dimensions for a projection length.
optionExplanations.3: The sum of the two vectors is a vector with no relation to a projection length.

formulaNotes: a . b = |a||b|cos(theta) -> projection of a on b = (a . b)/|b|.

shortExplanation: At 144 km/h = 40 m/s, each wheel of circumference pi*0.8 m ~ 2.51 m rolls 40/2.51 ~ 16 turns per second.
solutionSteps: Convert the speed: 144 km/h = 144/3.6 = 40 m/s.
With perfect rolling, in one wheel turn the train advances one circumference: C = pi * d = pi * 0.80 m ~ 2.51 m.
Turns per second = distance per second / circumference = 40 / 2.51 ~ 15.9.
Rounded, the wheels make about 16 turns per second.
keyConcept: Rolling without sliding links speed and rotation: v = C * f, so f = v/(pi*d).
commonMistake: Using the diameter (or the radius) instead of the circumference pi*d as the distance covered per turn.

optionExplanations.0: 8 corresponds to doubling the circumference, as if one turn covered 2*pi*d ~ 5 m.
optionExplanations.1: 57 arises from mixing units, for instance keeping km/h with meters.
optionExplanations.2: 32 comes from using half the circumference, e.g. treating the radius formula incorrectly, since 40/(pi*0.4) ~ 32.

shortExplanation: The idiom 'paving the way' means preparing conditions so that something can happen more easily, i.e. making it easier.
solutionSteps: Literally, paving a road lays a smooth surface so the road can be travelled more easily.
Figuratively, 'paving the way for something' means creating the conditions that make that thing possible or easier.
Only 'making it easier' captures this facilitating, preparatory sense.
The remaining choices describe hindering, instructing, contrasting, or illustrating, none of which fit the idiom.
keyConcept: 'Paving the way for X' = preparing the conditions that facilitate or enable X.
commonMistake: Reading 'way' as 'method' and choosing 'indicating the method'; the idiom is about easing something's arrival, not describing how to do it.

optionExplanations.0: 'Blocking the future' is the opposite of the idiom's enabling meaning.
optionExplanations.1: The expression does not point out a procedure; it describes clearing obstacles so something can happen.
optionExplanations.4: 'Giving an example' is illustrative, whereas paving the way is preparatory and enabling.

shortExplanation: Every square is a rectangle and every rectangle is a parallelogram, so the three sets form a chain of strict inclusions, drawn as three nested ovals: Figure 2.
solutionSteps: Establish the set relations: a square is a rectangle with equal sides, so squares are a proper subset of rectangles.
A rectangle is a parallelogram with right angles, so rectangles are a proper subset of parallelograms.
A chain of inclusions (squares inside rectangles inside parallelograms) is represented by three concentric ovals, one inside the other.
Figure 2 is the only diagram with three fully nested ovals, so it is the correct one.
keyConcept: Nested Euler diagrams represent chains of class inclusion: subset inside subset inside superset.
commonMistake: Treating squares and rectangles as merely overlapping classes; in fact every square is already a rectangle, so their ovals must be nested, not intersecting.

optionExplanations.0: Figure 1 shows two separate small ovals inside a large one, which would mean squares and rectangles are disjoint classes, but every square is a rectangle.
optionExplanations.2: Figure 3 shows three disjoint ovals, which would mean no square is a rectangle and no rectangle is a parallelogram.
optionExplanations.3: Figure 4 shows two partially overlapping ovals inside a larger one, which would mean only some squares are rectangles.

figureExplanation: Among the five numbered diagrams, only Figure 2 consists of three ovals nested one inside the other, matching the inclusion chain squares within rectangles within parallelograms.

shortExplanation: The rule says: more than 300 pupils implies gym and infirmary. Its contrapositive is certainly true: if a school lacks a gym (so it lacks 'gym and infirmary'), it cannot have more than 300 pupils, i.e. it has at most 300.
solutionSteps: Formalize the rule: pupils > 300 => (gym AND infirmary).
A conditional is logically equivalent to its contrapositive: NOT(gym AND infirmary) => pupils <= 300.
If a school doesn't have a gym, then 'gym AND infirmary' is false.
Therefore that school cannot have more than 300 pupils: it has 300 pupils at the most.
keyConcept: A conditional statement is equivalent to its contrapositive, not to its converse or inverse.
commonMistake: Reading the rule backwards (converse): having a gym or an infirmary does not tell you anything about the number of pupils.

optionExplanations.0: Nothing guarantees such a school exists; the rule only constrains schools with more than 300 pupils.
optionExplanations.3: The rule links pupil numbers to facilities; it never states that a gym implies an infirmary, since a small school could have a gym only.
optionExplanations.4: This is the converse: an infirmary is required for large schools, but small schools may also have one.

shortExplanation: Tracking the pile through the three moves: An,Bo,Ch,Di,El -> Ch,Di,El,An,Bo -> El,An,Bo,Ch,Di -> Bo,Ch,Di,El,An, so book An ends at the bottom.
solutionSteps: Start (top to bottom): An, Bo, Ch, Di, El.
Move 1: take the bottom three (Ch, Di, El) to the top keeping their order: Ch, Di, El, An, Bo.
Move 2: bottom three are El, An, Bo; move them up: El, An, Bo, Ch, Di.
Move 3: bottom three are Bo, Ch, Di; move them up: Bo, Ch, Di, El, An.
After the third move the bottom book is An.
keyConcept: Simulate the rearrangement step by step, rewriting the full order after each move.
commonMistake: Reversing the order of the three moved books, or applying the move only twice instead of three times.

optionExplanations.1: El is at the bottom only in the starting pile; after the first move it is no longer last.
optionExplanations.2: Di is at the bottom after the second move, not after the third.
optionExplanations.3: Bo ends at the top of the final pile, not the bottom.

shortExplanation: All Engineering students are diligent and Charlie is not diligent, so Charlie cannot be an Engineering student; nothing can be concluded about John, since diligence does not imply enrollment.
solutionSteps: Premise: every Engineering student is diligent (Engineering => diligent).
Charlie is not diligent; by contraposition, Charlie is not an Engineering student.
John is diligent, but the premise does not say all diligent people are Engineering students, so John's enrollment is undetermined.
The winter trip to the mountains gives no information about study habits in other seasons.
The only certain deduction is that Charlie isn't an Engineering student.
keyConcept: From 'all X are Y' and 'not Y', conclude 'not X'; but 'Y' alone does not give 'X'.
commonMistake: Affirming the consequent: assuming John must be an Engineering student just because he is diligent.

optionExplanations.1: The premises mention winter only; nothing follows about what John and Charlie do in summer.
optionExplanations.2: The first half is correct but the claim about John is unwarranted, making the whole conjunction not deducible.
optionExplanations.4: Diligence is necessary for Engineering students, not sufficient: a diligent person may study anything or nothing.

shortExplanation: A positive product of 12 nonzero integers requires an even number of negative factors, so the positive factors number 12 minus an even number, which is again even (possibly zero counts as even too).
solutionSteps: A product of integers is positive only if no factor is zero and the count of negative factors is even.
Let k be the number of negative factors: k is even (0, 2, 4, ..., 12).
The number of positive factors is 12 - k, and 12 minus an even number is even.
Hence the number of positive factors is necessarily even (with zero being possible, e.g. all 12 factors negative).
The other statements describe possible but not necessary sign distributions.
keyConcept: Sign of a product: positive iff the number of negative factors is even (and no factor is zero).
commonMistake: Assuming a positive product forces at least some specific number of negative or positive factors, when many even distributions work.

optionExplanations.0: All factors positive is one possibility, not a necessity: two negatives and ten positives also give a positive product.
optionExplanations.1: Zero negative factors (all positive) also yields a positive product, so at least two negatives is not required.
optionExplanations.3: Six and six is just one admissible split; it is not forced by the information given.

shortExplanation: Testing the sign pattern minus, plus, plus, plus, minus: -14 + 15 + 13 + 12 - 10 = 16, which matches the target.
solutionSteps: The numbers in order are 14, 15, 13, 12, 10 and the target is +16.
Check the alternatives: + + - - - gives 14+15-13-12-10 = -6; - - - + + gives -20; + + - - + gives 14; + - + - + gives 10.
Only the pattern minus, plus, plus, plus, minus produces +16.
keyConcept: Evaluate each candidate sign sequence by running the sum left to right.
commonMistake: Arithmetic slips when accumulating the running total, especially with consecutive subtractions.

optionExplanations.0: Plus, plus, minus, minus, minus gives 14 + 15 - 13 - 12 - 10 = -6, not 16.
optionExplanations.3: Plus, plus, minus, minus, plus gives 14 + 15 - 13 - 12 + 10 = 14, close but not 16.
optionExplanations.4: Plus, minus, plus, minus, plus gives 14 - 15 + 13 - 12 + 10 = 10, not 16.

shortExplanation: Substituting t = x^3 turns the equation into a perfect square, (2t - 3)^2 = 0, so t = 3/2 is the only value, and x^3 = 3/2 has exactly one real solution.
solutionSteps: Rewrite the equation with all terms on one side: 4x^6 - 12x^3 + 9 = 0.
Substitute t = x^3, giving the quadratic 4t^2 - 12t + 9 = 0.
Compute the discriminant: (-12)^2 - 4*4*9 = 144 - 144 = 0, so the quadratic is a perfect square: (2t - 3)^2 = 0.
The only solution is t = 3/2, i.e. x^3 = 3/2.
Every real number has exactly one real cube root, so x = (3/2)^(1/3) is the unique real solution.
keyConcept: A degree-6 equation in x^3 reduces to a quadratic by substitution; a real cube root is unique.
commonMistake: Assuming a degree-6 equation must have six (or at least two) real solutions; the degree only bounds the number of solutions.

optionExplanations.0: Six distinct real solutions is impossible here: the quadratic in x^3 has a double root, giving a single value of x^3.
optionExplanations.2: Two real solutions would need two distinct values of x^3 or an even-power root; x^3 = 3/2 yields only one real x.
optionExplanations.3: Degree six does not make an equation unsolvable; substitution reduces it to a quadratic that is solved directly.

shortExplanation: Rationalizing the denominator by multiplying numerator and denominator by (sqrt(2) - 1) gives x = 2 - sqrt(2).
solutionSteps: Start from x = sqrt(2)/(sqrt(2) + 1).
Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate (sqrt(2) - 1): x = sqrt(2)(sqrt(2) - 1) / ((sqrt(2) + 1)(sqrt(2) - 1)).
The denominator becomes 2 - 1 = 1.
The numerator becomes sqrt(2)*sqrt(2) - sqrt(2) = 2 - sqrt(2).
Therefore x = 2 - sqrt(2), about 0.586, which matches the value of the original fraction (1.414/2.414 is about 0.586).
keyConcept: Rationalize a denominator of the form sqrt(a) + b by multiplying by its conjugate sqrt(a) - b.
commonMistake: Sign errors when expanding sqrt(2)(sqrt(2) - 1), which lead to 2 + sqrt(2) instead of 2 - sqrt(2).

optionExplanations.1: 2 + sqrt(2) is about 3.41, but the original fraction is clearly less than 1 since its numerator is smaller than its denominator.
optionExplanations.2: x is about 0.586, an irrational number, so it is not an integer.
optionExplanations.3: (sqrt(2) + 1)/2 is about 1.21, again larger than 1, so it cannot equal a fraction with numerator smaller than denominator.

formulaNotes: (sqrt(a) + b)(sqrt(a) - b) = a - b^2; here (sqrt(2) + 1)(sqrt(2) - 1) = 2 - 1 = 1.

shortExplanation: The tourist gets 3900 NOK, spends 3000 NOK, and converts the remaining 900 NOK back at 0.12 EUR per NOK, obtaining 108 EUR.
solutionSteps: Convert to NOK: 500 EUR * 7.8 NOK/EUR = 3900 NOK.
Subtract the spending: 3900 - 3000 = 900 NOK remaining.
The return rate 10 NOK = 1.2 EUR means 1 NOK = 0.12 EUR.
Convert back: 900 NOK * 0.12 EUR/NOK = 108 EUR.
keyConcept: Currency conversion is multiplication by the exchange rate; note the two rates differ between the trips.
commonMistake: Reusing the first rate (1 EUR = 7.8 NOK) for the return conversion, which would give about 115 EUR instead of applying the new rate.

optionExplanations.1: 90 EUR comes from wrongly using a rate of 10 NOK = 1 EUR on the way back, ignoring the 1.2 factor.
optionExplanations.2: 120 EUR would need 1000 NOK left over, but only 900 NOK remain after spending 3000 of the 3900.
optionExplanations.4: 100 EUR would require a round rate of 9 NOK per EUR at the end, which is not what is given.

shortExplanation: By the double-angle identity, cos^2(a) - sin^2(a) = cos(2a); with a = 7pi/8 this is cos(7pi/4) = sqrt(2)/2.
solutionSteps: Recognize the double-angle identity: cos^2(a) - sin^2(a) = cos(2a).
Set a = 7pi/8, so the expression equals cos(2 * 7pi/8) = cos(7pi/4).
7pi/4 lies in the fourth quadrant, where cosine is positive, and cos(7pi/4) = cos(-pi/4) = cos(pi/4).
Therefore the value is sqrt(2)/2.
keyConcept: Double-angle identity cos(2a) = cos^2(a) - sin^2(a), plus the reference-angle value cos(pi/4) = sqrt(2)/2.
commonMistake: Forgetting the identity and trying to evaluate cos(7pi/8) and sin(7pi/8) separately, or getting the sign wrong in the fourth quadrant.

optionExplanations.1: The value 1 would require 2a to be a multiple of 2pi, but 2a = 7pi/4 is not.
optionExplanations.3: cos(7pi/16) halves the angle instead of doubling it; the identity gives cos(2a), not cos(a/2).
optionExplanations.4: (sqrt(2)/2)^2 equals 1/2, which is the value of cos^2(pi/4), not of cos(7pi/4).

formulaNotes: cos(2a) = cos^2(a) - sin^2(a); cos(7pi/4) = cos(2pi - pi/4) = cos(pi/4) = sqrt(2)/2.

shortExplanation: The equation means (x+5)^4 = 2^4 = 16, so x+5 = 2 or x+5 = -2, giving the two solutions x = -3 and x = -7.
solutionSteps: Rewrite in exponential form: (x+5)^4 = 2^4 = 16.
Take real fourth roots: since the exponent is even, x+5 = 2 or x+5 = -2.
Solve each case: x = -3 or x = -7.
Check the domain: the argument (x+5)^4 is positive for both values (16 in each case), so both are valid.
The equation therefore has the two solutions x = -3 and x = -7.
keyConcept: y^4 = 16 has two real solutions, y = 2 and y = -2, because the exponent is even; the log argument (x+5)^4 is positive whenever x is not -5.
commonMistake: Writing log_2((x+5)^4) = 4 log_2(x+5) forces x+5 > 0 and loses the solution x = -7; the correct simplification uses the absolute value, 4 log_2|x+5|.

optionExplanations.2: x = -7 alone misses x = -3, which satisfies ((-3)+5)^4 = 2^4 = 16.
optionExplanations.3: Real solutions do exist: any x with (x+5)^4 = 16 works, and there are two such values.
optionExplanations.4: x = -3 alone misses x = -7, which also satisfies ((-7)+5)^4 = (-2)^4 = 16.

formulaNotes: log_b(A) = c means A = b^c; also log_2(y^4) = 4 log_2|y| for y different from 0.

shortExplanation: Writing the two conditions as equations and adding them makes both children's ages cancel, leaving twice the man's age equal to 170, so he is 85.
solutionSteps: Let M, A, R be the ages of the man, Aldo, and Maria.
First condition: M + A = R + 80.
Second condition: M + R = A + 90.
Add the two equations: 2M + A + R = A + R + 170.
Cancel A + R from both sides: 2M = 170, so M = 85.
keyConcept: Adding the two linear equations eliminates both unknown children's ages at once.
commonMistake: Trying to find each child's age individually; the system has three unknowns and two equations, but the man's age is still uniquely determined.

optionExplanations.0: 45 would give 2M = 90, which corresponds to using only the second condition's difference, not the sum of both.
optionExplanations.1: 68 does not satisfy the combined equation 2M = 80 + 90.
optionExplanations.4: 70 comes from averaging 80 and 90 incorrectly as (80+90)/2 applied to a wrong setup; the correct sum gives 2M = 170, not 140.

shortExplanation: The bracket sums to 5/4 * a^2 b^2, and multiplying by -3/10 * a^2 b^2 c^2 gives -3/8 * a^4 b^4 c^2.
solutionSteps: Factor a^2 b^2 out of the bracket: (4/3 + 1/6 - 1/4) * a^2 b^2.
So the bracket equals 5/4 * a^2 b^2.
Multiply the coefficients: (-3/10) * (5/4) = -15/40 = -3/8.
Multiply the literal parts: a^2 b^2 c^2 * a^2 b^2 = a^4 b^4 c^2.
Result: -3/8 * a^4 b^4 c^2.
keyConcept: Combine like monomials first, then multiply coefficients and add exponents of matching bases.
commonMistake: Adding the exponents incorrectly or cancelling a^2 b^2, which is not allowed in a product (only in a quotient).

optionExplanations.2: -6/25 * a^4 b^2 c^2 has both a wrong coefficient (from multiplying 3/10 by something other than 5/4) and a wrong power of b.
optionExplanations.3: -3/8 * c^2 wrongly cancels all the a and b factors, but this is a product, not a fraction.
optionExplanations.4: -3/8 * a^2 b^2 c^2 forgets to add the exponents when multiplying a^2 b^2 c^2 by a^2 b^2.

shortExplanation: The graph has horizontal asymptote y = 1, y-intercept -3 and x-intercept x = -2. Only y = 1 - 4*2^x satisfies all three: 1 - 4*2^0 = -3 and 4*2^x = 1 gives x = -2.
solutionSteps: All the candidates have the form y = 1 - c*a^x, which tends to 1 as x -> -infinity, matching the dashed asymptote y = 1.
Use the y-intercept: the curve passes through (0, -3), so 1 - c*a^0 = -3, which forces c = 4.
Only one option has c = 4 with base 2: y = 1 - 4*2^x.
Check the x-intercept: 1 - 4*2^x = 0 gives 2^x = 1/4, so x = -2, exactly where the curve crosses the x-axis.
Both fixed points match, so the function is y = 1 - 4*2^x.
keyConcept: Identify an exponential graph by matching its horizontal asymptote and two fixed points (the intercepts).
commonMistake: Reading only the asymptote and picking any option of the form 1 - c*a^x without checking the intercepts.

optionExplanations.0: y = 1 - 2*4^x has y-intercept 1 - 2 = -1, but the curve passes through (0, -3).
optionExplanations.2: y = 1 - 4^x has y-intercept 0, so it would pass through the origin, which the curve does not.
optionExplanations.4: y = 1 - 2*2^x crosses the x-axis at x = -1 and has y-intercept -1, neither of which matches the graph.

figureExplanation: The curve approaches the dashed horizontal line y = 1 on the far left, crosses the x-axis at x = -2, and crosses the y-axis at y = -3; these three features pin down the formula.
formulaNotes: For y = 1 - c*a^x (a > 1, c > 0): asymptote y = 1 as x -> -infinity; y-intercept 1 - c; zero where a^x = 1/c.

shortExplanation: Among Engineering graduates there are 42 employed out of 42 + 14 = 56 in total, and 42/56 = 0.75, i.e. 75%.
solutionSteps: Total Engineering graduates: 42 employed + 14 unemployed = 56.
The requested percentage is employed Engineering graduates over all Engineering graduates: 42/56.
So 75% of Engineering graduates are employed.
keyConcept: A conditional percentage uses the subgroup total (Engineering graduates), not the overall total of 150.
commonMistake: Dividing 42 by 150 (the whole sample) or by 86 (all employed) instead of by the 56 Engineering graduates.

optionExplanations.0: 86% comes from reading the count of employed graduates (86 people) as a percentage; it is a total, not a rate.
optionExplanations.2: About 57% is 86/150, the share of employed among all graduates, not among Engineering graduates.
optionExplanations.3: About 43% is 64/150, the overall unemployment share; it mixes in graduates from other degrees, which the question excludes.

shortExplanation: Take the least common multiple of the coefficients (12) and each variable with its highest exponent: a^3, b^4, x^6, giving 12 a^3 b^4 x^6.
solutionSteps: Coefficients are 3, 4, 1; their least common multiple is 12.
Highest power of a among a^2, a^3, a^2 is a^3.
Highest power of b among b^4, b^3, b^4 is b^4.
Highest power of x among x^0, x^5, x^6 is x^6.
Combine: LCM = 12 a^3 b^4 x^6.
keyConcept: The LCM of monomials uses the LCM of the numerical coefficients and each variable raised to its maximum exponent.
commonMistake: Taking the minimum exponents (which gives the greatest common divisor, not the least common multiple).

optionExplanations.0: a^2 b^4 misses the coefficient 12 and the factors a^3 and x^6, so it is not divisible by the second and third monomials.
optionExplanations.1: The variable c does not appear in any of the three monomials, so it cannot appear in their LCM.
optionExplanations.2: 12 a^2 b^3 x^4 uses exponents that are too small: it is not a multiple of 4a^3 b^3 x^5 or of a^2 b^4 x^6.

shortExplanation: The line through (0,1) and (3,2) has slope (2-1)/(3-0) = 1/3, and 2x - 6y + 3 = 0 rewrites as y = x/3 + 1/2, which has the same slope.
solutionSteps: Compute the slope through the two points: m = (2 - 1)/(3 - 0) = 1/3.
Parallel lines must have slope 1/3.
Its slope is 1/3 and it is a different line (it passes through (0, 1/2), not (0,1)), so it is parallel to the given one.
keyConcept: Two lines are parallel exactly when they have the same slope; for ax + by + c = 0 the slope is -a/b.
commonMistake: Computing the slope of ax + by + c = 0 as a/b instead of -a/b, or comparing intercepts instead of slopes.

optionExplanations.0: 3x - 6y + 3 = 0 gives y = x/2 + 1/2, slope 1/2, not 1/3.
optionExplanations.1: x - 4y - 2 = 0 gives y = x/4 - 1/2, slope 1/4, not 1/3.
optionExplanations.4: x + 2y - 4 = 0 gives y = -x/2 + 2, a negative slope, so it cannot be parallel to a line of slope 1/3.

shortExplanation: The denominator x^2 + x + 1 is always positive, so dividing P(x) by it never changes the sign or the domain; hence A and B have exactly the same solutions.
solutionSteps: Check the sign of x^2 + x + 1: its discriminant is 1 - 4 = -3 < 0 and the leading coefficient is positive, so it is positive for every real x.
Dividing an inequality by a strictly positive quantity preserves the inequality: P(x)/(x^2 + x + 1) <= 0 holds exactly when P(x) <= 0.
The denominator never vanishes, so no points are excluded from the domain; A and B are equivalent.

By contrast, x^2 - 3x + 2 = (x - 1)(x - 2) is negative between 1 and 2 and vanishes at x = 1 and x = 2, so C can flip the sign of the quotient and excludes those two points; C is not equivalent to A in general.
keyConcept: A quadratic with negative discriminant and positive leading coefficient is positive everywhere, so it can be dropped from an inequality without changing its solutions.
commonMistake: Treating both denominators alike: x^2 - 3x + 2 has real roots, so it changes sign and removes x = 1 and x = 2 from the domain.

optionExplanations.0: A and C differ in general: for 1 < x < 2 the denominator (x-1)(x-2) is negative and reverses the sign of P(x), and x = 1, 2 are excluded in C but may solve A.
optionExplanations.2: All three cannot coincide in general, because C's denominator changes sign while B's does not.
optionExplanations.4: Knowledge of P(x) is not needed: the comparison between A and B rests only on the denominator being always positive.

shortExplanation: Since the distance from the centre to the plane (1) is smaller than the radius (2), the plane cuts the sphere in a circle of radius sqrt(2^2 - 1^2) = sqrt(3).
solutionSteps: Compare the distance d from the centre Q to the plane with the sphere's radius R: here d = 1 and R = 2.
If d < R the plane cuts through the sphere; if d = R it is tangent (one point); if d > R they do not meet.
Since 1 < 2, the intersection is a circle.
Its radius is sqrt(R^2 - d^2) = sqrt(4 - 1) = sqrt(3), by the Pythagorean theorem applied to the foot of the perpendicular from Q to the plane.
keyConcept: A plane at distance d from the centre of a sphere of radius R intersects it in a circle of radius sqrt(R^2 - d^2) when d < R.
commonMistake: Thinking a plane can cut a sphere in an ellipse: every plane section of a sphere is a circle (or a point, or empty).

optionExplanations.0: The intersection is empty only when the distance exceeds the radius, i.e. d > 2.
optionExplanations.1: Plane sections of a sphere are always circles; an ellipse with different axes can only come from cutting a non-spherical surface such as an ellipsoid or a cylinder at an angle.
optionExplanations.2: A single point occurs only when the plane is tangent, i.e. when the distance equals the radius (d = 2 here, not 1).

shortExplanation: The dashed curve is the solid curve reflected in the x-axis and then lowered by 3, so g(x) = -f(x) - 3. At x = 0, f(0) = -3 gives g(0) = -(-3) - 3 = 0, matching the dashed curve crossing near the origin.
solutionSteps: Where the solid curve rises the dashed curve falls, and vice versa, so a reflection in the x-axis, -f(x), is involved.
Read the solid curve at x = 0: f(0) = -3.
Read the dashed curve at x = 0: it passes through the origin, so g(0) = 0.
A pure reflection would give -f(0) = 3, but the dashed value is 0, which is 3 less; the reflection is followed by a downward shift of 3: g(x) = -f(x) - 3.

Check the flat part: the solid curve has a small wiggle near y = 0 (between x = 1 and x = 3); reflected it stays near y = 0, then lowered by 3 it sits near y = -3, exactly where the dashed plateau lies.

Check the ends: for large x the solid climbs steeply positive so g = -f - 3 plunges steeply negative (dashed drops for x > 3); for x < 0 the solid drops steeply so g rises steeply positive (dashed is high for x < 0). Both match.
keyConcept: Graph transformations: -f(x) reflects the curve in the x-axis; subtracting 3 afterwards shifts the whole graph vertically downward by 3 units.
commonMistake: Confusing the vertical operation -f(x) - 3 (reflect, then move down) with the horizontal one -f(x - 3) (move right, then reflect), which would displace features sideways instead of downward.

optionExplanations.0: g(x) = -f(x) reflects correctly but gives g(0) = 3 and leaves the wiggle centred on y = 0, whereas the dashed curve passes through the origin and its wiggle sits near y = -3.
optionExplanations.2: g(x) = -f(x - 3) shifts every feature 3 units to the right; the steep dashed drop would then appear near x = 3 rather than following the reflected shape, and g(0) would equal -f(-3), not 0.
optionExplanations.3: g(x) = 3 - f(x) is a reflection shifted up by 3, giving g(0) = -(-3) + 3 = 6, far above the dashed curve which is at 0 there.
optionExplanations.4: g(x) = -3f(x) is a reflection with a vertical stretch by 3, giving g(0) = -3(-3) = 9 and distorting the shape, unlike the rigid downward shift the dashed curve shows.

figureExplanation: The solid curve y = f(x) has y-intercept -3, drops steeply for x < 0, rises through a small wiggle near y = 0 (a slight local maximum around x = 1 and local minimum around x = 2.3), then climbs steeply for x > 2.5. The dashed curve is steeply positive for x < 0, crosses near the origin, holds a plateau near y = -3 for roughly 1 < x < 3, then plunges steeply for x > 3 - exactly the solid curve mirrored in the x-axis and lowered by 3.
formulaNotes: -f(x) reflects across the x-axis; the extra -3 shifts down. Anchor check: f(0) = -3 gives g(0) = -(-3) - 3 = 0; where f = 0 the value g = -3.

shortExplanation: Equal vertex angles make two isosceles triangles similar (all three angles match), and similar triangles with equal perimeters must have ratio 1, hence they are congruent.
solutionSteps: In an isosceles triangle the vertex angle determines the base angles: each base angle is (180 deg - vertex angle)/2.
So two isosceles triangles with the same vertex angle have all three angles equal, i.e. they are similar.
Similar triangles have proportional sides, with some ratio k; their perimeters are then in the same ratio k.
Equal perimeters force k = 1, so all corresponding sides are equal: the triangles are congruent.
keyConcept: Similarity plus one matching linear measurement (perimeter, a side, a height) forces congruence.
commonMistake: Believing that equal areas or equal perimeters alone fix the shape of a figure; they constrain size but not shape.

optionExplanations.1: Equiangular (similar) triangles can have different sizes, e.g. two equilateral triangles with sides 1 and 2.
optionExplanations.2: Two isosceles triangles can share the same area while having different base/height proportions, so equal area does not imply congruence.
optionExplanations.4: A long thin parallelogram and a square can have the same perimeter but completely different shapes.

shortExplanation: The circles have centres (0,2) with radius 1 and (1,2) with radius 3; the distance between centres is 1, which is less than 3 - 1 = 2, so the small circle lies strictly inside the large one.
solutionSteps: Complete the square for the first circle: x^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 1, so centre C1 = (0, 2) and radius r1 = 1.
Complete the square for the second: (x - 1)^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 9, so centre C2 = (1, 2) and radius r2 = 3.
Distance between centres: d = sqrt((1-0)^2 + (2-2)^2) = 1.
Compare d with the radii: d = 1 < r2 - r1 = 2.
When d < |r2 - r1| the circles do not meet and the smaller one (the first) is internal to the larger (the second).
keyConcept: Two circles' mutual position is decided by comparing the distance d between centres with r1 + r2 and |r1 - r2|.
commonMistake: Checking only d < r1 + r2 and concluding the circles intersect; intersection at two points also requires d > |r1 - r2|.

optionExplanations.0: Tangency requires d = r1 + r2 = 4 (external) or d = |r2 - r1| = 2 (internal), and d = 1 is neither.
optionExplanations.2: Two intersection points would need |r2 - r1| < d < r1 + r2, i.e. 2 < d < 4, but d = 1.
optionExplanations.4: Two distinct circles can meet in at most two points, never four.

formulaNotes: Circle x^2 + y^2 + ax + by + c = 0 has centre (-a/2, -b/2) and radius sqrt(a^2/4 + b^2/4 - c).

solutionSteps: Evaluate the bracket: 3^3 + 3^2 = 27 + 9 = 36.
Factor 36 into primes: 36 = 4 * 9 = 2^2 * 3^2.
Raise to the third power: (2^2 * 3^2)^3 = 2^6 * 3^6.
Multiply by 2^4 by adding exponents of 2: 2^(6+4) * 3^6 = 2^10 * 3^6.
keyConcept: Sums of powers must be evaluated (or factored) before applying exponent rules; (a^m)^n = a^(mn) and a^m * a^n = a^(m+n).
commonMistake: Treating 3^3 + 3^2 as 3^5: exponent rules apply to products of powers, not to sums.

optionExplanations.0: 2^8 * 3^8 mismatches both exponents; cubing 2^2 * 3^2 gives exponent 6, and only the exponent of 2 is increased by the extra 2^4.
optionExplanations.1: 2^6 * 3^10 keeps the correct exponent 6 on 2 but over-raises the 3-part, as if 36 were mis-cubed to 3^10 instead of 3^6.
optionExplanations.3: 2^6 * 3^6 is (36)^3 alone; it forgets to multiply by the factor 2^4.

shortExplanation: By the power rule for logarithms, log_7(2^(x^3)) = x^3 * log_7(2), and since 2^(x^3) is positive for every real x, the identity holds for all real x with no restriction.
solutionSteps: The argument 2^(x^3) is an exponential with positive base, so it is strictly positive for every real x; the expression is defined for all real x.
Apply the power rule log_b(a^t) = t * log_b(a) with a = 2, t = x^3.
This gives log_7(2^(x^3)) = x^3 * log_7(2), valid for every real x.
No sign condition on x is needed, because the positivity of the argument comes from the base 2, not from x.
keyConcept: log_b(a^t) = t log_b(a) holds whenever a > 0, for any real exponent t.
commonMistake: Adding the restriction x > 0 by reflex: the restriction would be needed only if x itself were the base of the power inside the logarithm.

optionExplanations.0: 3 log_7(2^x) equals 3x * log_7(2), which matches x^3 * log_7(2) only for special values of x, not identically.
optionExplanations.2: (log_7(2^x))^3 equals x^3 * (log_7 2)^3, which carries an extra factor (log_7 2)^2 compared with the correct value.
optionExplanations.4: The identity is not limited to x > 0: for example at x = -1 both sides equal -log_7(2).

formulaNotes: log_b(a^t) = t * log_b(a) for a > 0; 2^u > 0 for every real u.

shortExplanation: For orbits around the same star, Kepler's third law gives T^2 proportional to r^3, so T'/T = (r'/r)^(3/2) = 4^(3/2) = 8.
solutionSteps: For a circular orbit, gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm/r^2 = m v^2 / r, so v = sqrt(GM/r).
The period is T = 2*pi*r / v = 2*pi * sqrt(r^3 / (GM)).
Hence T^2 is proportional to r^3 (Kepler's third law), independent of the planet's mass.
Take the ratio: T'/T = (r'/r)^(3/2) = 4^(3/2).
keyConcept: Kepler's third law: T^2 proportional to r^3 for bodies orbiting the same central star; the orbiting mass cancels out.
commonMistake: Using T proportional to r (giving 4) or forgetting that the speed also changes with r; the 3/2 power comes from combining both effects.

optionExplanations.0: 1/4 inverts the dependence: larger orbits take LONGER, not shorter, so T'/T must exceed 1.
optionExplanations.1: A ratio of 4 would follow from T proportional to r, ignoring that the outer planet also moves more slowly (v proportional to 1/sqrt(r)).
optionExplanations.3: Equal periods would require equal radii; the period depends on r even though it does not depend on the planet's mass.

formulaNotes: GMm/r^2 = m v^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r); T = 2 pi r / v = 2 pi sqrt(r^3/(GM)); so T'/T = (r'/r)^(3/2).

shortExplanation: Electric power is P = V * I = 220 V * 10 A = 2200 W = 2.2 kW; the result must be in watts (power), not joules or kilowatt-hours (energy).
solutionSteps: Identify the known values: current I = 10 A, voltage V = 220 V.
Apply the power formula: P = V * I.
Convert: 2200 W = 2.2 kW.
Check units: volt * ampere = watt, the unit of power, consistent with the question asking for dissipated power.
keyConcept: P = V * I, and the watt (kW) is the unit of power, while J and kWh are units of energy.
commonMistake: Picking an answer in kJ or kWh: those measure energy, which would require knowing for how long the current flows.

optionExplanations.0: 2.2 kJ is an amount of energy; 2200 J would be dissipated only in exactly one second, and the question asks for power.
optionExplanations.1: 0.045 A/V is the conductance I/V = 10/220, not the power.
optionExplanations.4: 2.2 kWh is also energy (the energy delivered by 2.2 kW in one hour), not power.

formulaNotes: P = V * I; equivalently P = R * I^2 = V^2 / R. 1 W = 1 V * 1 A.

shortExplanation: Every point has a single value of potential, so a point lying on two equipotential surfaces would have both values at once; surfaces at different potentials therefore can never intersect.
solutionSteps: The electrostatic potential assigns exactly one value to each point in space.
Suppose the two surfaces intersected: any intersection point would belong to both surfaces.
That point would then have two different potential values simultaneously, which is impossible.
Therefore two equipotential surfaces at different potentials never intersect.
keyConcept: The potential is a single-valued function of position, so distinct equipotential surfaces are disjoint.
commonMistake: Confusing the two correct facts: field lines cross equipotential surfaces at 90 degrees, but the surfaces themselves neither intersect each other nor are parallel to the field lines.

optionExplanations.1: Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to the field lines, not parallel to them (moving along a field line changes the potential).
optionExplanations.2: It is the LINES OF FORCE that cross an equipotential surface at 90 degrees; two equipotential surfaces do not intersect at all.
optionExplanations.3: They need not be geometrically parallel: around two point charges, for example, the surfaces are non-parallel closed shapes; they merely never touch.

shortExplanation: For free fall from rest, h = (1/2)g t^2, so t = sqrt(2h/g) = sqrt(2*5/9.8) ≈ 1 s.
solutionSteps: The object starts at rest and falls under gravity, so h = (1/2) g t^2.
Solve for t: t = sqrt(2h/g).
Substitute h = 5 m and g ≈ 9.8 m/s^2: t = sqrt(10/9.8) = sqrt(1.02).
t ≈ 1.0 s, so the fall takes roughly one second.
keyConcept: Free fall from rest: h = (1/2)g t^2, so t = sqrt(2h/g).
commonMistake: Using h = g t (forgetting the 1/2 and the square on t), which gives t = 0.5 s.

optionExplanations.1: In two seconds a body falls about (1/2)*9.8*4 ≈ 20 m, four times the given height.
optionExplanations.3: Half a second comes from using h = g t or halving incorrectly; sqrt(2*5/9.8) is about 1, not 0.5.
optionExplanations.4: Five seconds would correspond to a fall of about 122 m, far more than 5 m.

formulaNotes: h = (1/2) g t^2 with g ≈ 9.8 m/s^2; t = sqrt(2h/g).

shortExplanation: Each click marks one 15 m rail, so 240 clicks in 120 s means 3600 m covered in 120 s, i.e. 30 m/s.
solutionSteps: Each join heard corresponds to the wheel having crossed one rail of length 15 m.
Distance covered: 240 * 15 m = 3600 m.
Time elapsed: two minutes = 120 s.
Speed = distance/time = 3600/120 = 30 m/s.
keyConcept: Constant speed: v = total distance / total time.
commonMistake: Forgetting to convert two minutes into 120 seconds, which inflates the answer by a factor of 60 or leads to a wrong round number.

optionExplanations.0: 60 m/s would require covering 7200 m in 120 s, twice the actual distance counted.
optionExplanations.3: 15 m/s treats the rail length as the speed; it ignores the 240 counts per 120 s rate.
optionExplanations.4: 45 m/s corresponds to 5400 m in two minutes, not the 3600 m actually travelled.

shortExplanation: By the parallelogram rule, FT = sqrt(F1^2 + F2^2 + 2 F1 F2 cos 60°) = sqrt(25 + 4 + 10) = sqrt(39) ≈ 6.2 N, so the resultant is a little more than 6 N.
solutionSteps: For two forces at angle θ, the resultant modulus is FT = sqrt(F1^2 + F2^2 + 2 F1 F2 cos θ).
Substitute F1 = 5 N, F2 = 2 N, cos 60° = 0.5.
sqrt(39) ≈ 6.24 N, which is a little more than 6 N.
keyConcept: Vector addition of forces: FT = sqrt(F1^2 + F2^2 + 2 F1 F2 cos θ).
commonMistake: Adding the moduli directly (5 + 2 = 7 N), which is only valid when the forces are parallel and in the same direction.

optionExplanations.0: About 5.5 N would require a larger angle between the forces; with cos 60° = 0.5 the resultant exceeds 6 N.
optionExplanations.1: 7 N is the simple sum of the moduli, correct only if the forces were aligned (θ = 0°), not at 60°.
optionExplanations.4: The data are sufficient: two moduli and the angle between the forces fully determine the resultant.

formulaNotes: Law of cosines for vector addition: FT^2 = F1^2 + F2^2 + 2 F1 F2 cos θ; cos 60° = 1/2.

shortExplanation: The heat needed is Q = m c ΔT; with the same material (same c) and the same ΔT = 200 K, the block with double the mass absorbs double the heat.
solutionSteps: Heat absorbed in warming: Q = m c ΔT, where c is the specific heat of the material.
Both blocks share the same c (same material) and the same temperature rise ΔT = 500 - 300 = 200 K.
Q is therefore proportional to the mass m.
The 10 kg block absorbs twice the heat of the 5 kg block, so it has absorbed more heat.
keyConcept: Q = m c ΔT: for equal material and equal ΔT, absorbed heat scales with mass.
commonMistake: Confusing temperature with heat: equal temperature rise does not mean equal heat when the masses differ.

optionExplanations.1: For uniform heating the shape is irrelevant; Q depends on mass, specific heat and ΔT.
optionExplanations.2: Same material fixes the specific heat c, but Q = m c ΔT still depends on the mass.
optionExplanations.4: Equal ΔT alone does not fix Q; heat also depends on mass, and the masses differ.

shortExplanation: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a material medium; the Moon has essentially no atmosphere, so engine noise cannot reach the astronaut through space.
solutionSteps: Sound propagates as a mechanical wave: it requires a medium (gas, liquid or solid) whose particles can oscillate.
The Moon has no atmosphere, so there is no air between the spaceship and the astronaut.
Without a medium the pressure oscillations of the engine cannot travel, so no sound is heard.
The scene is therefore physically inconsistent because sound cannot propagate in vacuum.
keyConcept: Sound is a mechanical wave and cannot propagate in vacuum.
commonMistake: Attributing the effect to the Moon's lower gravity, which affects motion of masses but not the possibility of sound propagation.

optionExplanations.0: Temperature does not forbid sound propagation; the real obstacle is the absence of any medium.
optionExplanations.1: Gravity affects how objects fall, not whether pressure waves can travel; lower g would not silence an engine.
optionExplanations.2: The laws of physics are universal; they hold on the Moon exactly as on Earth.

shortExplanation: In parallel both capacitors have the same voltage V, so Q = CV gives Q1 = C1 V > C2 V = Q2 because C1 > C2.
solutionSteps: The fundamental relation is Q = C V for each capacitor.
In a parallel connection the two capacitors share the same potential difference V.
Then Q1 = C1 V and Q2 = C2 V, and since C1 > C2 it follows Q1 > Q2.
In a series connection, instead, the two capacitors carry the same charge (Q1 = Q2), regardless of the capacitances.
keyConcept: Q = CV: parallel means equal V (charges proportional to C); series means equal Q.
commonMistake: Swapping the two rules: thinking charges are equal in parallel and different in series, when it is the opposite.

optionExplanations.1: In series the same charge flows onto both capacitors, so Q1 = Q2, not Q1 > Q2.
optionExplanations.3: Without knowing how the capacitors are connected or charged, no general ordering of Q1 and Q2 holds.
optionExplanations.4: In parallel the voltages are equal, so the charges are proportional to the capacitances and cannot be equal when C1 > C2.

formulaNotes: Q = C V; parallel: same V, Q proportional to C; series: same Q.

shortExplanation: Equal volume, pressure and temperature imply equal numbers of moles (Avogadro), and at the same temperature the average kinetic energy per molecule is the same for both gases.
solutionSteps: By the ideal gas law pV = nRT, equal p, V and T mean the two canisters contain the same number of moles, hence the same number of molecules.
Kinetic theory: the average translational kinetic energy per molecule is (3/2) k T, which depends only on temperature.
Since both gases are at the same T, N2 and H2 molecules have the same average kinetic energy.
The speeds, however, differ: equal kinetic energy with a mass 14 times larger means N2 molecules move more slowly (v proportional to 1/sqrt(m)).
keyConcept: Average molecular kinetic energy (3/2)kT depends only on temperature, not on the type of gas.
commonMistake: Concluding equal kinetic energy implies equal speed; heavier molecules have the same energy at lower speed.

optionExplanations.2: With equal mole numbers, the mass in grams of N2 is 14 times that of H2 (28 g/mol vs 2 g/mol), not equal.
optionExplanations.3: Same kinetic energy but a 14-times larger mass means N2 molecules are slower, not equally fast.
optionExplanations.4: Equal p, V, T give equal numbers of molecules by Avogadro's principle, not 14 times as many.

formulaNotes: pV = nRT; average kinetic energy = (3/2) k T; (1/2) m v^2 equal implies v proportional to 1/sqrt(m).

shortExplanation: With v^2 = 2 a s for a start from rest, v = sqrt(2 * 10 * 45) = sqrt(900) = 30 m/s.
solutionSteps: For uniformly accelerated motion from rest: v^2 = 2 a s.
Substitute a = 10 m/s^2 and s = 45 m: v^2 = 2 * 10 * 45 = 900.
keyConcept: Time-free kinematic relation: v^2 = v0^2 + 2 a s, with v0 = 0.
commonMistake: Using v = a t with a guessed time, or computing v = sqrt(a*s) = sqrt(450) ≈ 21 m/s by forgetting the factor 2.

optionExplanations.0: 20 m/s would give v^2 = 400, corresponding to only 20 m of travel at this acceleration.
optionExplanations.3: 50 m/s would require 125 m of travel; it overestimates by ignoring the square root.
optionExplanations.4: 40 m/s would require s = 1600/20 = 80 m, not 45 m.

shortExplanation: The passage says the core's recoil makes the star explode as a supernova and 'give birth to an enormous, superheated, shock wave', i.e. an extremely hot wave produced by the explosion.
solutionSteps: Locate the description of the explosion: the crushed iron core rebounds, causing the star to explode as a supernova.
The text states this explosion gives birth to an enormous, superheated shock wave.
'Superheated shock wave' matches 'an extremely hot wave produced as a result of the explosion'.

Check the alternatives against the text: iron atoms are crushed together, not expanded; a black hole arises only from the most massive stars, not usually; the core heats to billions of degrees 'in a microsecond', which is sudden, not gradual; black dwarfs are the fate of stars that never become supernovae.
keyConcept: Answer strictly from what the passage states: the explosion produces a superheated shock wave.
commonMistake: Choosing the gradual-heating option: the passage says the core reaches billions of degrees in a microsecond, the opposite of gradual.

optionExplanations.0: Iron atoms are described as being 'crushed so closely together', the opposite of expanding.
optionExplanations.1: A black hole forms only when an extremely massive star (at least ten times the sun) leaves a large core, so it is not the usual outcome.
optionExplanations.3: The passage says the core may reach billions of degrees 'in a microsecond', so the heating is sudden, not gradual.

shortExplanation: The passage says heavy elements like iron are produced only in supernovae and that we carry their remnants in our own bodies, so supernovae produce the iron in our blood.
solutionSteps: Find the relevant sentences: supernova blasts produce much of the material in the universe, including elements like iron that make up our planet 'and even ourselves'.
The text adds that heavy elements are only produced in supernovae, so all of us carry these remnants within our bodies.
Combining the two: the iron in the human body, including in blood, comes from supernovae.

Rule out the others: supernovae add elements to space clouds rather than absorbing matter from them; it is ordinary smaller stars that become white dwarfs; the shock wave compresses clouds of gas (helping form new stars), not existing stars; 25,000 miles refers to the ejection speed per second, not to spacing in space.
keyConcept: Inference from two combined statements: iron comes only from supernovae, and our bodies contain that iron.
commonMistake: Confusing what supernovae compress (clouds of gas that aid new star formation) with compressing new stars themselves.

optionExplanations.1: The passage says supernovae ADD enriching elements to space clouds, not that they absorb matter from them.
optionExplanations.2: White dwarfs are what many ordinary stars become as they cool; the passage never says supernovae become white dwarfs.
optionExplanations.4: The figure of 25,000 miles is a speed (per second) of ejected matter, not a distance between supernovae.

shortExplanation: The passage says that if a very massive star leaves behind a large burned-out core, that core may be engulfed by its own gravity and turn into a black hole.
solutionSteps: The question concerns supernovae originating from massive stars (core-collapse, not the binary white-dwarf type).
The final paragraph states that a star at least ten times the size of the sun leaves behind a large core.
Such a core has no energy source, produces no outward pressure, and may become 'a cosmic sinkhole for energy and matter -- a black hole'.
Hence supernovae from massive stars can eventually give rise to black holes.
keyConcept: The remnant of the most massive supernovae can collapse into a black hole.
commonMistake: Answering with what supernovae give to space (energy and matter) in general; the black-hole outcome is what the passage specifically ties to massive stars.

optionExplanations.0: Massive stars are said to leave behind LARGE cores; small cores are not attributed to them.
optionExplanations.2: The burned-out core is described as producing NO outward pressure, which is precisely why it collapses.
optionExplanations.3: The passage says typically a tiny core of neutrons remains, but 'a small amount of neutrons' distorts this, and for the most massive stars a large core (and possibly a black hole) remains instead.

shortExplanation: The study found cities with minimal public transport (like Perth) spent 17% of their wealth on transport, while cities with good public transport spent as little as 5%, i.e. less money.
solutionSteps: The ISTP study compared the proportion of money put into transport by thirty-seven cities.
Perth, an example of minimal public transport, devoted 17% of its wealth to transport costs.
Some European and Asian cities with well-developed public transport spent as little as 5%.
Therefore the report showed that cities with good public transport spent less on transport, freeing money for industry, jobs and quality of life.
keyConcept: The comparison 17% (car-dependent Perth) versus 5% (transit-rich cities) shows lower transport spending where public transport is developed.
commonMistake: Choosing the vaguer 'good example to other cities': the report's stated finding is the specific spending comparison, not a claim about setting an example.

optionExplanations.0: Being an example to other cities is not a finding of the report; the report measured the proportion of money spent on transport.
optionExplanations.1: The figures show the opposite: it is the car-dependent city (Perth) that spent more (17% versus 5%).
optionExplanations.4: Attracting industry and jobs is mentioned as what the saved money could be used for, not as something the report showed public transport cities 'offered people'.

shortExplanation: The passage says that in later-developing Asian cities the World Bank and Asian Development Bank discouraged public transport, forcing people to depend on cars — i.e. banks effectively supported private transport there.
solutionSteps: Locate the sentence about banks: in cities that developed later, the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank discouraged the building of public transport.
As a result, people in those (Asian) cities were forced to depend on cars.
Discouraging public transport while people turn to cars means private transport was, in effect, supported by those banks in some Asian cities.

Check the alternatives: in Stockholm car use has FALLEN, not increased; wealthy Europeans use their cars LESS than Americans; urban villages are a proposal for converting cities to rail use, not a product of cars; the massive traffic jams are attributed to developing cities like Jakarta and Bangkok, whereas Singapore is cited as a public-transport success.
