commonMistake: Using the full battery current (3 A) or the full 24 V in the power formula for R4 instead of the 1 A actually flowing in its branch.

optionExplanations.2: 18 W results from putting the full 12 V of the parallel section across R4 alone (12^2/8), ignoring the drop across R3 in the same branch.
optionExplanations.3: 32 W would follow from a 2 A branch current, which mixes up the split between the R2 branch and the R3-R4 branch.
optionExplanations.4: 72 W comes from applying P = I^2 * R with the total battery current 3 A (3^2 * 8), but only 1 A flows through R4.

figureExplanation: The figure shows the 24 V battery feeding R1 = 4 ohm to node X; between X and Y, R2 = 6 ohm sits in the middle branch while R3 = 4 ohm and R4 = 8 ohm are in series in the right branch.

shortExplanation: The ammeter reads 0.40 A in the 30 ohm branch, so the common parallel voltage is 0.40 * 30 = 12 V. The three branch currents are then 0.40 A, 0.60 A and 0.20 A, which add to 1.20 A.
solutionSteps: In a parallel circuit every branch has the same voltage as the battery.
From the metered branch: V = I1 * R1 = 0.40 A * 30 ohm = 12 V.
Branch with 20 ohm: I2 = 12/20 = 0.60 A.
Branch with 60 ohm: I3 = 12/60 = 0.20 A.
Total current from the battery: I = 0.40 + 0.60 + 0.20 = 1.20 A.
keyConcept: Parallel branches share the same voltage, and the source current is the sum of the branch currents.
commonMistake: Assuming all three branches carry the ammeter's 0.40 A even though their resistances differ.

optionExplanations.0: 0.40 A is only the current in the 30 ohm branch, not the total delivered by the battery.
optionExplanations.1: 0.80 A would follow from doubling the metered current, which has no basis in the actual resistor values.
optionExplanations.2: 1.00 A comes from adding only the 0.40 A and 0.60 A branches and forgetting the 60 ohm branch.
optionExplanations.3: This is the correct total once each branch current is computed from the shared 12 V.

figureExplanation: The figure shows three parallel branches with R1 = 30 ohm (carrying the ammeter reading 0.40 A), R2 = 20 ohm and R3 = 60 ohm, all across the same unmarked battery.
formulaNotes: V = I*R per branch; I_total = V/R1 + V/R2 + V/R3.

shortExplanation: C2 and C3 in parallel give 8 uF; in series with C1 = 4 uF the equivalent is 8/3 uF, so the total charge is 32 uC and 4 V appears across the parallel pair. C3 then stores Q = 6 uF * 4 V = 24 uC.
solutionSteps: Parallel pair: C23 = C2 + C3 = 2 + 6 = 8 uF.
Total charge from the battery: Q = C_eq * V = (8/3) * 12 = 32 uC.
This 32 uC sits on C1 and on the parallel pair as a whole, so V23 = Q/C23 = 32/8 = 4 V.
Charge on C3: Q3 = C3 * V23 = 6 * 4 = 24 uC.
keyConcept: Series capacitors share the same charge; parallel capacitors share the same voltage and split the charge in proportion to capacitance.
commonMistake: Putting the full 12 V across C3 (giving 72 uC) instead of only the 4 V that remains after the drop across C1.

optionExplanations.0: 8 uC is the charge on C2 (2 uF * 4 V), not on C3.
optionExplanations.3: 32 uC is the total charge delivered by the battery, which splits between C2 and C3; it is not the charge on C3 alone.
optionExplanations.4: 72 uC assumes C3 sees the entire 12 V, ignoring the series capacitor C1.

figureExplanation: The figure shows the 12 V battery feeding C1 = 4 uF, which then connects to C2 = 2 uF and C3 = 6 uF wired in parallel between the same two nodes.
formulaNotes: Series: 1/C_eq = 1/C1 + 1/C23. Parallel: C23 = C2 + C3. Q = C*V.

shortExplanation: The snapshot shows a 4 m wavelength in Medium 1 and a 6 m wavelength in Medium 2. Since the frequency (12/4 = 3 Hz) is unchanged at the junction, the speed in Medium 2 is v = f * lambda = 3 * 6 = 18 m/s.
solutionSteps: Read Medium 1 from the graph: successive crests at x = 1, 5, 9 m, so lambda1 = 4 m.
Read Medium 2: the pattern repeats every 6 m (zero crossings at 12, 15, 18, 21, 24 m), so lambda2 = 6 m.
Frequency is set by the source and does not change at a junction: f = v1/lambda1 = 12/4 = 3 Hz.
Speed in Medium 2: v2 = f * lambda2 = 3 * 6 = 18 m/s.
keyConcept: When a wave crosses into a new medium the frequency stays constant, so speed and wavelength change in the same ratio.
commonMistake: Assuming the wavelength stays the same across the junction, or letting the frequency change instead of the wavelength.

optionExplanations.1: 8 m/s comes from inverting the wavelength ratio (multiplying 12 by 4/6 instead of 6/4).
optionExplanations.2: 12 m/s would mean the speed is unchanged, but the visibly longer wavelength in Medium 2 shows the wave sped up.
optionExplanations.4: 27 m/s comes from squaring the ratio (12 * (6/4)^2), but speed scales linearly with wavelength at fixed frequency.

figureExplanation: Left of the dashed junction at x = 12 m the wave completes a full cycle every 4 m; right of it each cycle spans 6 m, so the wavelength grows by a factor 6/4 = 1.5.
formulaNotes: v = f * lambda with f constant across the junction, so v2 = v1 * (lambda2/lambda1).

shortExplanation: The graphs give lambda1 = 0.4 m and T = 0.2 s, so f = 5 Hz and v1 = 2 m/s. In the heavier section v2 = 1.5 * 2 = 3 m/s at the same 5 Hz, giving lambda2 = 3/5 = 0.6 m.
solutionSteps: From the snapshot (y vs x): one full cycle spans 0.4 m, so lambda1 = 0.4 m.
From the time graph (y vs t): one full cycle takes 0.2 s, so T = 0.2 s and f = 1/T = 5 Hz.
Speed in the first section: v1 = lambda1/T = 0.4/0.2 = 2 m/s.
In the second section: v2 = 1.5 * v1 = 3 m/s, with f unchanged at 5 Hz.
New wavelength: lambda2 = v2/f = 3/5 = 0.6 m.
keyConcept: Wavelength in a new medium follows from v = f * lambda with the source frequency fixed.
commonMistake: Dividing the wavelength by 1.5 (giving about 0.27 m) as if a faster wave meant a shorter wavelength.

optionExplanations.0: 0.27 m comes from dividing 0.4 m by 1.5; a faster medium stretches the wavelength, it does not compress it.
optionExplanations.1: 0.30 m confuses values: it is half of 0.6 m and does not follow from v = f * lambda here.
optionExplanations.2: 0.40 m is the wavelength in the first section; it must change when the speed changes at fixed frequency.

figureExplanation: The left panel shows one spatial period of 0.4 m (crest to crest); the right panel shows one temporal period of 0.2 s for a fixed point, and both describe the wave before it enters the heavier section.
formulaNotes: f = 1/T; v = f * lambda; lambda2 = (1.5 * v1)/f.

shortExplanation: The grid gives f = 20 cm and an object distance of 30 cm (between F and 2F). The lens equation gives an image at 60 cm, so m = -di/do = -60/30 = -2.0: a real, inverted image twice the object's height.
solutionSteps: Read the focal length: F is 2 squares from the lens, so f = 2 * 10 = 20 cm.
Read the object position: the arrow stands 3 squares left of the lens, so do = 30 cm (between F at 20 cm and 2F at 40 cm).
Apply the thin-lens equation: 1/di = 1/f - 1/do = 1/20 - 1/30 = (3 - 2)/60 = 1/60.
So di = 60 cm on the far side of the lens (real image).
Magnification: m = -di/do = -60/30 = -2.0 (inverted and enlarged).
keyConcept: An object between F and 2F of a converging lens forms a real, inverted, magnified image beyond 2F.
commonMistake: Dropping the minus sign for a real inverted image, or swapping di and do in the magnification formula.

optionExplanations.1: +2.0 has the right size but the wrong orientation: a real image from a converging lens with the object outside F is inverted, so m is negative.
optionExplanations.2: -0.5 would apply if the object were beyond 2F (image between F and 2F, reduced), but here the object is between F and 2F.
optionExplanations.3: -1.0 occurs only when the object sits exactly at 2F; the figure places it clearly inside 2F at 30 cm.

figureExplanation: On the 10 cm grid the object arrow stands one square right of the 2F mark (at 30 cm from the lens) and the focal points are two squares out, fixing do = 30 cm and f = 20 cm.
formulaNotes: 1/f = 1/do + 1/di; m = -di/do.

shortExplanation: Both rays enter at 50 degrees, but ray 2 refracts at 27 degrees (closer to the normal) while ray 1 refracts at 33 degrees. By Snell's law ray 2 experiences the larger refractive index, so it is the higher-frequency component and is deviated more overall.
solutionSteps: Apply Snell's law at the entry face: n = sin(50)/sin(r), with the same 50 degree incidence for both rays.
Ray 1: n = sin(50)/sin(33) which is about 0.766/0.545 = 1.41.
Ray 2: n = sin(50)/sin(27) which is about 0.766/0.454 = 1.69.
A smaller refraction angle means a larger refractive index, so ray 2 has the larger n.
Larger n corresponds to higher frequency (toward violet) and produces the greater total deviation through the prism.
keyConcept: At a fixed angle of incidence, the ray bent closer to the normal has the larger refractive index, hence the higher frequency and greater deviation.
commonMistake: Linking the larger refraction angle to the larger refractive index, when Snell's law says exactly the opposite.

optionExplanations.0: The ray refracted through the larger angle from the normal (ray 1, 33 degrees) has the smaller refractive index, not the larger one.
optionExplanations.1: Travelling closer to the normal means a larger n, which corresponds to the shorter-wavelength (bluer) component, not the redder one.
optionExplanations.3: Equal incidence angles do not force equal refractive indices; the different refraction angles prove the indices differ (dispersion).
optionExplanations.4: Ray 1 has been bent at the entry face and will bend again at the exit face, so its net deviation cannot be zero.

figureExplanation: The marked angles are the key data: 50 degrees incidence for the white beam, with ray 2 at 27 degrees and ray 1 at 33 degrees from the normal inside the glass, so ray 2 is bent more toward the normal.
formulaNotes: Snell's law: 1 * sin(50) = n * sin(r), so n is inversely related to sin(r).

shortExplanation: Ray P shows the larger deviation (52 degrees versus 48 degrees for ray Q). Since violet has the higher refractive index in this glass (1.532 versus 1.513 for red), it bends more at each face, so the more-deviated ray P is the violet component.
solutionSteps: Read the deviations from the figure: ray P has delta = 52 degrees, ray Q has delta = 48 degrees.
In a prism, the deviation increases with the refractive index of the light in the glass.
Given n_violet = 1.532 > n_red = 1.513, violet is refracted more strongly at both faces.
Therefore the ray with the larger deviation, ray P, is violet, and ray Q is red.
keyConcept: Dispersion: deviation through a prism grows with refractive index, and violet has the larger index in glass.
commonMistake: Reasoning that longer wavelengths bend more; in normal dispersion it is the shorter (violet) wavelength with the larger n that deviates most.

optionExplanations.1: Longer wavelength means a smaller refractive index in glass, so red is bent less, not more.
optionExplanations.2: Violet travels slowest in the glass (v = c/n with the largest n), and the least-deviated ray is red, not violet.
optionExplanations.3: The 52 and 48 degree labels show the deviations are unequal; the separation is genuine dispersion by refraction, not internal reflection.
optionExplanations.4: It reaches the right ray but with inverted physics: violet's deviation is larger because its refractive index is larger, not smaller.

figureExplanation: The two emergent rays diverge from the dashed undeviated direction with ray P labelled delta = 52 degrees and ray Q labelled delta = 48 degrees; the 4 degree difference is what identifies which colour is which.
formulaNotes: Larger n gives larger deviation delta; v = c/n.

shortExplanation: Since 1 - 1/n = (n-1)/n, its reciprocal is n/(n-1); adding n and combining over the common denominator gives n^2/(n-1).
solutionSteps: Rewrite the inner part: 1 - n^-1 = 1 - 1/n = (n-1)/n.
Take its reciprocal: (1 - n^-1)^-1 = n/(n-1).
Expand the numerator: n^2 - n + n = n^2.
Result: n^2/(n-1).
keyConcept: Reciprocal of a difference: invert the single combined fraction (a - b)/c, never term by term.
commonMistake: Reading (1 - n^-1)^-1 as 1 - n, i.e. inverting each term separately instead of the whole fraction.

optionExplanations.1: (n^2 + n - 1)/n comes from wrongly treating (1 - 1/n)^-1 as (1 - 1/n) and just adding, i.e. forgetting to invert.
optionExplanations.2: 2n/(n-1) would require the added n to also sit over (n-1) without being multiplied up; testing n = 2 gives 4, but n = 3 gives 3 while the original expression gives 4.5.
optionExplanations.3: The value 1 fails immediately at n = 2, where the expression equals 4.

shortExplanation: The L-shaped cross-section has area 4a*3a - 2a*1a = 10a^2, and its perimeter is 14a. With uniform depth 2a the total surface is 2*10a^2 + 14a*2a = 20a^2 + 28a^2 = 48a^2.
solutionSteps: Find the L cross-section area: full rectangle 4a * 3a = 12a^2, minus the notch 2a * 1a = 2a^2, giving 10a^2.
The two identical L-shaped faces (front and back) contribute 2 * 10a^2 = 20a^2.
Walk the outline of the L: bottom 4a, left side 3a, top of tall part 2a, step down 1a, step across 2a, right side 2a; perimeter = 4a + 3a + 2a + 1a + 2a + 2a = 14a.
The side faces form a band of width equal to the depth 2a: lateral area = 14a * 2a = 28a^2.
Total surface area = 20a^2 + 28a^2 = 48a^2.
keyConcept: For any prism, total surface = 2 * (cross-section area) + (cross-section perimeter) * depth.
commonMistake: Forgetting the two exposed walls of the notch (the 1a step and the 2a shelf) when summing the perimeter, or computing the surface of the uncut block.

optionExplanations.0: 36a^2 undercounts several faces, for example by treating the depth as a instead of the labelled 2a.
optionExplanations.1: 42a^2 is what remains if the two notch walls (the 1a and 2a segments, worth 6a^2 of lateral area) are left out of the perimeter.
optionExplanations.3: 52a^2 comes from using the full 12a^2 rectangle for both faces while keeping the notched perimeter, double-counting the removed material.

figureExplanation: The isometric drawing labels the L outline: bottom 4a, left height 3a, top of the tall part 2a, a 1a step down, a 2a horizontal shelf, and a 2a right side, all with a uniform depth of 2a.
formulaNotes: S_total = 2*A_cross + P_cross * depth.

shortExplanation: P lies in the third quadrant with a 30 degree reference angle, so cos theta = -sqrt(3)/2 and sin theta = -1/2. Then 2cos theta + sin theta = -sqrt(3) - 1/2 = -(1 + 2sqrt(3))/2.
solutionSteps: The terminal side passes through P in the third quadrant, 30 degrees below the negative x-axis, so the reference angle is 30 degrees (theta = 210 degrees).
In the third quadrant both cosine and sine are negative.
cos theta = -cos(30) = -sqrt(3)/2 and sin theta = -sin(30) = -1/2.
Compute: 2cos theta + sin theta = 2*(-sqrt(3)/2) + (-1/2) = -sqrt(3) - 1/2.
Write over a common denominator: -(2sqrt(3) + 1)/2, which is the option -(1 + 2sqrt(3))/2.
keyConcept: On the unit circle, cos and sin of an angle are the x and y coordinates of the terminal point, with signs fixed by the quadrant.
commonMistake: Swapping the roles of sin and cos of the 30 degree reference angle, or dropping a negative sign in the third quadrant.

optionExplanations.0: (1 - 2sqrt(3))/2 arises from making only the cosine negative while leaving sin theta = +1/2.
optionExplanations.1: -(2 + sqrt(3))/2 comes from swapping sine and cosine, i.e. using cos theta = -1/2 and sin theta = -sqrt(3)/2.
optionExplanations.4: (1 + 2sqrt(3))/2 has the correct magnitude but positive sign, which would require P to be in the first quadrant.

figureExplanation: P sits on the unit circle in the lower-left (third) quadrant, and the marked 30 degree arc between the terminal side and the negative x-axis fixes the reference angle, so P = (-sqrt(3)/2, -1/2).
formulaNotes: cos(210) = -sqrt(3)/2, sin(210) = -1/2; 2cos theta + sin theta = -sqrt(3) - 1/2.

shortExplanation: The two increases compound to a factor 1.20 x 1.50 = 1.80, so the final concentration must be multiplied by 1/1.8, a decrease of 0.8/1.8 ≈ 44.4%.
solutionSteps: Let the original concentration be C.
After +20%: 1.20·C. After a further +50%: 1.20 x 1.50 x C = 1.80·C.
To return to C, multiply the current value by C/(1.80·C) = 1/1.8 ≈ 0.5556.
The required decrease is 1 - 1/1.8 = 0.8/1.8 = 4/9 ≈ 44.4%.
keyConcept: Successive percentage changes multiply; the reversal percentage is computed relative to the new (larger) base.
commonMistake: Adding 20% + 50% = 70% and assuming a 70% (or 80/180 misread) decrease undoes the change.

optionExplanations.0: 35% treats the problem as halving a 70% total increase, but percentages of different bases cannot be averaged like that.
optionExplanations.2: 55.6% is 1/1.8 expressed as a percentage, i.e. the fraction that remains, not the amount removed.
optionExplanations.3: 70% comes from adding the two increases and using that sum as the required decrease, ignoring compounding and the changed base.

shortExplanation: From the table, L2 has 10 failures out of 50, so each sensor fails with probability 1/5 and passes with 4/5. P(at least one fails) = 1 - (4/5)^2 = 1 - 16/25 = 9/25.
solutionSteps: Read the L2 row of the table: 40 passed, 10 failed, 50 total.
Failure probability for one L2 sensor: p = 10/50 = 1/5; pass probability: 4/5.
Use the complement: P(at least one fails) = 1 - P(both pass).
P(both pass) = (4/5) * (4/5) = 16/25, using independence.
So P(at least one fails) = 1 - 16/25 = 9/25.
keyConcept: Compute 'at least one' probabilities via the complement of 'none'.
commonMistake: Adding 1/5 + 1/5 = 2/5, which double-counts the case in which both sensors fail.

optionExplanations.1: 16/25 is the probability that both sensors pass, the exact complement of the required event.
optionExplanations.2: 2/5 comes from adding the two individual failure probabilities without subtracting the overlap where both fail.
optionExplanations.3: 1/25 is the probability that both sensors fail, not that at least one fails.
optionExplanations.4: 1/5 is the failure probability of a single sensor, ignoring that two are drawn.

figureExplanation: The two-way table's L2 row (40 passed, 10 failed, total 50) supplies the single number needed: the failure rate 10/50 = 1/5.
formulaNotes: P(at least one) = 1 - (1 - p)^2 with p = 1/5.

shortExplanation: The marked x-intercepts (-1, 0) and (3, 0) with y-intercept (0, -3) give g(x) = (x + 1)(x - 3) = x^2 - 2x - 3. Testing the candidates, g(4) = 16 - 8 - 3 = 5, so (4, 5) lies on the curve.
solutionSteps: Use the intercept form with roots -1 and 3: g(x) = k(x + 1)(x - 3).
Fix k from the y-intercept: g(0) = k(1)(-3) = -3k = -3, so k = 1.
Hence g(x) = (x + 1)(x - 3) = x^2 - 2x - 3; check the vertex: g(1) = 1 - 2 - 3 = -4, matching V(1, -4).
Test the candidate points: g(4) = 16 - 8 - 3 = 5, so (4, 5) is on the curve.
Cross-check the rest: g(-2) = 5 (not -3), g(3) = 0 (not -3), g(0) = -3 (not 3), g(1) = -4 (not 4).
keyConcept: A parabola is pinned down by its two roots plus one more point, via g(x) = k(x - r1)(x - r2).
commonMistake: Sign slips such as reading the y-intercept as +3 or evaluating x^2 - 2x - 3 with the wrong sign at negative x.

optionExplanations.1: g(-2) = 4 + 4 - 3 = 5, not -3, so that point sits well above the curve's value there.
optionExplanations.2: x = 3 is a root, so the curve passes through (3, 0), not (3, -3).
optionExplanations.3: The y-intercept of the curve is (0, -3), the reflection of this candidate across the x-axis.
optionExplanations.4: At x = 1 the curve reaches its vertex value -4, not +4.

figureExplanation: The labelled lattice points, roots at (-1, 0) and (3, 0), y-intercept (0, -3) and vertex V(1, -4), determine the equation g(x) = x^2 - 2x - 3 uniquely.

shortExplanation: The marked central angle is 30 deg, so the polygon has 360/30 = 12 sides. The dodecagon's area is (1/2)*12*R^2*sin(30 deg) = 3R^2, so the region between circle and polygon has area (pi - 3)R^2.
solutionSteps: Read the central angle of the shaded triangle from the figure: 30 deg.
The number of sides is n = 360/30 = 12, a regular dodecagon.
Apply the given formula: area = (1/2)*n*R^2*sin(2*pi/n) = (1/2)*12*R^2*sin(30 deg).
Since sin(30 deg) = 1/2, the polygon area is 6*R^2*(1/2) = 3R^2.
The circle has area pi*R^2, so the region inside the circle but outside the polygon is pi*R^2 - 3R^2 = (pi - 3)R^2.
Sanity check: pi - 3 is about 0.14, a small positive sliver, matching the thin gap visible between the circle and the 12-gon.
keyConcept: Central angle 360/n identifies n; inscribed regular polygon area (1/2)*n*R^2*sin(2*pi/n).
commonMistake: Assuming the polygon is a hexagon (60 deg central angle) instead of reading 30 deg, which leads to the 3*sqrt(3)/2 term.

optionExplanations.2: This subtracts the area of a regular hexagon, (3*sqrt(3)/2)R^2, but the marked 30 deg central angle means 12 sides, not 6.
optionExplanations.3: This is the area of the polygon itself, not the leftover region between circle and polygon.
optionExplanations.4: This is the sliver next to a single triangle (one twelfth of the answer), not the total region for all 12 sides.

figureExplanation: The figure marks a 30 deg angle at the centre O between two radii of length R joining adjacent vertices; 360/30 = 12 gives the number of sides, and the thin gap between circle and polygon is the region asked for.

shortExplanation: ax^2 + b = 0 has a real solution exactly when the parabola touches or crosses the x-axis. Sketches I, III and IV meet the x-axis, while II floats entirely above it.
solutionSteps: The solutions of ax^2 + b = 0 are the x-intercepts of the graph y = ax^2 + b.
Sketch I: opens upward with vertex below the x-axis, so it crosses the axis twice — real solutions exist.
Sketch II: opens upward with vertex above the x-axis, so it never meets the axis — no real solution.
Sketch III: opens downward with vertex above the x-axis, so it crosses the axis twice — real solutions exist.
Sketch IV: opens upward with its vertex exactly on the x-axis (b = 0), giving the single real solution x = 0.
Therefore I, III and IV have at least one real solution.
keyConcept: Real roots of a quadratic correspond to points where its graph meets the x-axis.
commonMistake: Forgetting that a vertex sitting exactly on the axis (case IV) still counts as one real (repeated) solution.

optionExplanations.1: Leaving out IV ignores that its vertex touches the x-axis, which is a genuine (double) real root x = 0.
optionExplanations.3: II never meets the x-axis, so its equation has no real solution; this pair is wrong on both counts.
optionExplanations.4: Including II is wrong: an upward parabola whose minimum is above the axis can never reach y = 0.

figureExplanation: What matters in each sketch is whether the curve meets the x-axis: I dips below it, III arches above and comes back down through it, IV touches it at the origin, while II stays strictly above it.

shortExplanation: On 0 < x < 1 raising a proper fraction to a higher power makes it smaller, so x^3 < x < x^(1/3). The top curve I is the cube root, the straight middle curve II is y = x, and the bottom curve III is the cube; Q confirms this since 0.5^(1/3) is about 0.794.
solutionSteps: For 0 < x < 1, multiplying by x (a number less than 1) shrinks a value, so x^3 < x.
Cube both sides of x < x^(1/3) equivalence: since x < 1, the cube root of x is larger than x, so x < x^(1/3).
Combined ordering on the whole interval: x^3 < x < x^(1/3).
In the figure, curve I lies highest, curve II is the straight diagonal, and curve III lies lowest, so I = x^(1/3), II = x, III = x^3.
Check with the marked point: 0.5^(1/3) = 0.7937..., matching Q = (0.5, 0.79) on curve I.
This matches the statement identifying I as the cube root, II as y = x and III as the cube, with x^3 < x < x^(1/3).
keyConcept: For 0 < x < 1, higher powers give smaller values and roots give larger values: x^3 < x < x^(1/3).
commonMistake: Carrying over the behaviour for x > 1 (where cubing enlarges) into the interval 0 < x < 1, where cubing shrinks.

optionExplanations.0: Cubing a proper fraction makes it smaller, not larger, so the cube is the lowest curve, not the highest.
optionExplanations.2: Taking a root of a proper fraction gives a larger number, not a smaller one, so this reverses the actual behaviour.
optionExplanations.3: The three curves meet only at the endpoints x = 0 and x = 1; strictly inside the interval the ordering x^3 < x < x^(1/3) never changes.

figureExplanation: The figure shows curve I bowing above the diagonal, straight curve II from (0,0) to (1,1), and curve III bowing below it; the point Q = (0.5, 0.79) sits on the top curve, and 0.5^(1/3) is approximately 0.794.

shortExplanation: log2(256) = 8 bits and log2(16) = 4 bits, so a symbol from the 256-state source carries 8 - 4 = 4 more bits.
solutionSteps: Write both state counts as powers of 2: 256 = 2^8 and 16 = 2^4.
Information per symbol: source A gives log2(2^8) = 8 bits and source B gives log2(2^4) = 4 bits.
Difference: 8 - 4 = 4 bits.
keyConcept: log2(2^k) = k, so for a power-of-two state count the information in bits is simply the exponent.
commonMistake: Dividing the state counts (256/16 = 16) and reporting 16, instead of subtracting the two logarithms.

optionExplanations.0: The value 2 comes from dividing the two bit counts (8/4) rather than subtracting them.
optionExplanations.2: The value 12 comes from adding the two bit counts (8 + 4) instead of subtracting.
optionExplanations.3: The value 16 is the ratio of the state counts (256/16), not the difference of their base-2 logarithms.

formulaNotes: Information difference = log2(256) - log2(16) = 8 - 4 = 4.

shortExplanation: The two given angles are co-interior (same side of the transversal, between the parallels), so they sum to 180 deg, giving x = 30. Then the angle at line l2 measures 80 deg, and theta is its supplement on the straight line: 100 deg.
solutionSteps: From the figure, (x + 70) deg sits below l1 and (2x + 20) deg sits above l2, both on the same side of t, between the parallel lines: they are co-interior angles.
Co-interior angles between parallels are supplementary: (x + 70) + (2x + 20) = 180.
Then (2x + 20) deg = 80 deg.
theta and the 80 deg angle are adjacent angles on the straight line l2, so theta = 180 - 80 = 100 deg.
Check: theta = 100 deg equals (x + 70) deg = 100 deg, consistent with alternate-angle relationships.
keyConcept: Co-interior (same-side interior) angles between parallel lines sum to 180 deg.
commonMistake: Setting the two expressions equal (treating them as corresponding angles) instead of supplementary, which gives x = 50 and the wrong angle.

optionExplanations.0: 60 deg comes from wrongly equating x + 70 = 2x + 20 and then taking a supplement incorrectly.
optionExplanations.1: 80 deg is the angle (2x + 20) deg itself, not theta, which lies on the other side of the transversal.
optionExplanations.3: 120 deg results from treating the marked angles as equal (x = 50) rather than supplementary.

figureExplanation: Both marked angles lie between the parallels on the right of the transversal, making them co-interior; theta is the angle on the left of the transversal above l2, forming a straight line with the (2x + 20) deg angle.

shortExplanation: The rows form an arithmetic progression with common difference 5 and first term 14; rows 8 through 20 are 13 rows summing to 13*(49 + 109)/2 = 1027.
solutionSteps: Number of rows from 8 to 20 inclusive: 20 - 8 + 1 = 13.
keyConcept: Arithmetic series: the sum of consecutive terms = count * (first term + last term)/2.
commonMistake: Counting 20 - 8 = 12 rows instead of 13, which gives 12*79 = 948.

optionExplanations.0: The value 948 uses 12 rows, forgetting that a range inclusive of both ends has 20 - 8 + 1 = 13 terms.
optionExplanations.2: The value 978 sums rows 9 through 20, starting one row late and omitting row 8.
optionExplanations.4: The value 1230 sums all rows 1 through 20 (20*(14 + 109)/2) instead of only rows 8 through 20.

formulaNotes: a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d; S = k*(a_first + a_last)/2 with k = 13.

shortExplanation: With L + W = 17 and LW = 60, the diagonal satisfies d^2 = L^2 + W^2 = (L+W)^2 - 2LW = 289 - 120 = 169, so d = 13 cm.
solutionSteps: Perimeter 34 cm gives L + W = 17.
Area 60 cm^2 gives L·W = 60.
By Pythagoras, d = sqrt(L^2 + W^2) = sqrt(169) = 13 cm.
keyConcept: The identity (L+W)^2 = L^2 + 2LW + W^2 lets you find L^2 + W^2 without solving for L and W.
commonMistake: Setting the diagonal equal to half the perimeter (17 cm) or forgetting to subtract 2LW.

optionExplanations.1: 17 cm is just L + W (half the perimeter); the diagonal of a rectangle is always shorter than the sum of its sides.
optionExplanations.2: sqrt(229) comes from subtracting only LW = 60 once instead of 2LW = 120.
optionExplanations.4: sqrt(409) comes from adding 2LW instead of subtracting it: 289 + 120 = 409.

shortExplanation: From the grid the large bracket is 2.5 times the small one linearly (15 vs 6, 10 vs 4), so its area is 2.5^2 = 6.25 times larger: 8 * 6.25 = 50 cm² of coating.
solutionSteps: Read matching dimensions from the grid: small bracket height 6 and base 4; large bracket height 15 and base 10.
Linear scale factor k = 15/6 = 10/4 = 2.5.
Areas of similar figures scale by k^2 = 2.5^2 = 6.25.
Coating needed = 8 cm² * 6.25 = 50 cm².
keyConcept: For similar figures, area scales with the square of the linear scale factor.
commonMistake: Multiplying the area by the linear factor 2.5 (giving 20) instead of by its square 6.25.

optionExplanations.0: 20 cm² uses the linear factor 2.5 directly on the area; area must scale by 2.5^2.
optionExplanations.1: 32 cm² corresponds to a scale factor of 2, but the grid shows 15/6 = 2.5.
optionExplanations.4: 125 cm² applies the cube of the factor (volume scaling), but coating covers an area, not a volume.

figureExplanation: The grid shows the small L-shape 6 units tall and 4 wide and the large L-shape 15 units tall and 10 wide, fixing the scale factor at 2.5 in both directions.
formulaNotes: If linear dimensions scale by k, areas scale by k^2: A_large = k^2 * A_small = 2.5^2 * 8 = 50.

shortExplanation: In the after-promotion scenario apprentices are 4/7 of 84 = 48. Undoing the 6 promotions gives 54 apprentices now and 84 - 54 = 30 mentors, a ratio of 54 : 30 = 9 : 5.
solutionSteps: The total stays 84 throughout, since promotions only move people from apprentice to mentor.
After the hypothetical promotions, apprentices = (4/7) x 84 = 48, so mentors = 84 - 48 = 36.
Reverse the 6 promotions to recover the current split: apprentices = 48 + 6 = 54, mentors = 36 - 6 = 30.
Current ratio = 54 : 30, and dividing both by 6 gives 9 : 5.
keyConcept: A hypothetical transfer changes both group sizes but never the total; solve the hypothetical split first, then step backward to the current counts.
commonMistake: Applying the fraction 4/7 to the current situation instead of the after-promotion scenario.

optionExplanations.1: 4 : 3 equals 48 : 36, which is the ratio AFTER the hypothetical promotions, not the current one.
optionExplanations.2: 3 : 2 does not match the actual counts of 54 apprentices to 30 mentors; it is a simple-looking ratio with no valid derivation here.
optionExplanations.3: 5 : 9 is the correct pair of numbers but written in reverse, listing mentors before apprentices.

shortExplanation: Line r through (-3,-1) and (3,3) is y = (2/3)x + 1; line s through (2,5) and (5,2) is y = 7 - x. Setting them equal gives x = 3.6, y = 3.4.
solutionSteps: Cable r passes through (-3, -1) and (3, 3): slope = (3 - (-1))/(3 - (-3)) = 4/6 = 2/3.
Equation of r: y = (2/3)x + 1 (check: x = 3 gives y = 3).
Cable s passes through (2, 5) and (5, 2): slope = (2 - 5)/(5 - 2) = -1.
Equation of s: y = -x + 7 (check: x = 2 gives y = 5).
Then y = 7 - 3.6 = 3.4, so the weld point is (3.6, 3.4).
Check on r: (2/3)(3.6) + 1 = 2.4 + 1 = 3.4. Consistent.
keyConcept: Find each line's equation from two points, then solve the two equations simultaneously.
commonMistake: Swapping the coordinates of the intersection, reporting (3.4, 3.6) instead of (3.6, 3.4).

optionExplanations.1: (3.0, 3.0) is just the marked anchor point (3,3) on line r; line s does not pass through it since 7 - 3 = 4, not 3.
optionExplanations.3: (3.4, 3.6) swaps x and y; substituting shows it fails both equations.

figureExplanation: The grid marks anchors (-3,-1) and (3,3) on the rising cable r and (2,5) and (5,2) on the falling cable s; the crossing visibly occurs between x = 3 and x = 4 slightly above y = 3, consistent with (3.6, 3.4).

shortExplanation: An odd number k of consecutive integers sums to k times the middle integer, so k·m = 100; the only odd factorization keeping every term above 1 is k = 5, m = 20.
solutionSteps: For an odd count k of consecutive integers, the sum equals k x (middle integer m), so k·m = 100.
k must be an odd divisor of 100 greater than 1: k = 5 or k = 25.
If k = 25, m = 4 and the set runs from 4 - 12 = -8 to 16, which includes integers not greater than 1: rejected.
If k = 5, m = 20 and the set is 18, 19, 20, 21, 22 — all greater than 1 and summing to 100.
Therefore the middle integer is 20.
keyConcept: The sum of an odd number of consecutive integers equals the count times the middle term.
commonMistake: Choosing k = 25, m = 4 without checking that the smallest terms of that run violate the 'each greater than 1' condition.

optionExplanations.0: 4 would be the middle of a 25-term run, but that run starts at -8, breaking the condition that every integer exceeds 1.
optionExplanations.1: 5 divides 100 but as a middle value it would need 20 terms, an even count, contradicting the odd-count condition.
optionExplanations.3: 50 would require just two integers (not an odd count) or a single term, contradicting the stated conditions.

shortExplanation: The two facts give b + 3r = 47 and b + r = 23; subtracting yields 2r = 24, so the hourly rate is 12 euros.
solutionSteps: Cost model: cost(h) = b + r·h.
The 3-hour rental: b + 3r = 47.
The first hour alone costs 23: b + r = 23.
Subtract the equations: (b + 3r) - (b + r) = 47 - 23, so 2r = 24 and r = 12.
Check: b = 23 - 12 = 11, and 11 + 3 x 12 = 47, consistent.
keyConcept: Two linear conditions on b and r are solved by elimination: subtracting removes the fixed fee.
commonMistake: Treating 23 euros as the fixed fee b rather than as the total cost of a 1-hour rental (b + r).

optionExplanations.0: 8 euros comes from computing (47 - 23)/3, wrongly spreading the difference over three hours instead of two.
optionExplanations.1: 11 euros is the booking fee b, not the hourly rate.
optionExplanations.4: 23 euros is the total price of the first hour (fee plus one hour), not the rate alone.

shortExplanation: Matching dimensions on both sides leaves the length balance p + 1 - 3 + 1 = 1, so p = 2.
solutionSteps: Left side: [v] = L T^-1.
Right side dimensions: [r^p] = L^p, [g] = L T^-2, [ρ] = M L^-3, [η] = M L^-1 T^-1.
Mass: M^1 from ρ cancels M^1 from η — consistent with no mass on the left.
Time: T^-2 from g divided by T^-1 from η gives T^-1 — matches the left side.
Length: L^p x L x L^-3 / L^-1 = L^(p - 1); this must equal L^1, so p - 1 = 1 and p = 2.
keyConcept: Dimensional homogeneity: each base dimension (M, L, T) must balance separately on both sides.
commonMistake: Forgetting that dividing by η with L^-1 ADDS one power of length to the right side.

optionExplanations.0: p = 0 removes the radius entirely and leaves L^-1 T^-1, which cannot be a speed.
optionExplanations.1: p = 1 leaves the right side as L^0 T^-1, a frequency rather than a speed.
optionExplanations.3: p = 3 gives L^2 T^-1, the dimensions of kinematic viscosity, not velocity.

formulaNotes: This is Stokes' terminal velocity v = (2/9) r^2 g (ρ_s - ρ)/η, confirming the r^2 dependence.

shortExplanation: The maximum error in P = V^2/R is 2(ΔV/V) + (ΔR/R); voltage counts double, so halving its 2% to 1% gives 2x1 + 3 = 5%, better than halving R's error (2x2 + 1.5 = 5.5%).
solutionSteps: For P = V^2/R the maximum fractional error is ΔP/P = 2(ΔV/V) + (ΔR/R).
Without recalibration: 2 x 2% + 3% = 7%.
Option 1 — improve V to 1%: error = 2 x 1% + 3% = 5%.
Option 2 — improve R to 1.5%: error = 2 x 2% + 1.5% = 5.5%.
5% < 5.5%, so improving the voltmeter is better and yields a 5% maximum error.
keyConcept: In a product/quotient formula each variable's percentage error is weighted by its exponent; V appears squared, so its error counts twice.
commonMistake: Improving the instrument with the larger raw error (3% on R) while ignoring that V's error is doubled by the exponent 2.

optionExplanations.1: Improving R does give about 5.5%, but that is worse than the 5% achievable by improving V.
optionExplanations.2: 3.5% ignores the doubling of V's contribution: it computes 2% + 1.5% as if V entered to the first power.
optionExplanations.3: The two choices are not equivalent, because the exponent 2 makes each percent on V twice as valuable as a percent on R.

formulaNotes: ΔP/P = |2| ΔV/V + |-1| ΔR/R for P = V^2 R^-1 (worst-case error addition).

shortExplanation: On an x-t graph the velocity is the slope, so the sled is momentarily at rest where the slope is zero and changes sign — at the minimum of the curve, which occurs at t = 3 s.
solutionSteps: Velocity is the slope of the position-time graph.
From t = 0 to t = 3 s the curve falls (negative slope): the sled moves in the negative direction.
From t = 3 s to t = 6 s the curve rises (positive slope): the sled moves in the positive direction.
At the lowest point of the curve, at t = 3 s (x = -4 m), the slope is zero and the direction reverses.
Therefore the sled is momentarily at rest at t = 3 s.
keyConcept: Zero slope on an x-t graph means zero velocity; a slope sign change marks a reversal of direction.
commonMistake: Picking the instants where x = 0 (t = 1 s and t = 5 s): crossing the origin is not the same as being at rest — the sled moves fastest through those points.

optionExplanations.1: At t = 1 s the graph crosses x = 0 with a steep negative slope, so the sled is moving quickly, not at rest.
optionExplanations.3: At t = 5 s the position is zero but the slope is steep and positive, so the sled is moving, not stopped.
optionExplanations.4: At t = 6 s the curve is still rising steeply (x back at 5 m), so the sled has a large positive velocity.

figureExplanation: The curve starts at x = 5 m, descends through zero at t = 1 s, bottoms out at about x = -4 m at t = 3 s, then rises back through zero at t = 5 s to x = 5 m at t = 6 s; the flat turning point at t = 3 s is the instant of zero velocity.

shortExplanation: P lies in the second quadrant with horizontal displacement -3 and vertical displacement 3*sqrt(3), so tan theta = (3*sqrt(3))/(-3) = -sqrt(3).
solutionSteps: From the figure, the right triangle has a horizontal leg of length 3 measured to the left of the origin and a vertical leg of length 3*sqrt(3) going up, so P = (-3, 3*sqrt(3)).
tan theta = y/x for any point on the terminal side.
tan theta = (3*sqrt(3))/(-3) = -sqrt(3).
Sign check: in the second quadrant sine is positive and cosine negative, so the tangent must be negative, confirming -sqrt(3).
This corresponds to theta = 120 deg, consistent with the drawn angle just past the vertical axis.
keyConcept: tan theta = y/x, with the sign determined by the quadrant of the terminal side.
commonMistake: Dropping the negative sign by using the leg lengths as pure distances and ignoring that x = -3 in the second quadrant.

optionExplanations.0: sqrt(3)/2 is the sine of the reference angle 60 deg, not the tangent of theta.
optionExplanations.2: Positive sqrt(3) ignores the quadrant: with the terminal side in the second quadrant the x-coordinate is negative, forcing a negative tangent.
optionExplanations.3: Negative sqrt(3)/3 inverts the ratio, computing x/y = -3/(3*sqrt(3)) instead of y/x.

figureExplanation: The blue legs mark 3 units left along the x-axis and 3*sqrt(3) units up to P in the second quadrant, while theta opens counterclockwise from the positive x-axis past 90 deg; the ratio rise/run = 3*sqrt(3)/(-3) drives the answer.
formulaNotes: tan theta = y/x = 3*sqrt(3) / (-3) = -sqrt(3).

shortExplanation: The asymptote x = 1 and the points (2,0), (3,1), (5,2) identify f(x) = log2(x - 1). The equation becomes (x-1)(x-3) = 8, whose roots are 5 and -1, but only x = 5 lies in the domain.
solutionSteps: The vertical asymptote x = 1 and the marked points (2, 0), (3, 1), (5, 2) fit f(x) = log2(x - 1): log2(1) = 0, log2(2) = 1, log2(4) = 2.
The equation f(x) + f(x - 2) = 3 becomes log2(x - 1) + log2(x - 3) = 3.
Domain requirement: x - 1 > 0 and x - 3 > 0, so x > 3.
Combine the logs: log2[(x - 1)(x - 3)] = 3, hence (x - 1)(x - 3) = 2^3 = 8.
Expand: x^2 - 4x + 3 = 8, so x^2 - 4x - 5 = 0, factoring as (x - 5)(x + 1) = 0.
Candidates x = 5 and x = -1; only x = 5 satisfies x > 3.
Check: log2(4) + log2(2) = 2 + 1 = 3. Correct.
keyConcept: Identify a shifted logarithm from its asymptote and integer points, then enforce the log domain before accepting roots.
commonMistake: Keeping both roots of the quadratic: x = -1 makes both logarithm arguments negative and must be rejected.

optionExplanations.0: At x = 4 the sum is log2(3) + log2(1) = log2(3), about 1.58, not 3.
optionExplanations.1: At x = 6 the sum is log2(5) + log2(3) = log2(15), about 3.9, which overshoots 3.
optionExplanations.3: Listing both 5 and -1 forgets the domain check: at x = -1 the expressions x - 1 and x - 3 are negative, so f is undefined there.

figureExplanation: The dashed vertical asymptote at x = 1 and the integer points (2, 0), (3, 1) and (5, 2) pin the curve down as y = log2(x - 1); no other marked feature is needed.
formulaNotes: log2(A) + log2(B) = log2(A*B); log2(x-1) + log2(x-3) = 3 means (x-1)(x-3) = 8.

shortExplanation: Tangency at x = -2 means y = (x + 2)^2 = x^2 + 4x + 4, so b = 4 and c = 4, giving c - b = 0.
solutionSteps: The parabola touches the x-axis at exactly one point, read from the figure as x = -2.
A monic quadratic tangent to the x-axis at x = -2 is a perfect square: y = (x + 2)^2.
Expand: y = x^2 + 4x + 4, so b = 4 and c = 4.
Check against the marked intercept: at x = 0, y = 4, matching the point (0, 4) in the figure.
Therefore c - b = 4 - 4 = 0.
keyConcept: A parabola tangent to the x-axis has a double root, so x^2 + bx + c = (x - r)^2 with b = -2r and c = r^2.
commonMistake: Using r = -2 with the wrong signs (e.g. writing (x - 2)^2) and getting b = -4, which contradicts the vertex lying at negative x.

optionExplanations.1: 8 is b + c, not c - b.
optionExplanations.3: -6 would need b and c to differ by 6, impossible here since tangency forces c = (b/2)^2 with vertex at -2, making them equal.
optionExplanations.4: 4 is the value of b (or of c) alone, not their difference.

figureExplanation: The curve touches the x-axis only at the point marked at x = -2 (labelled tangent) and crosses the y-axis at (0, 4); these two features force y = (x + 2)^2.

shortExplanation: Setting 40 - 3t = 28 + t gives 12 = 4t, so the tanks hold equal volumes after t = 3 minutes.
solutionSteps: Tank A volume: 40 - 3t (draining at 3 L/min).
Tank B volume: 28 + t (filling at 1 L/min).
Set equal: 40 - 3t = 28 + t.
Solve: 40 - 28 = 4t, so 12 = 4t and t = 3.
Check: at t = 3, A holds 40 - 9 = 31 L and B holds 28 + 3 = 31 L.
keyConcept: Equal-value problems: model each quantity as a linear function of time and set the expressions equal.
commonMistake: Dividing the 12-litre gap by 3 L/min only, forgetting the tanks approach each other at the combined rate 3 + 1 = 4 L/min.

optionExplanations.0: 6 minutes comes from using a closing rate of 2 L/min (subtracting the rates instead of adding them).
optionExplanations.2: 12 minutes treats the 12-litre difference as if it closed at 1 L/min.
optionExplanations.3: 4 minutes divides the gap by the 3 L/min drain rate alone, ignoring tank B's filling.

shortExplanation: Each factor is a power of 2: 4^5 = 2^10, 8^2 = 2^6, 16^3 = 2^12; adding the exponents gives 2^28.
solutionSteps: Rewrite the bases: 4 = 2^2, 8 = 2^3, 16 = 2^4.
Multiply by adding exponents: 2^(10 + 6 + 12) = 2^28.
commonMistake: Adding the original exponents 5 + 2 + 3 = 10 without first converting each base to a power of 2.

optionExplanations.0: 2^10 keeps only the first factor's converted exponent (or adds the raw exponents 5+2+3), ignoring the base conversions.
optionExplanations.2: 2^20 comes from an arithmetic slip such as 10 + 6 + 4, using the base exponent of 16 instead of 4 x 3.
optionExplanations.3: 2^25 arises from miscomputing 8^2 as 2^9 or 16^3 as 2^9 while converting.

shortExplanation: The marked values 20,000, 14,000 and 9,800 show the printer keeps 70% of its value each year; the end of year 3 value is 9,800 * 0.7 = 6,860 euros.
solutionSteps: Read the marked points on the solid curve: 20,000 at year 0, 14,000 at year 1, 9,800 at year 2.
Compute the yearly ratio: 14,000/20,000 = 0.7 and 9,800/14,000 = 0.7, confirming a constant 30% loss of the remaining value each year.
Apply the ratio once more for year 3: 9,800 * 0.7 = 6,860.
So the actual resale value at the end of year 3 is 6,860 euros.
keyConcept: Constant-percentage decay is geometric: each year's value is the previous value times the same ratio.
commonMistake: Following the dashed straight line (fixed loss of 6,000 per year), which gives 2,000 at year 3 instead of applying the 0.7 ratio.

optionExplanations.0: 2,000 euros comes from the dashed fixed-loss model (20,000 minus 3 * 6,000), not from the actual percentage-loss curve.
optionExplanations.3: 9,800 euros is the value already reached at the end of year 2, not year 3.
optionExplanations.4: 4,802 euros is the value at the end of year 4 (one application of 0.7 too many).

figureExplanation: The solid curve's dots read 20,000, 14,000 and 9,800 at years 0, 1 and 2, fixing the yearly ratio at 0.7; the question mark at year 3 asks for the next point on that curve, while the dashed line is the distractor model.

shortExplanation: The blank cell is 260 - 150 = 110 Electrical students who passed. Everyone else, 400 - 110 = 290 students, is 290/400 = 72.5% of the survey.
solutionSteps: Fill the blank: Electrical passed = column total 260 minus Mechanical passed 150 = 110 (check by row: 180 - 70 = 110).
The complement of 'Electrical AND passed' is every other student: 400 - 110 = 290.
Convert to a percentage: 290/400 = 0.725 = 72.5%.
keyConcept: P(not A) = 1 - P(A): subtract the single cell from the grand total, then divide.
commonMistake: Reading 'not Electrical students who passed' as 'Mechanical students who passed' (150/400 = 37.5%) or as all who failed, instead of the complement of one cell.

optionExplanations.0: 27.5% is the share who ARE Electrical students that passed (110/400), the complement of the answer.
optionExplanations.2: 55% is the share of all Mechanical students (220/400), which is not the requested complement.
optionExplanations.3: 62.5% is 250/400, obtained by wrongly subtracting Mechanical passed (150) instead of Electrical passed (110).

figureExplanation: The table gives n = 400 with the Electrical-passed cell blank; the column total 260 and Mechanical-passed 150 (or row total 180 and Electrical-failed 70) both force the blank to be 110, and the question asks for everyone outside that single cell.

shortExplanation: The two cuts leave 0.75 x 0.80 = 0.60 of the list price, so the original price is 360/0.60 = 600 euro.
solutionSteps: After the first cut the price is 75% of the original: factor 0.75.
After the second cut it is 80% of the reduced price: overall factor 0.75 x 0.80 = 0.60.
Let the original price be x: 0.60·x = 360.
Solve: x = 360 / 0.60 = 600 euro.
Check: 600 -> 450 after 25% off -> 360 after a further 20% off.
keyConcept: Successive discounts multiply their remaining fractions; they never simply add.
commonMistake: Adding 25% + 20% = 45% and computing 360/0.55, or applying the discounts forward to 360.

optionExplanations.0: 450 euro is the intermediate price after only the first 25% reduction, not the original list price.
optionExplanations.1: 480 euro undoes only the 25% cut from 360 (360/0.75), ignoring the second reduction.
optionExplanations.3: 540 euro treats the total discount as a single 25% + 20% = 45% cut miscomputed, or divides 360 by 2/3.

shortExplanation: Line r passes through (0, 5) and (5, 0), giving y = 5 - x; line s passes through (0, -1) and (1, 1), giving y = 2x - 1. Setting them equal gives x = 2, y = 3, so the lines cross at (2, 3).
solutionSteps: Find the equation of r: it passes through (0, 5) and (5, 0), so its slope is (0 - 5)/(5 - 0) = -1 and its y-intercept is 5, giving y = -x + 5.
Find the equation of s: it passes through (0, -1) and (1, 1), so its slope is (1 - (-1))/(1 - 0) = 2 and its y-intercept is -1, giving y = 2x - 1.
Solve the system: set -x + 5 = 2x - 1.
Add x and 1 to both sides: 6 = 3x, so x = 2.
Substitute back: y = -2 + 5 = 3 (check with s: 2*2 - 1 = 3).
The intersection point is (2, 3), which matches where the two lines visibly cross on the grid.
keyConcept: The solution of a system of two linear equations is the point where their graphs intersect; find each line's equation from two marked points, then solve.
commonMistake: Swapping the coordinates and reporting (3, 2) instead of (2, 3), or misreading the slope of s by using only one marked point.

optionExplanations.1: (3, 2) swaps the x- and y-values of the true intersection; at x = 3 line r gives y = 2 but line s gives y = 5, so the lines do not meet there.
optionExplanations.2: (4, 1) lies on line r (5 - 4 = 1) but not on line s (2*4 - 1 = 7), so it is not a simultaneous solution.
optionExplanations.4: (2, 2) has the correct x but the wrong y; both lines pass through x = 2 at height y = 3, not y = 2.

figureExplanation: The marked points (0, 5) and (5, 0) fix line r, and (0, -1) and (1, 1) fix line s; the unlabelled crossing sits exactly at the grid point (2, 3).

shortExplanation: Rescaling both ratios to a common Senior value gives Junior : Senior : Open = 12 : 15 : 10. Junior + Open = 22 parts = 66 teams, so one part = 3 and Senior = 15 x 3 = 45.
solutionSteps: Junior : Senior = 4 : 5, multiplied by 3, becomes 12 : 15.
Senior : Open = 3 : 2, multiplied by 5, becomes 15 : 10.
Senior now has 15 parts in both, so Junior : Senior : Open = 12 : 15 : 10.
Junior + Open = 12 + 10 = 22 parts correspond to 66 teams, so 1 part = 3 teams.
Senior = 15 parts x 3 = 45 teams.
keyConcept: To chain two ratios that share a quantity, rescale both so the shared quantity (Senior) has the same number of parts before combining.
commonMistake: Combining 4 : 5 and 3 : 2 directly without first rescaling Senior to a common value.

optionExplanations.0: 30 is the number of Open teams (10 parts x 3), obtained by answering for the wrong division.
optionExplanations.1: 36 is the number of Junior teams (12 parts x 3), again the count for the wrong division rather than Senior.
optionExplanations.4: 55 comes from not rescaling: treating the chain as Junior : Senior : Open = 4 : 5 : 2, so Junior + Open = 6 parts = 66, giving 1 part = 11 and Senior = 55.

shortExplanation: With vertical sides 12 cm and 6 cm and base b, the slanted top has length sqrt(b^2 + 6^2). The perimeter condition 12 + 6 + b + sqrt(b^2 + 36) = 36 gives b = 8 cm, so the area of the trapezoid is (12 + 6)/2 * 8 = 72 cm^2.
solutionSteps: Call the unknown base b. The two vertical sides are 12 cm and 6 cm, and the base meets them at right angles, so the shape is a right trapezoid.
The slanted top spans a horizontal run of b and a vertical drop of 12 - 6 = 6 cm, so its length is sqrt(b^2 + 36) by the Pythagorean theorem.
Write the perimeter equation: 12 + 6 + b + sqrt(b^2 + 36) = 36, so sqrt(b^2 + 36) = 18 - b.
Square both sides: b^2 + 36 = 324 - 36b + b^2.
The b^2 terms cancel: 36b = 288, so b = 8 cm (and the slant is sqrt(64 + 36) = 10 cm; check: 12 + 6 + 8 + 10 = 36).
Area of a trapezoid = (sum of parallel sides)/2 * distance between them = (12 + 6)/2 * 8 = 9 * 8 = 72 cm^2.
keyConcept: Use the Pythagorean theorem to express the slant side in terms of the unknown base, solve the perimeter equation, then apply the trapezoid area formula.
commonMistake: Treating the slant as equal to the base or forgetting it entirely in the perimeter, which leads to b = 18 and a wildly wrong area.

optionExplanations.0: 48 cm^2 comes from using only the shorter side (6 * 8), treating the plate as a low rectangle and discarding the taller portion.
optionExplanations.3: 96 cm^2 comes from multiplying 12 * 8 as if the plate were a full rectangle, ignoring the slanted cut that removes a triangle.
optionExplanations.4: 108 cm^2 results from using the slant length 10 or a wrong base such as 12 in the area formula instead of the correct base of 8 cm.

figureExplanation: The figure shows right-angle marks at both base corners, a left side of 12 cm, a right side of 6 cm, a base marked '?', and a single straight slanted top joining the two vertical sides — so the vertical sides are the parallel sides of a right trapezoid.
formulaNotes: Trapezoid area = (a + b)/2 * h, where a and b are the parallel sides (12 and 6) and h is the perpendicular distance between them (the base, 8).

shortExplanation: After draining, 400 mL of 20% mixture retains 80 mL of antifreeze; adding 100 mL of pure antifreeze gives 180 mL in 500 mL, i.e. 36%.
solutionSteps: Initial antifreeze: 20% of 500 mL = 100 mL.
Draining 100 mL of well-mixed coolant removes 20% of 100 mL = 20 mL of antifreeze, leaving 80 mL in 400 mL.
Top up with 100 mL of pure antifreeze: antifreeze = 80 + 100 = 180 mL; total volume back to 500 mL.
Concentration = 180/500 = 0.36 = 36%.
keyConcept: Track the absolute amount of solute through each step; the drained liquid carries solute away in proportion to its concentration.
commonMistake: Assuming the drained 100 mL removes no antifreeze (or removes 100 mL of it), instead of 20 mL.

optionExplanations.0: 16% treats the topping-up as if it were water, diluting instead of enriching the mixture.
optionExplanations.1: 20% would only hold if the replacement liquid had the same 20% composition as what was removed.
optionExplanations.3: 40% assumes the drained coolant contained no antifreeze, so that 100 + 100 = 200 mL would remain.

shortExplanation: Writing the integers as n-2 to n+2, the condition 3n - 3 = 2n + 3 gives n = 6, so the largest is 8.
solutionSteps: Let the five consecutive integers be n-2, n-1, n, n+1, n+2.
Sum of the three smallest: (n-2) + (n-1) + n = 3n - 3.
Sum of the two largest: (n+1) + (n+2) = 2n + 3.
Set equal: 3n - 3 = 2n + 3, so n = 6.
The integers are 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; check 4 + 5 + 6 = 15 = 7 + 8. Largest = 8.
keyConcept: Centering consecutive integers on the middle value n turns the condition into a one-step linear equation.
commonMistake: Reporting the middle integer (6) or the smallest (4) instead of the largest of the five.

optionExplanations.0: 4 is the smallest integer of the run.
optionExplanations.1: 6 is the middle integer of the run, not the largest.
optionExplanations.2: 7 is the second-largest; the question asks for the maximum, which is 8.

shortExplanation: The courier ends 110 km from the depot after a total elapsed time of 5 hours, so the average speed is 110/5 = 22 km/h.
solutionSteps: Read the endpoints of the whole trip from the graph: it starts at (0 h, 0 km) and ends at (5 h, 110 km).
Average speed for the entire trip = total distance covered / total elapsed time, including the stop.
Total distance = 110 km; total time = 5 h.
Average speed = 110 km / 5 h = 22 km/h.
keyConcept: Average speed over a whole journey is total distance divided by total time, and the time spent at rest must be included.
commonMistake: Averaging the speeds of the two riding legs (50 km/h and 20 km/h) or excluding the 1-hour rest from the total time.

optionExplanations.2: 27.5 km/h comes from dividing 110 km by only the 4 hours of actual riding, wrongly excluding the rest hour.
optionExplanations.3: 35 km/h is the simple average of the two leg speeds (50 and 20), which ignores that the legs last different times and that the stop counts.
optionExplanations.4: 50 km/h is the speed of the first leg only (50 km in 1 h), not the average over the whole trip.

figureExplanation: The graph rises from 0 to 50 km in the first hour, stays flat at 50 km from hour 1 to hour 2 (labelled 'rest'), then rises to 110 km at hour 5 — so the full trip covers 110 km in 5 hours.

shortExplanation: The sides 15, 20 and 25 satisfy 15^2 + 20^2 = 25^2, so the triangle has a right angle between the 15 m and 20 m sides and its area is (1/2)(15)(20) = 150 m^2.
solutionSteps: Read the side lengths from the figure: AB = 15 m, AC = 20 m, BC = 25 m.
Test the Pythagorean relation: 15^2 + 20^2 = 225 + 400 = 625 = 25^2.
Since the relation holds, the angle at A (between the 15 m and 20 m sides) is a right angle even though no square symbol is drawn.
Cross-check with the coordinates A(0, 12), B(9, 24), C(16, 0) using the shoelace formula: (1/2)|0*(24 - 0) + 9*(0 - 12) + 16*(12 - 24)| = (1/2)|-108 - 192| = 150 m^2.
keyConcept: A 15-20-25 triangle is a scaled 3-4-5 right triangle, so its area is half the product of the two legs; the shoelace formula on the coordinates confirms it.
commonMistake: Using the hypotenuse 25 as a leg, e.g. (1/2)(15)(25) = 187.5 or (1/2)(20)(25) = 250, instead of multiplying the two perpendicular sides.

optionExplanations.0: 192 m^2 is (1/2)(16)(24), taken from the raw coordinate extents rather than a valid base-height pair of the triangle.
optionExplanations.2: 187.5 m^2 is (1/2)(15)(25), which wrongly pairs a leg with the hypotenuse instead of the two perpendicular sides.
optionExplanations.3: 250 m^2 is (1/2)(20)(25), again treating the hypotenuse as if it were a leg.

figureExplanation: The figure gives the vertices A(0, 12), B(9, 24), C(16, 0) and marks the side lengths 15, 25 and 20; recognizing 15-20-25 as a 3-4-5 multiple identifies the hidden right angle at A.

shortExplanation: The constant-volume leg is A to B (V fixed at 2 L while p rises from 100 kPa to 400 kPa). With no work done, Q = deltaU = (3/2)(p_B - p_A)V = (3/2)(300 kPa)(2 L) = +900 J absorbed.
solutionSteps: Identify the constant-volume leg from the diagram: A(2 L, 100 kPa) to B(2 L, 400 kPa) is the vertical segment.
At constant volume the gas does no work: W = 0, so the first law gives Q = deltaU.
For a monatomic ideal gas U = (3/2)pV, so deltaU = (3/2)(p_B V_B - p_A V_A).
Compute: p_B V_B = 400 kPa * 2 L = 800 J and p_A V_A = 100 kPa * 2 L = 200 J (1 kPa * 1 L = 1 J).
Since pressure (and hence temperature) rises, the gas absorbs heat: Q = +900 J.
keyConcept: At constant volume W = 0, so all heat exchanged goes into internal energy: Q = deltaU = (3/2) * delta(pV) for a monatomic ideal gas.
commonMistake: Concluding that zero work means zero heat — internal energy still changes at constant volume, so heat must flow in.

optionExplanations.0: Zero work does not imply zero heat: the pressure (and temperature) rises at fixed volume, so the internal energy increases and that energy must enter as heat.
optionExplanations.1: +600 J is delta(pV) alone, missing the factor 3/2 in the monatomic internal-energy formula.
optionExplanations.3: -900 J has the right magnitude but the wrong sign: pressure increases at constant volume, so the gas absorbs heat rather than releasing it.

figureExplanation: The vertical arrowed segment from A(2 L, 100 kPa) up to B(2 L, 400 kPa) is the only leg with unchanging volume; its endpoint pressures and the fixed 2 L volume supply all the numbers needed.
formulaNotes: First law: Q = deltaU + W. Isochoric: W = 0. Monatomic gas: U = (3/2)pV, so Q = (3/2)(p_B - p_A)V. Unit fact: 1 kPa * 1 L = 1 J.

shortExplanation: Equal pulls at the midpoint's distances mean the planet is 9 times as massive as the moon; the balance point then satisfies 3(d - x) = x, i.e. x = 3d/4 from the planet.
solutionSteps: At the midpoint both bodies are at the same distance d/2, so the force ratio equals the mass ratio: M_planet = 9·M_moon.
At the balance point at distance x from the planet: G·M_planet/x^2 = G·M_moon/(d - x)^2.
Substitute M_planet = 9·M_moon and cancel: 9/(x^2) = 1/(d - x)^2.
Take square roots: 3(d - x) = x.
Solve: 3d = 4x, so x = (3/4)d — three quarters of the way from planet to moon.
keyConcept: The gravitational null point lies closer to the lighter body, at distances in the ratio sqrt(M_planet) : sqrt(M_moon) = 3 : 1.
commonMistake: Splitting the separation in the mass ratio 9 : 1 (giving 9/10) instead of the square-root ratio 3 : 1.

optionExplanations.1: The midpoint cannot be the balance point, since there the planet already pulls 9 times harder.
optionExplanations.2: 1/4 of the way puts the probe closer to the massive planet, where its pull would dominate even more.
optionExplanations.3: 9/10 uses the mass ratio directly rather than its square root, forgetting the inverse-square law.

formulaNotes: M_p/x^2 = M_m/(d-x)^2 with M_p = 9 M_m gives x/(d-x) = 3, hence x = 3d/4.

shortExplanation: The parabola opens upward and its vertex (3, 4) sits exactly on the line y = 4, so f(x) >= 4 for every real x. The strict inequality f(x) < 4 is therefore never satisfied.
solutionSteps: Read the graph: the solid curve is an upward-opening parabola whose lowest point is the marked vertex (3, 4).
The dashed line y = 4 passes exactly through this vertex, so the curve touches the line at x = 3 and lies above it everywhere else.
Hence f(x) > 4 for all x not equal to 3, and f(3) = 4.
The strict inequality f(x) < 4 requires the curve to dip below the line, which never happens.
The solution set is empty: no real x satisfies f(x) < 4.
keyConcept: When an upward parabola is tangent to a horizontal line at its vertex, the function value never falls strictly below that line.
commonMistake: Answering x = 3 — but at x = 3 the function equals 4, which fails a strict 'less than' inequality.

optionExplanations.0: At x = 3 the graph touches the line, so f(3) = 4; equality does not satisfy the strict inequality f(x) < 4.
optionExplanations.1: 1 < x < 5 would be correct only if the line crossed the parabola at x = 1 and x = 5, but the graph shows tangency at a single point, not two crossings.
optionExplanations.4: Every x except 3 is where f(x) is strictly greater than 4, i.e. the solution of f(x) > 4, not f(x) < 4.

figureExplanation: The key feature is that the dashed line y = 4 touches the parabola only at the labelled vertex (3, 4) — the curve never goes below the dashed line.

shortExplanation: By the remainder theorem the remainder of R(x) on division by (x - 1) is R(1) = P(1) + 3 - 1; since the sum of P's coefficients is P(1) = 7, the remainder is 7 + 2 = 9.
solutionSteps: The sum of all coefficients of P equals P(1), so P(1) = 7.
By the remainder theorem, dividing R(x) by (x - 1) leaves remainder R(1).
The condition about division by x (which gives P(0) = -5) is not needed for this remainder.
keyConcept: Remainder theorem: the remainder of a polynomial on division by (x - a) is its value at x = a; the coefficient sum is the value at x = 1.
commonMistake: Using P(0) = -5 (the remainder on division by x) instead of P(1) when evaluating at x = 1.

optionExplanations.0: 7 is just P(1), forgetting to add the contribution 3(1) - 1 = 2 from the added terms.
optionExplanations.1: 11 adds 3 + 1 instead of 3 - 1, mishandling the sign of the constant term.
optionExplanations.3: -3 comes from evaluating with P(0) = -5: -5 + 3 - 1 = -3, which answers division by x, not by (x - 1).

shortExplanation: From the grid, AB and AC both have length sqrt(5) and the marked right angle is at A, so the triangle is right isosceles with angles 90, 45, 45. The sum of cosines is 0 + sqrt(2)/2 + sqrt(2)/2 = sqrt(2).
solutionSteps: Read the vertices: A(2, 1), B(4, 2), C(1, 3), with the small square marking a right angle at A.
Compute AB = sqrt((4-2)^2 + (2-1)^2) = sqrt(4 + 1) = sqrt(5).
Compute AC = sqrt((1-2)^2 + (3-1)^2) = sqrt(1 + 4) = sqrt(5).
Confirm perpendicularity: vector AB = (2, 1) and vector AC = (-1, 2) have dot product 2*(-1) + 1*2 = 0.
The triangle is right isosceles: angle A = 90 degrees, angles B and C are each 45 degrees.
Sum: cos 90 + cos 45 + cos 45 = 0 + sqrt(2)/2 + sqrt(2)/2 = sqrt(2).
keyConcept: In a right isosceles triangle the angles are 90-45-45, and cos 90 = 0 while cos 45 = sqrt(2)/2.
commonMistake: Using cos 90 = 1 (confusing it with cos 0), which adds a spurious 1 and gives 1 + sqrt(2).

optionExplanations.0: 1 would follow from treating the base angles as 60 degrees (cos 60 = 1/2 each), but the equal legs force 45-degree base angles.
optionExplanations.1: sqrt(2)/2 counts only one of the two 45-degree angles instead of both.
optionExplanations.3: 1 + sqrt(2) results from taking cos 90 = 1 instead of 0.

figureExplanation: The square symbol at A(2, 1) marks the right angle, and counting grid squares shows both legs AB and AC span a 2-by-1 step, so they are equal in length — this makes the two remaining angles 45 degrees each.

shortExplanation: Adding numerator exponents and subtracting denominator exponents gives (n+3)+(2n-1)-(n+2)-(n-4) = n+4, and n+4 is divisible by 4 exactly when n is a multiple of 4.
solutionSteps: Combine the numerator: 2^(n+3) · 2^(2n-1) = 2^(3n+2).
Combine the denominator: 2^(n+2) · 2^(n-4) = 2^(2n-2).
Divide by subtracting exponents: P = 2^((3n+2)-(2n-2)) = 2^(n+4).
Require 4 | (n + 4). Since 4 | 4, this holds exactly when 4 | n, i.e. n ≡ 0 (mod 4).
Check: n = 4 gives exponent 8 (multiple of 4); n = 2 gives exponent 6 (not a multiple of 4).
keyConcept: Same-base exponent rules (add when multiplying, subtract when dividing) plus modular reasoning: n + 4 ≡ n (mod 4).
commonMistake: Concluding that any even n works, e.g. from testing n = 4 and generalizing, though n = 2 gives exponent 6.

optionExplanations.1: Even n is not sufficient: n = 2 makes the exponent 6, which 4 does not divide.
optionExplanations.2: n = 0 works but is not the only case: n = 4, 8, -4, ... all give exponents divisible by 4.
optionExplanations.3: The exponent is n + 4, not n; the simplification loses the +4 only if the denominator exponents are added instead of subtracted incorrectly.

shortExplanation: The kite PAOB is two congruent right triangles of area (1/2)*20*PA, so 20*PA = 300 gives PA = 15 m and OP = sqrt(20^2 + 15^2) = 25 m. The chord AB is twice the altitude from A to OP: AB = 2*(20*15/25) = 24 m.
solutionSteps: Read the radius from the figure: OA = OB = 20 m, with right angles at A and B because a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the contact point.
PAOB splits along OP into two congruent right triangles OAP and OBP, each with legs OA = 20 and PA (tangent length).
Area condition: 2 * (1/2) * 20 * PA = 300, so 20 * PA = 300 and PA = 15 m.
Hypotenuse: OP = sqrt(20^2 + 15^2) = sqrt(400 + 225) = sqrt(625) = 25 m.
By symmetry OP is the perpendicular bisector of chord AB, and half of AB is the altitude from A to the hypotenuse in triangle OAP: h = (leg1 * leg2)/hypotenuse = (20 * 15)/25 = 12 m.
Therefore AB = 2 * 12 = 24 m.
keyConcept: Tangent-radius perpendicularity plus kite symmetry: AB equals twice the altitude to the hypotenuse of right triangle OAP, i.e. AB = 2*OA*PA/OP.
commonMistake: Stopping at a partial result — reporting the tangent length 15 m or the half-chord 12 m instead of the full chord AB = 24 m.

optionExplanations.0: 12 m is only half of AB — the perpendicular distance from A to the line OP — and must be doubled.
optionExplanations.1: 15 m is the length of each tangent walkway PA (or PB), not the chord joining the contact points.
optionExplanations.3: 25 m is the distance OP from the centre to the gate, the hypotenuse of the right triangle, not the chord AB.

figureExplanation: The figure marks the radius 20 m, right angles at A and B where the tangents touch the circle, and the dashed symmetry line OP; the green segment AB is the chord whose length is asked, bisected perpendicularly by OP.
formulaNotes: Altitude to the hypotenuse of a right triangle: h = (product of legs)/hypotenuse. Here AB = 2h = 2*(20*15)/25 = 24.

shortExplanation: The red curve passes through (1, 2) and (10, -1). Writing h(x) = a + b*log10(x), the point (1, 2) forces a = 2 and the point (10, -1) forces 2 + b = -1, so b = -3 and h(x) = 2 - 3*log10(x) = log10(100/x^3).
solutionSteps: Read the marked points: the blue curve f(x) = log10(x) passes through (1, 0) and (10, 1); the red curve h passes through (1, 2) and (10, -1).
Model the transformation as h(x) = a + b*log10(x) (a vertical stretch/reflection plus a shift).
Thus h(x) = 2 - 3*log10(x).
Rewrite with log laws: 2 - 3*log10(x) = log10(100) - log10(x^3) = log10(100/x^3).
Check the shape: the red curve is decreasing, consistent with the negative coefficient -3.
keyConcept: Two marked points determine the transformation h(x) = a + b*log10(x); log laws convert 2 - 3*log10(x) into the single expression log10(100/x^3).
commonMistake: Dropping the sign when combining logs and writing log10(100*x^3), which increases with x while the red graph clearly decreases.

optionExplanations.1: log10(100*x^3) = 2 + 3*log10(x) is increasing and gives 5 at x = 10, but the red curve is decreasing and passes through (10, -1).
optionExplanations.2: log10(2/x^3) gives log10(2), about 0.3, at x = 1, not the marked value 2.
optionExplanations.3: log10(100/x^2) = 2 - 2*log10(x) fits (1, 2) but gives 0 at x = 10 instead of -1.

figureExplanation: The decisive data are the two red points: (1, 2) fixes the vertical shift (since log10(1) = 0) and (10, -1) fixes the multiple of log10(x) (since log10(10) = 1); the downward trend of the red curve confirms the negative coefficient.

shortExplanation: A = (-2, 1) and B = (4, 5), so the midpoint is (1, 3) and the slope of AB is 2/3. The perpendicular bisector has slope -3/2 and passes through (1, 3), giving y = -3/2*x + 9/2.
solutionSteps: Read the endpoints from the grid: A(-2, 1) and B(4, 5).
Midpoint of AB: ((-2 + 4)/2, (1 + 5)/2) = (1, 3) — this matches the open circle labelled 'equidistant from A & B'.
The perpendicular bisector has the negative reciprocal slope: -3/2.
Point-slope form through (1, 3): y - 3 = -3/2*(x - 1), so y = -3/2*x + 9/2.
Verify with the other open circles: at x = 3, y = -9/2 + 9/2 = 0 (the point on the x-axis), and at x = -1, y = 3/2 + 9/2 = 6 (the upper-left point) — both lie on the line.
keyConcept: The set of points equidistant from two points is the perpendicular bisector: it passes through the midpoint with slope equal to the negative reciprocal of the segment's slope.
commonMistake: Using the segment's own slope 2/3 instead of the negative reciprocal -3/2, which produces the line through A and B rather than its bisector.

optionExplanations.1: y = 2/3*x + 7/3 has the slope of segment AB itself, not the perpendicular slope; a bisector must be perpendicular to AB.
optionExplanations.3: y = -3/2*x - 2 has the correct slope but the wrong intercept: it misses the midpoint (1, 3), giving -3/2 - 2 = -7/2 there.
optionExplanations.4: y = -2/3*x + 11/3 uses the negative of the original slope without taking the reciprocal, so it is not perpendicular to AB.

figureExplanation: The filled dots give A(-2, 1) and B(4, 5); the three open circles — at (1, 3), (3, 0) and (-1, 6) — all satisfy y = -3/2*x + 9/2, confirming that this is the equidistant line.

shortExplanation: E equals the fourth root of 3/2, and rationalizing 3/2 to 24/16 inside the fourth root gives ∜24 / 2.
solutionSteps: Write everything with fractional exponents: E = ((3/2) · (2/3)^(1/2))^(1/2).
Distribute the outer square root: E = (3/2)^(1/2) · (2/3)^(1/4).
Combine powers of the same fraction: (3/2)^(1/2) · (3/2)^(-1/4) = (3/2)^(1/4).
So E = ∜(3/2). Rationalize by multiplying inside by 8/8: 3/2 = 24/16.
keyConcept: A square root of a square root is a fourth root; combine (3/2)^(1/2) x (2/3)^(1/4) via exponent arithmetic.
commonMistake: Multiplying 3/2 by 2/3 first (getting 1) and forgetting that the inner factor sits under an extra square root.

optionExplanations.1: √6 / 2 equals (3/2)^(1/2), the value obtained if the inner square root is ignored entirely.
optionExplanations.2: ∜6 / 2 has fourth power 6/16 = 3/8, not 3/2, so it is too small.
optionExplanations.4: ∜24 / 4 has fourth power 24/256 = 3/32; the denominator should be ∜16 = 2, not 4.

shortExplanation: Joining midpoints quarters the area: DEF has area 48/4 = 12 cm^2 and GHI has area 12/4 = 3 cm^2. The shaded region is DEF with GHI removed, so its area is 12 - 3 = 9 cm^2.
solutionSteps: Joining the midpoints of a triangle creates a medial triangle similar to the original with ratio 1/2, so its area is 1/4 of the original.
Area of DEF = 48/4 = 12 cm^2.
Repeat for the inner triangle: area of GHI = 12/4 = 3 cm^2.
From the figure, the shaded region consists of the three corner triangles of DEF (DGI, IHF and GEH) — that is, all of DEF except the central triangle GHI.
Shaded area = area(DEF) - area(GHI) = 12 - 3 = 9 cm^2.
Check: each corner triangle of DEF is congruent to GHI (area 3), and 3 * 3 = 9 cm^2.
keyConcept: The medial triangle of any triangle has one quarter of its area, and this quartering can be applied repeatedly.
commonMistake: Shading-set confusion: reporting the whole of DEF (12 cm^2) or only the central triangle GHI (3 cm^2) instead of DEF minus GHI.

optionExplanations.0: 3 cm^2 is the area of the innermost triangle GHI, which is exactly the part left white, not the shaded part.
optionExplanations.1: 6 cm^2 would correspond to only two of the three shaded corner triangles; the figure shades all three.
optionExplanations.3: 12 cm^2 is the entire area of DEF, but the central triangle GHI is unshaded and must be subtracted.

figureExplanation: The shading covers the three outer triangles of DEF — between D, G and I, between I, H and F, and between G, E and H — while the central triangle GHI and the three corner regions of ABC remain white.

shortExplanation: Take the full amount as 100 units: after draining 20% then 25% of the remainder, 60 units are left. Refilling to 90 units means adding 30 units, and 30/60 = 50% of what was present at the start of the third phase.
solutionSteps: Let the full system hold 100 units of coolant.
Phase 1 drains 20%: 100 - 20 = 80 units remain.
Phase 2 drains 25% of the 80 units present: 80 - 0.25*80 = 80 - 20 = 60 units remain.
Phase 3 must bring the level to 90% of the original: target = 90 units.
Fresh coolant added = 90 - 60 = 30 units.
Percentage of the volume at the start of phase 3: 30/60 = 0.50 = 50%.
keyConcept: Successive percentage changes act on the current amount, and a requested percentage must use the stated reference base (here, the phase-3 starting volume).
commonMistake: Computing 30 units as a percentage of the original 100 units (giving 30%) instead of the 60 units actually present when the refill begins.

optionExplanations.1: 30% comes from dividing the 30 added units by the original full volume of 100 units, but the question asks for a percentage of the 60 units present at the start of the third phase.
optionExplanations.2: 45% would follow from mishandling the second drain (e.g. removing 25% of the original instead of 25% of the remainder), which changes both the remaining amount and the ratio.
optionExplanations.4: 67% is roughly 40/60, which arises from wrongly assuming the tank must be refilled all the way to 100% of the original amount rather than to 90%.

shortExplanation: The 5 large statues can be arranged on the 5 large pedestals in 5! = 120 ways, and independently the 2 small statues on the 2 small pedestals in 2! = 2 ways, giving 120 * 2 = 240 arrangements.
solutionSteps: From the figure, the row has 5 large pedestals (positions 1, 3, 4, 6, 7) and 2 small pedestals (positions 2 and 5).
Size restrictions split the placement into two independent sub-problems: large statues onto large pedestals, small statues onto small pedestals.
Arrange the 5 distinct large statues on the 5 large pedestals: 5! = 120 ways.
Arrange the 2 distinct small statues on the 2 small pedestals: 2! = 2 ways.
By the multiplication principle, total arrangements = 120 * 2 = 240.
keyConcept: When constraints split objects into independent groups, multiply the number of arrangements of each group (multiplication principle with permutations).
commonMistake: Ignoring the size restriction and computing 7! = 5040, or adding the two counts (120 + 2) instead of multiplying them.

optionExplanations.2: 122 comes from adding 5! + 2! instead of multiplying the two independent choices.
optionExplanations.3: 5040 = 7! counts free placement of all statues on all pedestals, ignoring that small statues cannot use large pedestals and vice versa.
optionExplanations.4: 21 is the binomial coefficient C(7, 2), which would count choices of positions for identical statues, but the statues are distinct and positions are already fixed by size.

figureExplanation: The pedestal row reads L, S, L, L, S, L, L from left to right — exactly five large and two small pedestals in fixed positions, which is what makes the two permutation counts independent.

shortExplanation: Both bodies feel the same net force of 10 N (B = 15 N vs W = 5 N for P, W = 25 N vs B = 15 N for Q), but their masses differ by a factor of 5, so the accelerations are in the ratio 5 : 1.
solutionSteps: Read the forces from the diagram: P has B = 15 N up and W = 5 N down; Q has B = 15 N up and W = 25 N down.
Net force on P: 15 - 5 = 10 N upward (P accelerates upward).
Net force on Q: 25 - 15 = 10 N downward (Q accelerates downward).
Find the masses from the weights with g = 10 m/s^2: m_P = 5/10 = 0.5 kg; m_Q = 25/10 = 2.5 kg.
keyConcept: Newton's second law a = F_net/m: equal net forces produce accelerations inversely proportional to the masses.
commonMistake: Seeing equal net forces (10 N each) and concluding the accelerations are equal, forgetting that the two bodies have different masses.

optionExplanations.0: Equal net forces do not mean equal accelerations: the masses (from W = mg) are 0.5 kg and 2.5 kg, so the accelerations differ.
optionExplanations.1: A 5 : 2 ratio does not follow from any correct combination of the given forces and masses; the mass ratio is exactly 1 : 5, so the acceleration ratio is exactly 5 : 1.
optionExplanations.4: The liquid's density is not needed: the buoyant force is already given numerically (15 N) in the diagram.

figureExplanation: The scaled arrows show B = 15 N up on both bodies (equal volumes, same liquid), while the weight arrows differ: 5 N for P (shorter than B, so P rises) and 25 N for Q (longer than B, so Q sinks). The numbers on the arrows supply everything needed.

shortExplanation: The graph gives v = 20 m/s at t = 2 s, and its slope gives g = 10 m/s^2, so the mass is 60/10 = 6 kg and KE = 0.5*6*20^2 = 1200 J.
solutionSteps: From the graph, the line passes through v = 20 m/s at t = 2 s (marked with dashed lines).
The slope of the v-t line is the gravitational acceleration: g = 20/2 = 10 m/s^2.
Find the mass from the weight: m = P/g = 60/10 = 6 kg.
Read the speed at t = 2 s directly from the graph: v = 20 m/s.
keyConcept: On a velocity-time graph for free fall, the slope equals the local g; combining it with the weight gives the mass needed for KE = (1/2)mv^2.
commonMistake: Using the weight 60 N directly as the mass (60 kg), or assuming g = 9.8 m/s^2 instead of reading g from the graph.

optionExplanations.1: 2400 J omits the factor 1/2 in the kinetic energy formula (6*400 instead of 0.5*6*400).
optionExplanations.2: 12000 J comes from treating the 60 N weight as a 60 kg mass; the mass is P/g = 6 kg.
optionExplanations.3: 300 J would result from using v = 10 m/s (the value at t = 1 s) instead of the speed at t = 2 s.
