A plane through the centre O perpendicular to VW is preserved by this 120° rotation, so the cross-section must have 3-fold symmetry.
The plane through O perpendicular to VW misses both endpoints' corners and instead crosses all six faces of the cube, one edge of the section per face.
Six sides with 3-fold symmetry and, by the cube's additional point symmetry about O, all sides and angles equal: the section is a regular hexagon.
Concretely, for a unit cube from (0,0,0) to (1,1,1) with diagonal along (1,1,1), the plane x + y + z = 3/2 cuts the edges at their midpoints, giving six vertices equally spaced: a regular hexagon.
keyConcept: The central cross-section of a cube perpendicular to a body diagonal passes through the midpoints of six edges and is a regular hexagon.
commonMistake: Expecting a square or triangle: squares come from cuts parallel to a face, and equilateral triangles come from cuts near a corner perpendicular to the diagonal, not from the central cut.

optionExplanations.0: A square section arises from planes parallel to a face (or certain other orientations), not from a plane perpendicular to a space diagonal.
optionExplanations.1: An equilateral triangle appears only when the perpendicular cut is close to vertex V or W (slicing off a corner), not when it passes through the centre.
optionExplanations.3: A rectangle arises from planes containing a pair of parallel edges; the perpendicular-to-diagonal cut has 3-fold symmetry, which a rectangle lacks.

figureExplanation: The figure shows the cube drawn along the diagonal VW (V top vertex, W bottom vertex) with O marked at its midpoint; viewed along VW the cube's outline is already a hexagon, hinting that the central perpendicular cut meets all six faces.

shortExplanation: Folding the staircase net shows each face pairs with the one two steps away along the zigzag: P with S, Q with T, and R with U.
solutionSteps: Take S as the bottom face of the cube.
R (attached above S) folds up to become the back face, and T (attached to the right of S) folds up to become the right face.
U hangs from T, so it wraps around to become the front face - opposite R.
Q is attached to R, so it wraps to the left face - opposite T.
P is attached to Q and folds over to close the top - opposite the bottom S.
The three opposite pairs are therefore P-S, Q-T and R-U.
keyConcept: In a staircase (zigzag) cube net, faces separated by two squares along the zigzag end up on opposite sides of the cube.
commonMistake: Pairing squares that share an edge in the net (such as P with Q, or S with T); net neighbours always remain adjacent on the folded cube, never opposite.

optionExplanations.0: The pairing that puts Q with R and T with U is wrong because Q-R and T-U share edges in the net, so those faces are adjacent on the cube.
optionExplanations.2: P and U are at the two extreme ends of the zigzag, four steps apart, and folding brings them onto adjacent faces (top and front), not opposite ones.
optionExplanations.3: The pairing that puts P with Q, R with S and T with U matches net neighbours exactly, and neighbouring squares can never be opposite faces.

figureExplanation: The net is a diagonal staircase: P above Q, then Q-R side by side, S below R, S-T side by side, and U below T; each opposite pair (P-S, Q-T, R-U) is separated by exactly two squares along this zigzag.

solutionSteps: Raise to the third power: (2 * 5^2 * 13)^3 = 2^3 * 5^6 * 13^3.
keyConcept: Factor common terms before applying the power: (ab)^n = a^n b^n and a^m * a^n = a^(m+n).
commonMistake: Adding exponents inside the sum (treating 5^4 + 5^2 as 5^6) instead of factoring out 5^2.

optionExplanations.0: The exponent of 2 must be 3 + 4 = 7 and 13 must appear cubed; this option has 2^4 and 13^2.
optionExplanations.1: 5^2 inside the parentheses becomes 5^6 after cubing, not 5^2, and 13 appears cubed, not squared.
optionExplanations.2: Cubing multiplies every exponent by 3, so 13 appears as 13^3 and the total power of 2 is 2^7.

shortExplanation: Equation A has solution set {0} (x = 3 is excluded because it annuls the denominator x^2 - 9), while equation B has solution set {0, 3} (its denominator never vanishes), so the solutions of A are included in those of B.
solutionSteps: Both numerators equal x^2 - 3x = x(x - 3), which vanishes at x = 0 and x = 3.
Equation A: the denominator x^2 - 9 vanishes at x = 3 and x = -3, so x = 3 must be excluded; solutions of A: {0}.
Equation B: the denominator x^2 - 3x + 9 has discriminant 9 - 36 = -27 < 0, so it never vanishes; solutions of B: {0, 3}.
Since {0} is contained in {0, 3}, the set of solutions of A is included in the set of solutions of B.
keyConcept: A fraction equals zero when the numerator is zero AND the denominator is nonzero; always check the domain.
commonMistake: Solving only the numerator and forgetting that x = 3 makes the denominator of the first equation vanish.

optionExplanations.0: The two solution sets are {0} and {0, 3}; they are not equal because x = 3 is excluded from the first equation.
optionExplanations.1: The inclusion goes the other way: {0, 3} is not contained in {0}.
optionExplanations.3: They share only one solution, x = 0; x = 3 solves the second equation but not the first.

formulaNotes: Discriminant of x^2 - 3x + 9: (-3)^2 - 4*1*9 = -27 < 0, so the denominator of B never vanishes.

shortExplanation: log_5((x+3)^2) = 2 means (x+3)^2 = 5^2 = 25, so x + 3 = 5 or x + 3 = -5, giving x = 2 and x = -8; both keep (x+3)^2 > 0.
solutionSteps: Rewrite the logarithmic equation in exponential form: (x+3)^2 = 5^2 = 25.
Take both square roots: x + 3 = 5 or x + 3 = -5.
First case: x = 2. Second case: x = -8.
Check the domain: (x+3)^2 must be positive; at x = 2 it equals 25 and at x = -8 it equals 25, both valid.
The equation has the two solutions x = 2 and x = -8.
keyConcept: The argument of the log is a square, so both signs of x + 3 must be considered.
commonMistake: Writing log((x+3)^2) = 2 log(x+3) without absolute value, which silently discards the solution x = -8.

optionExplanations.0: At x = -2 the argument is (1)^2 = 1 and log_5 1 = 0, not 2.
optionExplanations.1: (x+3)^2 = 25 clearly has real solutions; the equation is solvable.
optionExplanations.3: x = 2 is a solution but not the only one; x = -8 also gives (x+3)^2 = 25.

formulaNotes: log_b(y) = c is equivalent to y = b^c; here (x+3)^2 = 25.

shortExplanation: With f + s = 60 and f + 80 = 3f - 2s, the second equation gives f - s = 40, so f = 50 and s = 10.
solutionSteps: Let f be the father's current age and s the son's: f + s = 60.
Condition in eighty years: f + 80 = 3f - 2s.
Simplify: 80 = 2f - 2s, hence f - s = 40.
Add the equations: (f + s) + (f - s) = 60 + 40, so 2f = 100 and f = 50.
keyConcept: Translate age conditions into a linear system and solve by elimination.
commonMistake: Adding 80 years to both people's ages; the condition compares the father's future age with current ages only.

optionExplanations.1: 48 and 12: 48 + 80 = 128 but 3*48 - 2*12 = 120; the second condition fails.
optionExplanations.3: 45 and 15: 45 + 80 = 125 but 3*45 - 2*15 = 105; the second condition fails.
optionExplanations.4: 52 and 8: 52 + 80 = 132 but 3*52 - 2*8 = 140; the second condition fails.

shortExplanation: Simplifying each radical: sqrt(75) = 5sqrt(3), 3sqrt(18) = 9sqrt(2), 2sqrt(12) = 4sqrt(3), 2sqrt(50) = 10sqrt(2); combining gives (5-4)sqrt(3) + (9-10)sqrt(2) = sqrt(3) - sqrt(2).
solutionSteps: sqrt(75) = sqrt(25*3) = 5 sqrt(3).
3 sqrt(18) = 3 sqrt(9*2) = 9 sqrt(2).
2 sqrt(12) = 2 sqrt(4*3) = 4 sqrt(3).
Combine like radicals: (5 - 4) sqrt(3) + (9 - 10) sqrt(2) = sqrt(3) - sqrt(2).
keyConcept: Extract perfect squares from each radicand, then combine like radicals.
commonMistake: Sign slip when collecting the sqrt(2) terms: 9 sqrt(2) - 10 sqrt(2) is -sqrt(2), not +sqrt(2).

optionExplanations.0: sqrt(3) + sqrt(2) comes from dropping the minus sign on the sqrt(2) contribution.
optionExplanations.3: sqrt(2) - sqrt(3) has both signs flipped; the sqrt(3) terms give +1, the sqrt(2) terms give -1.
optionExplanations.4: 9 sqrt(3) + 19 sqrt(2) comes from adding all coefficients instead of respecting the minus signs.

shortExplanation: The factor 2x^2 - 11 gives x = +sqrt(11/2) and x = -sqrt(11/2); the factor x^4 - x^2 + 5, seen as a quadratic in x^2, has negative discriminant and is always positive, so there are exactly two real solutions.
solutionSteps: A product is zero when at least one factor is zero.
First factor: 2x^2 - 11 = 0 gives x^2 = 11/2, hence x = sqrt(11/2) or x = -sqrt(11/2): two real solutions.
Second factor: set u = x^2, then u^2 - u + 5 has discriminant 1 - 20 = -19 < 0.
So u^2 - u + 5 > 0 for all real u, and the second factor never vanishes for real x.
The equation therefore has exactly two real solutions, one positive and one negative.
keyConcept: Solve each factor separately; a biquadratic with negative discriminant in x^2 contributes no real roots.
commonMistake: Counting the degree (degree 6) and expecting six real solutions; complex roots of the quartic factor are not real solutions.

optionExplanations.0: 2x^2 - 11 = 0 clearly has real solutions, so the equation is not without real roots.
optionExplanations.2: The two real solutions are sqrt(11/2) and -sqrt(11/2), which have opposite signs.
optionExplanations.3: The polynomial has degree six, but four of its roots are complex; only two are real.

formulaNotes: Discriminant of u^2 - u + 5: 1 - 20 = -19 < 0, so x^4 - x^2 + 5 > 0 for all real x.

shortExplanation: x^2 + y^2 - 2xy = (x - y)^2, so the equation is (x - y)^2 = 0, i.e. y = x: a single straight line through the origin.
solutionSteps: Recognize the perfect square: x^2 - 2xy + y^2 = (x - y)^2.
The equation becomes (x - y)^2 = 0.
A square is zero only when its base is zero: x - y = 0.
The solution set is all points with y = x, which is one straight line (the bisector of the first and third quadrants).
keyConcept: A perfect-square equation (x - y)^2 = 0 collapses to the single condition x - y = 0.
commonMistake: Treating the degree-two equation as automatically representing two distinct lines; here the two factors coincide.

optionExplanations.0: Every point of the form (t, t) satisfies the equation, so the set is infinite, not a single point.
optionExplanations.2: The factorization gives (x - y)(x - y): the two factors coincide, so the locus is one line, not a pair of separate lines.
optionExplanations.3: Points like (1, 1) satisfy the equation, so the solution set is certainly not empty.

shortExplanation: Evaluating left to right, the first bracket is (16b^5)^2 = 256b^10 and the second is (-4b)^5 = -1024b^5; dividing gives 256b^10 / (-1024b^5) = -(1/4) b^5.
solutionSteps: First bracket, left to right: b^3 * (2b)^4 = b^3 * 16 b^4 = 16 b^7; then divide by b^2: 16 b^5.
Second bracket, left to right: (-2b)^2 = 4 b^2; divide by (-b)^6 = b^6: 4 b^(-4); multiply by (-b)^5 = -b^5: -4 b.
Raise to the fifth power: (-4b)^5 = -1024 b^5.
keyConcept: Multiplication and division have equal precedence and are performed left to right; even powers erase signs, odd powers keep them.
commonMistake: Losing a sign: (-b)^6 = +b^6 (even exponent) while (-b)^5 = -b^5 and (-4b)^5 = -1024b^5 (odd exponents).

optionExplanations.0: -1/(8b) would arise from mishandling the exponents; the powers of b give b^(10-5) = b^5 in the numerator, not a reciprocal.
optionExplanations.2: (1/4) b^5 has the wrong sign: the odd power (-4b)^5 is negative, making the whole quotient negative.
optionExplanations.4: -(1/2) b^2 does not match either the coefficient 256/1024 = 1/4 or the exponent 10 - 5 = 5.

formulaNotes: a^m * a^n = a^(m+n); a^m : a^n = a^(m-n); (-x)^even = x^even, (-x)^odd = -x^odd.

shortExplanation: By the double angle formula, 2 sin θ cos θ = sin(2θ); here 2θ = 11π/6, and sin(11π/6) = -sin(π/6) = -1/2.
solutionSteps: Apply the identity 2 sin θ cos θ = sin(2θ) with θ = 11π/12.
Compute 2θ = 11π/6.
11π/6 lies in the fourth quadrant, where sine is negative; its reference angle is 2π - 11π/6 = π/6.
keyConcept: Double angle identity sin(2θ) = 2 sin θ cos θ, plus quadrant sign of sine.
commonMistake: Forgetting the sign: 11π/6 is in the fourth quadrant, so the sine is negative, not +1/2.

optionExplanations.0: The product of a sine and cosine can never reach 2, since sin(2θ) is bounded between -1 and 1.
optionExplanations.2: sin(11π/24) would come from halving the angle instead of doubling it; the identity produces sin(2θ).
optionExplanations.4: +1/2 ignores that 11π/6 is in the fourth quadrant, where sine is negative.

formulaNotes: sin(2θ) = 2 sin θ cos θ; sin(11π/6) = -sin(π/6) = -1/2.

shortExplanation: In an isosceles triangle the two base angles are equal, so if two isosceles triangles share the measure of a base angle, all three angles match (the apex is 180° minus twice the base angle) and the triangles are similar by the angle-angle criterion.
solutionSteps: In an isosceles triangle both base angles equal some value β, and the apex angle is 180° - 2β.
If two isosceles triangles have congruent base angles β, each has angles β, β, 180° - 2β.
Equal corresponding angles imply similarity (AA criterion).

The other statements fail: equal perimeter or equal area does not fix the shape of scalene triangles, rectangles, right trapezoids or rhombuses (e.g. a 1x6 and a 2x3 rectangle have equal area but different proportions).
keyConcept: Similarity of triangles follows from equal angles (AA); one base angle determines all angles of an isosceles triangle.
commonMistake: Believing equal perimeter or equal area forces equal shape; both conditions leave the proportions free.

optionExplanations.0: Perimeter fixes only the sum of the sides; scalene triangles with equal perimeter can have completely different angles.
optionExplanations.1: A 1x6 rectangle and a 2x3 rectangle have the same area 6 but different side ratios, so they are not similar.
optionExplanations.4: Rhombuses with the same area can have different angles (a square and a flat rhombus), hence different shapes.

shortExplanation: A cube circumscribed to a sphere of radius 5 has edge equal to the sphere's diameter, 10; the diagonal of a face is then 10 sqrt(2).
solutionSteps: When a cube is circumscribed to a sphere, the sphere touches all six faces, so the edge of the cube equals the diameter of the sphere.
Diagonal of a face: L sqrt(2) = 10 sqrt(2).
For comparison, the space diagonal of the cube is L sqrt(3) = 10 sqrt(3), not 10 sqrt(2).
keyConcept: Inscribed sphere of a cube: edge = diameter; face diagonal = edge * sqrt(2); space diagonal = edge * sqrt(3).
commonMistake: Confusing the face diagonal (L sqrt(2)) with the space diagonal of the cube (L sqrt(3)).

optionExplanations.0: The diagonal of the cube (space diagonal) is 10 sqrt(3), not 10 sqrt(2).
optionExplanations.1: 10/sqrt(2) would be the side if 10 were the face diagonal, but 10 is the sphere's diameter, hence the side itself.
optionExplanations.2: The side equals the sphere's diameter, 10, not 10 sqrt(2).

formulaNotes: Edge L = 2r = 10; face diagonal = L sqrt(2) = 10 sqrt(2); space diagonal = L sqrt(3).

shortExplanation: A common divisor must use each variable with the smallest exponent present in all monomials: a appears at least squared, b at least cubed, and x is absent from the first monomial, so a^2 b^3 works.
solutionSteps: Compare exponents of a: 2, 3, 2; the minimum is 2, so at most a^2.
Compare exponents of b: 4, 3, 4; the minimum is 3, so at most b^3.
Compare exponents of x: 0 (absent), 5, 6; the minimum is 0, so x cannot appear in a common divisor.
Therefore a^2 b^3 divides 3a^2 b^4, 4a^3 b^3 x^5 and a^2 b^4 x^6, and is a common divisor.
keyConcept: The GCD of monomials takes each variable with its minimum exponent across all terms.
commonMistake: Including x in the divisor even though the first monomial contains no x at all.

optionExplanations.1: This contains x^4, but the first monomial 3a^2 b^4 has no factor x, so it is not divisible by any power of x.
optionExplanations.2: a^2 b^4 does not divide 4a^3 b^3 x^5, whose power of b is only 3.
optionExplanations.4: a^3 exceeds the power of a in 3a^2 b^4 and a^2 b^4 x^6, and x^4 does not divide the x-free first monomial.

shortExplanation: The truck takes 6 h 20 min, so the car, travelling twice as fast, needs half that time: 3 h 10 min. Leaving 4 h later, the car arrives 7 h 10 min after the truck's departure, which is 50 minutes after the truck.
solutionSteps: Truck time: 6 h 20 min = 19/3 h for 400 km, so truck speed = 400/(19/3) = 1200/19 km/h.
The car is twice as fast, so it covers the same 400 km in half the time: (19/3)/2 = 19/6 h = 3 h 10 min.
Measure everything from the truck's departure: the truck arrives at 6 h 20 min.
The car departs at 4 h 00 min and travels 3 h 10 min, arriving at 4 h + 3 h 10 min = 7 h 10 min.
Difference: 7 h 10 min - 6 h 20 min = 50 min, so the car arrives 50 minutes after the truck.
keyConcept: At double the speed the travel time over the same distance is exactly halved; then compare arrival instants on a common clock.
commonMistake: Comparing travel times instead of arrival times, forgetting to add the 4-hour delayed start of the car.

optionExplanations.0: 45 minutes comes from a rounding or misreading of 6 h 20 min; the exact gap is 7 h 10 min - 6 h 20 min = 50 min.
optionExplanations.3: They would arrive together only if the car's delay equalled the time saved, but 4 h delay exceeds the 3 h 10 min saving.
optionExplanations.4: The car cannot arrive 50 minutes before the truck: its 4-hour head-start deficit is larger than the 3 h 10 min time it saves.

shortExplanation: Write 6^(x-y) as 3^(x-y) * 2^(x-y); the powers of 3 combine to 3^(2y) = 9^y and the powers of 2 give 2^(y-x).
solutionSteps: Factor the base 6: 6^(x-y) = (3*2)^(x-y) = 3^(x-y) * 2^(x-y).
So the expression is 3^(x+y) / (3^(x-y) * 2^(x-y)).
Combine the powers of 3: 3^(x+y) / 3^(x-y) = 3^((x+y)-(x-y)) = 3^(2y).
Handle the powers of 2: 1 / 2^(x-y) = 2^(-(x-y)) = 2^(y-x).
Rewrite 3^(2y) = (3^2)^y = 9^y, giving 9^y * 2^(y-x).
keyConcept: Split a composite base into prime factors, then subtract exponents when dividing powers of the same base.
commonMistake: Dividing 3^(x+y) by 6^(x-y) as if the bases were equal, subtracting exponents directly to get a power of 18 or of 1/2.

optionExplanations.1: 18^x would require multiplying the bases 3 and 6 and adding exponents in a way the laws of exponents never allow for a quotient.
optionExplanations.2: 1/2^y ignores the entire contribution of the powers of 3, which do not cancel out.
optionExplanations.3: 18^y = 9^y * 2^y keeps a 2^y factor but loses the 2^(-x) part coming from dividing by 2^(x-y).

shortExplanation: The line passes through (0, 4) and (2, 0), so f(x) = 4 - 2x. The parabola has zeros at x = 0 and x = 4 with vertex (2, 2), which forces g(x) = -(1/2) x (x - 4).
solutionSteps: Line: it crosses the y-axis at 4 and the x-axis at 2, so the slope is (0 - 4)/(2 - 0) = -2 and f(x) = 4 - 2x.
Parabola: it crosses the x-axis at x = 0 and x = 4, so g(x) = a*x*(x - 4) for some a.
Therefore g(x) = -(1/2) x (x - 4); check: g(2) = -(1/2)*2*(-2) = 2, correct.
The pair f(x) = 4 - 2x and g(x) = -(1/2) x (x - 4) matches both graphs.
keyConcept: Reconstruct a parabola from its roots with y = a*x*(x - r) and fix the coefficient a using one more point (the vertex).
commonMistake: Taking g(x) = 4x - x^2 because it has the same zeros 0 and 4, without checking that its vertex height is 4 while the drawn maximum is 2.

optionExplanations.1: g(x) = 4x - x^2 has the right zeros but its maximum is g(2) = 4, while the drawn parabola peaks at height 2.
optionExplanations.2: f(x) = 2 - x gives a y-intercept of 2, but the drawn line crosses the y-axis at 4.
optionExplanations.3: g(x) = 2x - (1/2)x^2 + 1 gives g(0) = 1, so it would not pass through the origin as the drawn parabola does.

figureExplanation: The dashed line meets the axes at (0, 4) and (2, 0); the solid parabola opens downward, passes through (0, 0) and (4, 0), and reaches its maximum 2 at x = 2. These intercepts and the vertex height determine both formulas.
